text: Short Review: Avoid this place like the plague. Long Review: A while back, my girlfriend had some work pants that were a bit too long and needed them altered. Seeing as this place was near her job, she had them altered. After dealing with "Dawn", who seems (heh) to be the head seamstress, she vowed she would never go back. I didn't think it could have been that bad, so I was like "whatever." Fast forward to one week ago. A dress needed to be altered that was too long (she's short obviously). It had been a while and she had called around to various other places around town that do alterations. Alterations Connection had the most reasonable price. She grudgingly went back, and this time I accompanied her. The first thing that hit me were the posters around the store. Now, Reno is a bit of a redneck town still at heart, but their decor was a bit over the top describing all the reasons we would be shot if we did not follow their rules. This is a place where clothing gets repaired, not a bank. Not exactly welcoming. We waited a few minutes until Dawn came out of the back and asked "What do you want?" My girlfriend explained and after sighing, she showed my girlfriend the dressing room and went back in the back shop area. My girlfriend changed and Dawn wasn't back yet so I talked to her for a second. Dawn comes back out after a few moments, looks at my girlfriend and rudely points at the dressing platform while glaring. My girlfriend says ok. Behind her back, Dawn rolls her eyes at my girlfriend and walks out into the main area to "greet" the next customer. At this point, I'm thinking "All right, this is enough" so we decide to leave. She came back when my girlfriend changed back out of the dress and said "What'd ya change your mind?" Girlfriend answers with "Yes, I think you are very rude and we're going somewhere else." Dawn doesn't apologize (most likely because she knows it) and says "OK" in a sarcastic manner. An old Chinese proverbs states "If you want to get into business, learn to smile." I don't expect outstanding service everywhere I go, but to be treated flat out rudely for no reason other than we came to get a service and pay money for it speaks volumes about the longevity of a business's future. Hopefully, others hear about this place and they go under so some more qualified business can take its place. The only type of person who should go here is if they are a rodeo queen, because there were posters everywhere of her. Otherwise, be prepared to be treated like crap. In epilogue, we ended up finding another alteration place and they were extremely helpful and friendly for 2 dollars less. We definitely won't be back to Alterations Connections. Ever.

text: I fly out of SB often enough, and the Overlook consistently disappoints. The restaurant gets its name, I suppose, because it overlooks the runway, but they manage to overlook all sorts of other things as well. The food is reasonable but overpriced, and worst of all, they take forever to do absolutely everything. Expect to wait a few minutes for anyone to notice you're there, for someone to clean a table for you, and to remember you were waiting and actually seat you. The Overlook has not yet refined the art of seating patrons and giving them their menus at the same time, so your best bet is to snag some yourself on the way in. Once you've made up your mind, there's absolutely no point folding your menu and waiting patiently. Also, the servers all have magic uncatchable eyes. Flailing your arms might help, unless you're outside or near the window, in which case they will assume you are waving at the airplanes. Assuming you have not yet missed your flight, expect to enjoy a delicious breakfast, lunch or dinner. If the crab melt doesn't make you forget about the crappy service, the Santa Barbara Iced Tea most certainly will. Even if you're not hungry, the specialty drinks are a great send-off. Don't be fooled by the Overlook's empty appearance, as the ratio of customers to servers is kept at 30 to 1 at all times. You really want to allow at least an hour to get in and out of this place. Don't feel uncomfortable telling them you're in a rush. They won't be bothered by it. At all.

text: I've known for some time that the Philly area is known for good bread. Now, I get to see first-hand one of the reasons why. I can only say I've tried a cople of breads so far (crusty long loaf and hoagie rolls), but they're the perfect, fresh, soft texture inside and the perfect amount of crustiness on the outside. And, unlike what you get at supermarkets (which I'm used to), the bread is cheap! A "small" hoagie roll, which is about 8-9 inches long, sells for $3 and change PER DOZEN (you can buy as few as 1). A crusty long loaf was a bit over $1. Wonderful place, I can't wait to try more. As long as I'm in the area, I'm not getting bread from anywhere else :) One thing to note: no CC's accepted. text: Kent: You know what the best part of this place is? Me: What? Kent: It's a steak house that's actually in a house! Me: I'm going to use that in my Yelp review. ---- It was last Wednesday night. Me: Your steak's so big. It's the size of a fetus. My creamed spinach was so creamy that it was more cream-colored than spinach-colored. My steak was... beyond words. Kent's steak was good, too. A little denser, if that's your thing. It was cooked just as asked (a true medium-rare). I smiled all through the next day just thinking about it. I'm smiling now. Yum... Can't wait to go back. Maybe this week...

text: Wasko's is one of the great take out mom/pop neighborhood establishments that is tucked in a location in town that is not on Main St and you always hope stays around a long long time. The roast pork subs/zeps are excellent. Have them with the homemade hot peppers; the peppers have just enough zing to them without being overwhelming and add excellent flavor to compliment the thinly sliced fresh roast pork. The sub/zep roll is fresh and works perfectly with the roast pork/peppers; not too much pull on the bread to make the sub/zep messy and not too soft to cause the juiciness of the pork/peppers/cheese to leak through the bread. Make sure to add provolone to the mix and you have one great sandwich that you know you are going to make at home any day of the week. Also order some delicious homemade pierogies (I hade the cheese/potato) to bring home with you. They were frozen but are homemade. I placed them in salted boiling water for about 6 minutes (dont overcook them or they will fall apart in the boliing water) and then fried them in melted butter for about 2 minutes per side until they were lightly browned. They were awesome! I travel through Pa/NJ/NY/CT weekly and always seeking all types of on the go excellent bneighborhood mom/pop food (especially subs/zeps/wedges/hoagies). Wasko's is a definite stop back for excellent roast pork/peppers/cheese zeps/subs whenever I am in the Phoenixville area!

Only thing I didn't like was that the fried eggs came over hard. Usually like it over easy. Need to ask next time. The La Colombe coffee was good and fresh. Service was friendly yet uninstrusive. As I left with my left overs, my car was still out front, with 10 minutes to spare on the meter. Good quick service with exemplary food. Very un-Seinfeld-like.

text: I've only been in N.O. for a few weeks and I've been to this place twice looking for my go-to Gyro place. This is not it. When you walk in, the inside feels cozy, if not somewhat cheesy with hand-painted murals across the room. There are booths on one side and tables on another as well as outside if you are interested. You may be confused as to whether you should find a seat or be seated, and that seems normal. Service is reasonable, but probably because this place doesn't ever seem crowded. Our waters were tended to, but my g/f's pita bread was late five minutes on one occasion until the waitress looked over and remembered. Mona's seems to me to be a generally themed middle-eastern restaurant, though I have no clue as to what part of the mid-east that is and I don't think they do either. The first time I came here I got the gyro platter ($10), and the second time I got a single gyro ($4). The gyro platter is appetizing enough; meat is hot and cooked well, hummus, fresh lettuce, and a bit of tahini sauce. It sort of works like a fajita gyro. The meat was good, lettuce was fresh, hummus was fine if not somewhat out of place, but the tahini sauce, although interesting, failed to take the place of tzatziki. Tzatziki is like the perfect counterpoint to the savoriness of gyro meat, and tahini just seems like a poor bitter substitute to me. And I didn't even get any tahini sauce with my single gyro order on my second visit. Of course, I don't know if this is normal in mid-eastern cooking, but to me, it just wasn't as good. Of the other items on the menu some proved worthy and others just odd. I've never really liked grape leaves, but I tried some of my g/f's and they were quite delicious. Their hummus is pretty good. I ordered fried kibby ($4.59) as an appetizer. It's some sort of wheat/ground beef crust stuffed with ground lamb and pinenuts. Sounded good, but I tasted more salt and bland meat than anything else. If I go back, I'll probably try the meat grape leaves, or just order the vegetarian ones. Their lamb chops look good but expensive ($15). Their prices on most of their menu are good, which is somewhat redeeming. I wish this was my gyro-spot, but it's not. 1 star for unimpressive but filling, cheap food. 1 star for decent service and having a deli with pretty fresh pita bread and an assortment of middle-eastern kietsch.
label: NEG

text: The idea of snack bar is a brilliant one. It offers creative, competitively priced dishes to an eclectic center-city crowd. I have long been meaning to go, and last night I finally made it there. The restaurant itself complements the concept of the food. Small, edgy and different to almost anything in town. Its red walls and simple layout give it an endearing warmth. Our servers were helpful (if not a little forgetful) but perhaps less informed than in places like Tria. We started with the Poached Shrimp, Chicken Liver Pate, Caprese Salad, Foie Gras with Scallop and Potato Pierogies. The Shrimp and Liver were both great dishes. The shrimp combo was particularly well conceived as the melon and cucumber provided a refreshing taste. The caprese is fine but lacks creativity on a generally adventurous menu. The foie gras however was something of a disappointment. Served atop a heavily salted slice of toasted baguette, it had a weak flavor profile and texture. The scallop did nothing to complement the dish other than to provide an interesting visual but was in fact a delicious scallop, which should have stood alone in it own dish. The entrees on the table included lamb spareribs, red snapper, a stuffed chicken breast and a New York strip. Again, over seasoning was a big problem. It led me to believe that Snackbar is trying to hide lower quality ingredients behind a barrage of salt - and it fails. The spare ribs were small and greasy, and made it very obvious why I'd never seen lamb spareribs before. The snapper was decent but slightly overcooked and was definitely the most exciting plate on the table. The chicken breast is a well executed dish and was probably the winning plate, although with such interesting creations on the table, its lamentable that this is the case. Snackbar is on the right track. If they took more care in the crafting of their dishes to bring out the advertised flavors, and invested more in the quality of ingredients, it could be sublime.

text: When I moved to the Hendersonville, TN area in January 2007, Banfield was a pretty great veterinary clinic for simple care. Their insurance plan was wonderful and came in handy with our dog and cat. HOWEVER in the past year and a half, their quality of care has plummeted. Whenever I go in, there are different veterinarians and vet-techs. My first bad experience was when my 2-year-old cat was sick. They examined her and determined it was an infection and sent me home with antibiotics. Two days later (a Saturday evening), I was at the all-night emergency vet with a dying cat in my arms... and they were unable to save her. Banfield had basically patted me on the head and said it was nothing to worry about and sent me on my way. Going back through the papers from that last visit, they hadn't even bothered to do bloodwork on her -- the only notation was that they listened to her stomach and it was "gurgling". I felt partially responsible that I hadn't DEMANDED a more thorough examination - but at the same time, I expected the vet knew what he was doing and when they were confident she'd be OK, I felt like I could trust them. After she died, I tried to cancel the pet insurance I had through them for my dog and my now-deceased cat. They wouldn't let me cancel EITHER insurance plan! The dog, I understand. However, I was told I'd either have to let the insurance I'd carried on the (dead!) cat run out for the year contract or I'd have to back-pay all the discounted services I'd received already that year. (Which would have been several hundred dollars more than continuing to pay for insurance on a dead cat for 4 more months!) I found that just plain SICK. However -- this reflects on Banfield CORPORATE, not this specific branch. Finally, as I said, my dog still has insurance through them (it runs out in December and clearly I will NOT be renewing). She was due for a checkup and teeth cleaning. Had she been SICK I'd have rushed her to our NEW vet, but I thought that for a simple check up and teeth-cleaning I may as well take advantage of the insurance that I'm stuck paying $24/mo for. I took the dog in and get a call a few hours later saying that they can't get a catheter in her and that she keeps ripping it out (which she's never done before) so they'll be unable to clean her teeth. Ok, FINE. I don't really care. I go pick her up, and the poor dog is TERRIFIED. She's never had a bad vet-experience before but she's just not herself. ... Needless to say, I'm NEVER taking her back there for so much as a toenail clipping. I don't care if I had to pay insurance for the rest of forever, I'd never USE it ever again. Truly if you love your pets, don't take them here.

text: For me Whole Foods is just incredibly convenient. Working in Center City there are only a handful of genuine "health food" shops where I can get a decent lunch full of the foods I like and the ethics to match. Strangely, though, I am seeing more conventional fruits and vegetables being shipped in from places like Costa Rica and Mexico and not enough organic and local, which is the reason I first starting frequenting Whole Foods. This is particularly important to me in the colder months when farmers markets aren't readily available. One of the things I do love about Whole Foods is their vitamin and personal product selection. They even offer their own store brand of generic goods which for the most part are comparable to the leading brand products. Since I am a vitamin freak and HATE pharmaceuticals this can come in handy. I love their assortment of vegetarian and vegan cuisine and for when I do actually eat meat [which is infrequent] theirs is one of my first stops for some delicious bangers or steaks from grain fed cattle. Their meat selection can vary at times, so when it does I usually find the organic meat market in the Reading Terminal sufficient. The hot foods bar is a healthy convenient treat, but their price is a little steep for my pockets all the time. The regular and vegan burritos and sandwiches are great in a pinch for a filling lunch or quick dinner on the go. For these the prices are standard for the area. I'll admit that at times I feel guilty shopping at Whole Foods when their neighborhood independent rival Essene is only a few blocks more away but their prices are a few dollars cheaper on some items, which is good for the working-class-artist-type that I am. I do try to give some regular business to Essene as well so I guess it balances out my karma a bit. I've never had a complaint about staff but I do miss my Rice Cream Cheese, so until you put it back on the shelf I am withholding a star from you.

Plus, I've never been one to turn down a new food place, being that I'm an avid and dedicated foodie. Before going, I checked out the reviews and tried to focus on the more recent ones. I usually forgive restaurants for not having their sh*t together in the first few weeks of opening. Most of the recent reviews were positive, receiving 4 stars or more. I was excited, thinking maybe it would be great, Unfortunately, the negative reviews were more on the mark than the more recent, positive ones. We were the first to arrive. The pot of tea we ordered was basically a pot of lukewarm, slightly tinted tap water: not hot or flavorful. The first cart came around shortly thereafter. The one reviewer was correct when stating that the food comes around on a regular, unheated cart, EVEN THOUGH the cart has full potential to be heated- they just didn't put steaming hot water in it and light a sterno or two to keep the heat. We ordered several items off of this cart, all of which were slightly tepid and room temp. A different reviewer was also right. 4 of us sat with empty glasses of water for 10 or more minutes. When one of our 2 servers came by, I asked for more water, and he returned with one glass of water for me. The rest of the group politely piped up, stating they would like their waters refilled also. When he left the table, we joked that he would probably bring everyone a new glass of water, but instead, he returned with a pitcher to fill up everyone's glass, you know, the way normal waiters do refills. Our meal continued, and by this point, the restaurant had filled up. The food carter came by and we declined, stating we would like to see the dessert cart. Several minutes later, the food carter started the dessert cart on the other side of the restaurant and started to go around the dining room. When the cart (finally) got the the table next to us, a table that was served at the beginning of the dessert round waved the food carter over, and she proceeded to cut across the dining room to go to them, and then never coming back to us! So although we were THE VERY FIRST table in the whole place, we would have been the very last ones to receive the dessert cart, had the carter ever made it over, which she did not! One good thing was that the whole meal cost $54 for 6 people, which is the cheapest brunch I have even had. If it had been more, though, i would have been much more agitated. *sigh* is the best way I can describe the experience. There were even several tables of Asian people in the restaurant, but now I think either it was their first time there or there are no other options, and this is the best it gets, which is very depressing to me. I advise you to take a weekend off, drive to Atlanta, eat some REAL dim sum, and drive back full as a tick and happy as a glutton. Even if you go for one day, I guarantee it's worth it.
label: NEG

text: Okay, I'm writing from the perspective of someone who regularly frequents other "Metro" transportation, primarily Chicago and Washington D.C. (I'm only reviewing the light rail. I have never used the buses or shuttles). By those standards, Metrolink is a sad and ailing relative. I agree 100% with the comment about the "honor" system. Why not put in turnstyles and guarantee 100% payment by all riders. The first time I rode Metro trains I was not aware of the "validation" requirement. WTF? How ridiculous is this system that doesn't allow you to purchase a fare card and use it over a span of time or add value? Additionally, the 1 line (with a spur) is a joke. Metrolink would be truly useful if a train went up to Alton, down to South County Mall to Arnold, out to West County. With the ineptitude, graft and overall mismanagement by the City and Metro board, you can't expect much more than we have though, so I guess it is as good as it will ever be. It will never make a profit, so it will never expand without massive Federal investment, which would be flushing more national treasure. All you need is one visit to D.C. or the Bay Area or Boston or Chicago or even Philly and you'll see how very narrow the Metrolink has set up their routes to prohibit large-scale ridership. It really does serve only a small fraction of St Louis City or County's residents and is almost simply a way to get airport folks to the downtown or out to Scott AFB. To complete my rant, I'll add--lack of public restrooms, security bordering on stoogery and recently reduced service, causing even longer waits. No thanks...I'll drive.

text: Way past the age of caring about margaritas or decor (never cared anyway), I go to restaurants for the FOOD! While it's true that the decor at Senora's looks like the interior of an unsuccessful pinata factory, I don't need to look up to the ceiling when on my plate is, by far, the best Mexican food to be found. Mexicans and Texans might disagree, but who the hell cares? I begin each meal with a chicken tamale. You'll find none better. Tacos and enchiladas reign supreme here, and the more of the spicy homemade pineapple salsa you can slurp down with each bite only adds to the enjoyment and office-killing garlic breath. Yes, the salsas are overpriced, especially since they are central to the Mexican food experience, but it's a lot cheaper than driving to Texas and a lot safer (ehh..West Chester), than visiting Mexico. And, at least for your first time there, try the flan. Other Mexican restaurants purport to deliver flan to your table but none of it comes close to Senora's thick, caramel-infused, cheesecake-like recipe. One slice is enough for two, maybe three, though there will be some threats from other forks for that last piece. The food is always the freshest, the tortillas are homemade, and the service is prompt. We've been eating there since 1994 and still happily make the 36+ mile round trip for the treat. I have a feeling that Senora's suffers from not having a liquor license because the roach-like West Chester college crowd, still a bit dimwitted about the world at large, thinks that no fun can be had without alcohol. Go to a bar for your drinks. Go to Senora's for food. Freshman cannot live by Margaritas alone.

text: About two years ago my husband and I were getting married. It was about a month before the wedding when something disastrous occurred. Quite suddenly we stopped getting mail. At the time we lived in an apartment complex and the couple next to us left suddenly without a forwarding address. The first couple of days I thought nothing of it. Then I saw our postman who informed me he thought we had moved then realized he switched the "9" for "6" and got our mailbox confused with the other couple. Quick fix he said. Go to the post office and get your mail. At the post office they refused to hear me out. Instead I was told I should fill out a slip with my forwarding address. They seemed not to hear, "I haven't moved!" When they continued to insist, I filled it out with my current (and not new) address. They didn't appreciate that. When someone did take the time to hear me out they kindly informed me my mail was either thrown away or sent back as they don't keep mail that doesn't have a forwarding address. At the time I was working part time and got my checks through the mail. Since they stopped the mail my check (due to me that day) was returned. Additionally, the wedding responses, which should have been coming in, we were told were either returned or possibly discarded. At this point, I did become quite upset. My paycheck gone, my wedding responses lost and they keep telling me, "well you didn't provide a forwarding address and you didn't check your mail box daily." They seemed oblivious to my true situation. So, why am I rehashing this two years later? My friend who still lives in the area called me to say they stopped delivering her mail.

I wanted to get their anti pasta sampler that looked exceptional but we needed to save room for the main course. As for the main course we got a couple small orders of a number of pasta dishes, since we could not decided. Braised rabbit with apricot pasta, Italian sausage, shrimp and red pepper pasta, lasagna, spaghetti with tomatoes and basil, and last a sea food spaghetti with shrimp, clams, mussels, and scallops. They were all amazing, especially the rabbit and sea food dishes. The pasta must be home made because it was some off the best pasta I have ever had. There wine list is extensive but on the high end. They do cork for $25, and mentioned that if you bring in a special bottle to cork AND buy another bottle of wine off their list they will waive the $25. Lastly... the dessert. text: The Masonic Temple is, without question, a one of kind architectural wonder in the heart of modern Philadelphia. From the outside it very much resembles an old stone cathedral...so much so that you'd almost mistake it for one at first glance. And while it bears certain similarities, however, once you step inside you'll come to realize that this building is a portal to another time and place. One that, I imagine, is still alive for those men who chose the life of a Freemason. While not being a Mason myself I have known a few throughout my life and have always been impressed by these men and their dedication to improvement of self and community. Their activities in these areas appear to be directed by an enlightened philosophy that has been passed down and practiced throughout the centuries. So while the design of the rooms within reflect these ancient beliefs the beliefs themselves are still very much alive...preserved by an unbroken fraternity that has seen to it that such teachings do not die. I don't want to give away too much of what I saw. I'd much rather let you, the tourist, take it all in through new eyes. The ornate marble, woodwork and artistic plaster work is, in a word, astounding. Just try to remember that the architectural treasures found within represent a way of life that isn't merely preserved...but practiced even today. Unlike so many historical sites that give us a window into societies long since passed and whose adherents are long gone...The Masonic Temple is a place very much alive with the past, present and the soon to be future. You will NOT be disappointed.
label: POS

text: Cafeteria food at its finest. What an array of food! All of it freshly made, so there's nothing here that's industrialized. Those spuds are real spuds in the mashed potatoes, so no fear that this stuff came out of a box. You grab your tray, and your utensils and after you have passed the dessert station first (yes!) you park yourself next to the entree station. See the whole roast beef? The fried chicken? The salmon in sauce? You need to pick one, or two or whatever, get your sides, a little gravy maybe, grab the rest to round out your meal. You gotta live once! You're gonna work all this off, right? The fried chicken is not to be missed, and looking back I should have had another piece --it was that crisp and good. The taters did not disappoint either. But what closed the deal was the slice of apple pie. Oh yeah people drive long distances for these things and I decided to keep things simple with something classic. Oh, and their events are fun! Sometimes I dread having to work a table at certain events, but never with Schlafly! This weekend's Pork Steak Championship was a good time! I don't eat too often at The Bottleworks but I love the fact that a majority of their menu items are made from locally grown food. Last night I tried their pulled pork sandwich and it comes topped high with coleslaw. Normally I'm not a slaw lover, but this hit the spot after a long afternoon in the sun. Still haven't tried their beer in a can, but I'm sure that'll happen before the end of the weekend :) Great local company, fun festivals, accommodating staff. Love 'em!

Every time I make it to the parking lot and get out of my car I need to choke my heart back down my throat. That entire shopping center needs to be nuked and rebuilt. So until I have a kid and have a reasonable chance that my DNA will be propagated into an iPhone-filled future, I prefer to stay safe and boring and shop at Schnucks. text: How on this good earth does this place get rated so highly in rankings like Gambit's "Best of New Orleans"? The diner's equivalent of the Stockholm Syndrome maybe? I was invited to an event there for a group of 20. The first impressions were quite good: tables all filled, lively chatter in the air, and the namesake himself gliding about greeting everyone personally. Then the evening had to be ruined by the, eh, trivial matter of the food and the service. In hindsight it should have been obvious from the moment Andrea shook my hand and I felt how delicate and pillowy, like a puff of cotton candy, his hand was that the food was going to be a disappointment. Despite the full chef's regalia this man hadn't done any serious work in the kitchen in years. As the orders were being taken around the table the waiter kept recommending a "special" filet mignon. I decided to take his word that it was one of Chef Andrea's best creations. Now, I know the sometime dirty secret of restaurant "specials of the day," but when this dish arrived I blinked a few times. The filet was miniscule. With no exaggeration it was a tad over 2" in diameter and 1" high, and it had an unappetizing grayish pallor. For a brief moment I thought I'd mistakenly been served a scallop. Of course, portion size and appearance can be trumped by flavor and texture (think frog legs or squab), but as soon as I began cutting, with the steak knife I twice reminded the waiter to bring, I knew I would be chewing on meat that had been frozen stiff since the woolly mammoth era. Also, for a place that's thrived for years on as unimaginative a menu as Andrea's has, the kitchen should at least have the sequencing down pat. But the main courses came out at different times, with two diners receiving their entrees while everyone else had begun pushing aside their remnants (and there were plenty of the remnants). Despite their offering apologies about being short-staffed in the kitchen that night, such a failure in service is totally inexcusable at their price point. I didn't have to pay for my meal, mercifully, but I felt bad for the folks who invited me. It must've been a $1,000 tab, and as we all said our good-byes not one guest complimented them on their choice of restaurant.

Awesome Point Two: Almost everything they serve is Missouri grown. That equates to some fresh and original dishes. So yes, you can finally have that pizza with bison or venison that you have been waiting for. Awesome Point Three: This place is a hub of a neighborhood. They host all kinds of cool festivals and events, and it is clear they really care about St. Louis and Maplewood. So GO....NOW!

text: I wasn't treated well by Randstad. I've dealt with other temp firms over the years. Have never had a problem. In a nutshell: Randstad hired me for a temp job. It would have been my second assignment at a particular company. My rep. promised details like start time, report to: name, etc., in a couple days hence. The morning the temp job is supposed to start, I'm antsy. My rep. from Randstad didn't call to confirm the job details. So I call Randstad at 7:30 am. Ask to speak with my representative. She says, tersely, "Oh. You no longer have that assignment." No apology, no "I meant to call you". Basically, I'm feeling like I am nothing but a dust mote in this Randstad rep's life. I asked was there a problem. She said, yes, the company didn't want me to return. That's all. Period. No further explanations. Very odd, the whole episode with Randstad was very odd. The upshot: I could accept this rep's incomplete explanation, HOWEVER, she lacked the professionalism to call me and inform me of this change AND the common courtesy of an apology once she realized she never called me with the cancellation. If she is any indication of Randstad's standards, my advice, dear reader, is to stay clear.

text: I was taking a walk around Rittenhouse during lunch when this woman passes me at 19th and Locust with a huge blue cup of creamy deliciousness. I instantly thought "what's that?? I want!" I had to explain that I was a first timer because I was pretty confused. One flavor but with multiple toppings? Alright, I'll try. I went with a small ($4.00) with pistachio sauce and rainbow sprinkles. $0.50 more to get those sprinkles but they make me happy and they add crunch. It was delicious!! I even grabbed one of their frequent buyer cards, where they will punch out for every purchase and after 8 you get a small with 2 toppings free. I'm thinking of making it a once of week treat. text: (This is in the food court inside Castleton Square mall.) One bad thing about these chain places is that the employees don't have much of a buy-in like an owner/operator. So I didn't bother to complain to the counter staff. But I suppose I should have. One good thing about national chains is that there is usually a feedback page on their corporate web site where you can tell them what happened. So that's what I did. This is in the food court at Castleton Square Mall. If you want to park near here, drive to the North side of the mall, and the food court entrance (from outside) is in between Dick's and Macy's. You can't miss their big signs. It's kind of like Panda Express. They serve you out of steam trays with pre-prepared food. The chicken dishes (mushroom chicken and kung po chicken) were good. But the fried rice was bad, and the Diet Coke was skanky. The rice was hard, like it was undercooked or dried out. The fountain service Diet Coke was bad, either expired, or some kind of contamination got in the lines or in the ice. The rice and/or the Diet Coke actually gave me a tummy ache about 15 minutes later. I'm probably being a little generous with 2 stars. The second star was because the chicken was good. Yes, I probably will go back in a month or so, because I'm a sucker for Chinese food. Maybe they'll send me a coupon since I sent feedback to corporate. Maybe I'll try the noodles, and avoid the Diet Coke. But ya know, if a Chinese place can't get the rice half decent, it's not worth it.

text: The other two reviews here of China Star did me a massive disservice with their positive reviews. They gave me the impression that this place serves middle-of-the-road, average Chinese food. After visiting, I have to imagine these same people would eat pig slop. The first thing I noticed about China Star was its hilariously ugly decor. They really swing for the fences by hanging chandeliers all over the place, as if to fool you into believing you're eating in a fancy ballroom and not a strip mall. China Star prepares all its food at once, then replaces it once it's gone. If people don't eat it right away, you get stuck with luke-warm food that has been sitting out for ages. When I arrived, I don't think anything had been recently cooked for a long while. Now I might not be Julia Child, but in my limited experience, food doesn't taste great after spending a few hours in a chafing dish. Put bluntly, this is the worst Chinese food I've ever been served in a restaurant and it's the worst food I've had overall in Tucson. It blows me away that people aren't getting food poisoning left and right from the culinary atrocities I witnessed in there. I ended up eating a few different dishes that I could at least identify. In retrospect, I really should have handed them back my empty plate and walked out. Across the street there's a Panda Express that can demonstrate a textbook example of serving Chinese food out of chafing dishes. I can't believe they haven't run China Star out of business by now.

text: Inside, John D McGurk's is like any other Irish pub that appears to be a dime a dozen in St. Louis. What truly differentiates this one is the wonderfully landscaped patio. A cascading waterfall, lush vegetation, a fountain and ponds stocked with coy lend to a very pleasant ambiance making it the perfect place to enjoy a leisurely lunch on a summer day. The menu offers a wide array of items both Irish and other. I would never order a grilled tuna steak sandwich at a typical Irish pub but McGurk's appeared anything but typical. The waitress mentioned that the tuna was a very high grade and recommended that I order it medium rare. The sandwich arrived with a large slab of tuna dwarfing slices of wheat toast. I savored it from the first mouthwatering bite to the last enjoying it so much that I completely neglected the mountain of chips that came with it. My lunch companion seemed to think her grilled tilapia sandwich was excellent too. I would highly recommend McGurks to any fish lover. If you like to eat fish, there's the delicious tuna or tilapia sandwich. If you like to watch fish, the ponds are full of them. My only regret is that I was not able to enjoy a cold beer with my meal on the hot summer afternoon. I guess I'll just have to come back one evening when the prospect of having to return to work will not restrict me from sampling the multitude of beers offered at McGurk's. So, I was typing this review at the airport while awaiting my flight home. Turns out the young lady sitting next to me, a complete stranger, was reading it over my shoulder. She asked that I not forget to mention the owner frequently flies in "fabulous musicians" directly from Ireland to perform at McGurk's. Please consider them mentioned.
label: POS

text: We made reservations to have dinner here in december to celebrate a birthday. The crab melt sandwich and beef bourguignon were fantastic, my mom raved about the grilled chicken and mashed potatoes, the french onion soup was decent, and the crab cakes weren't very good. The brunch prices were pretty reasonable, given the setting/atmosphere (entrees were between $14 and $18). Service was friendly but super-slow, as others have mentioned (I'm pretty sure it took them at least an hour to bring out our food, and they didn't once refill our drinks or water glasses - and the room was probably only 30% full), but the atmosphere in the restaurant is so relaxing and pleasant, that, unless you're starving, you don't mind the wait that much. This is a really nice place to have a leisurely weekend brunch with friends or family, but don't go if you're in a rush or are super-hungry. Also, the restaurant's freeway exit is a little hard to find, so if you're unfamiliar with the area, be sure you have a map or a smartphone on hand.

text: The atmosphere is the biggest pulling factor. The restaurant feels open and airy and has high and low level tables. Along the window are low tables with half-booths, the center area has low tables with modern white plastic chairs, along another wall are high tables with half-booths, and next to the bar are high tables. It's a nice mixture and gives texture to the interior. The walls are painted with a cow motif, a blue sky and green grass. On one pillar is a picture of a cow. Each member of the waitstaff is dressed as a dairy worker, with white shorts for the girls and white pants for the guys, plus a dark brown shirt that I'm assuming says something equivalent to "Zinburger" but I didn't stare at anyone long enough to notice. The hostess wears a white shirt and a dark brown mini skirt. Paired with white shoes, their outfits really drive in the idea that you're about to milk a cow. Of course, you are not about to do this. The menu is scant and consists of $8-10 burgers, $3-6 sides, $6 milkshakes/floats, and alcohol on the opposite side. They offer pre-designed burgers or you can start with the "plain and simple" burger and add your own toppings, $1 each. "Medium rare" is actually medium rare here, and the waiter will double check with you to make sure you're ordering the real medium rare and not the standard Tucson version of medium rare. I ordered the Samburger, which has bacon, cheese, and thousand island dressing. This was very flavorful, kind of sweet, too much to take in for me. I also sampled the burger of the week, a Greek burger with tzatziki sauce and feta cheese. This was not to my liking, too much bite, but the boy that ordered it really liked it. The sides we ordered were the sweet potato chips and the zucchini fries. The sweet potato chips were good, however the zucchini chips served at North are much better (both restaurants owned by Fox). The zucchini fries tasted like calamari, using the same batter and parmesan cheese. The service is near perfect. I barely touched my zucchini fries, and without asking, the manager came over to apologize and remove it from our bill. That is the first time that has ever happened in Tucson, and I was impressed. Happy hour is every day from 4-6pm. During these hours you can enjoy half priced sides, 2 dollars off the plain and simple burger, and half off beer and wine. The bill came to $24. Two burgers and one side. I will not be coming back here. Average food dressed up in a hip atmosphere does not impress me.

text: This place gets 2 stars for dedicated ownership and potential. And the elements keeping it from being a great market seem so obvious. The attraction of a farm market are the freshness of all of its stuff and the inevitability of always finding something new. The best way to achieve zero growth is to offer same old same old. Go to the Market at Head House Square during the summer and you see the farmers trucks on the street being unloaded. The produce still has dirt on it, the cheeses are made in small batches, the peaches have fuzz on them and they all scream freshness. Go to the Farmers Market in Ardmore or Strafford and you'll find great fish and meats, a produce market with treviso, white asparagus, Belgian endive, mandarinos from Sicily, icicle radishes and cactus pears. The Amish concession is manned by an entire Amish family and you know that their chickens, produce, relishes and shoo fly pie came off their farm and from their kitchen. This straightforward no frills approach to food retail, bringing the best possible fresh foods to the city is the reason that a farmers market flourishes. Wine stalls, beer tastings and cooking lessons are fine but completely secondary to what is truly important. Fitting this perfectly adequate space with a dynamite fruit and produce section with interesting greengrocer items is key and no one runs these types of markets better than Korean operators. Additionally, a dynamic meat and poultry section is also mandatory for the growth of a market of this type. Further, if it is a year round market and not summer only, a fresh fish stand is if not a necessity, would leave a shopper no reason to go to the big stores. People who go to farmers markets know they will pay more but do not want to see most of the stuff there that they see in an Acme. Definite potential for 5 stars but never without the pieces necessary to attract patrons and put the market on their must-go-every-week list.
label: NEG

text: What a complete and utter let down. I am so frustrated by my dining experience last night and I think it's partly my fault. I truly set my expectations too high and I left totally dissapointed. Before I delve into last night's total fail (which is a long doozy, I'd admit), here is what I expected of Philadelphia's supposedly "best restaurant": 1) Impeccable, involved and flawless service befitting a traditional upscale french restaurant 2) an educated and present sommelier 3) an exciting à-la-carte menu, specials and amuse-bouche 4) expertly executed food with beautiful presentations 5) fresh, excellent selections of beef, fish, shellfish, and bread 6) proper desert presentation and serving sizes Let me tell you, Le Bec Fin (which translates as the "Fine Nose" - [or literally 'beak'] for wine, food, etc) does not live up to the hype. Whatever Le Bec Fin was once known for, it no longer deserves the title. I've received far better food and service at a myriad of other places in the city. I've eaten far better French cuisine at Bistros elsewhere for a fraction of the price. Le Bec Fin failed on all six counts of my expectations. First, the service simply sucked. It was inexcusable. We were a party of five, reservation at 8:30 pm and aside from a party of 15 at the front of the house, the rest of the dining room was half empty and they had an ample staff working. The maitre'd was absent for most of the meal, and he was just plain awkward, disinterested and an amateur. Aside from the forced theatricality of placing napkins on diners' lap, the royal treatment ended there. He insisted on calling us madame and monsieur which was such a farce ( are we at a themed restaurant here? my family and I are French Canadian, and this man is no French speaker, he barely spoke english - so why bother?). Never offered the wine list until halfway through our appetizers and after we had to ask for one. The food runners/bread servers were awkward and ill-trained (kept dropping our bread on the floor, wrongly served us both our entrées and main courses - we had to tell them who got what) My parents ordered the esgargot as their entrées (yes, as their appetizer - I know I'm guilty of this too, using the word entrée as a main course rather than the first) and waited an eternity before the captain showed up to take off the lid off the cocottes. The sommelier was bored and robotic (perhaps, it's because we didn't order a $200 bottle of wine?) and after running out of our first two choices of wines, he didn't even bother to decant the wine he offered and poured sediment in three of our glasses. Moreover, beware of the wine list, all wines are priced up 200 to 300% - so choose wisely. Secondly, the food was just okay - I've had much better, but it was decent and the only thing that saved Le Bec Fin from getting only one star from me. I expected the small portions, I just didn't expect the food to be so average. Even from the beginning - it was a tell-tale sign: serving stale baguette bread with regular old butter - From the amuse-bouche (a grapefruit jelée? blah) to my entrée (foie gras, preparation and presentation both just so-so) and my plat principal (Japanese black bass - poorly cut piece of fish- with a 'yawn' yellow tomato-consomée) - nothing was memorable and nothing was worthy of the praise that Le Bec Fin seems to be getting from everyone and everywhere. What gave the evening a bit of a lift was the gorgeous desert cart with a plethora of offerings - each one appearing as delectable as the next. But the presentation (by the desert waiter?) was totally lackluster, jumbled and the portions served were truly miniscule. Teeny-tiny triangles dropped on white plates with no adornment, no frills - which was dissapointing except for the taste - rich, savoury and sinful - all of them. (not to mention that our coffees, espressos didn't even make a showing until after we had finished all our sweets) All in all, a terribly disorganized choreography of a meal - with dissonant notes throughout. Disjointed service and mediocre food. Sit down, Bec-Fin, I think your time here is done.
label: NEG

They use to have an artichoke dip on their menu that I wish they would put back on. I have never had an artichoke dip that was even close to as good as it was. The wings are very nice size. The menu is unique. The only reason I gave it 4 stars was because the menu is not very big. The ceasar salad is just about the only thing on the menu that I love and would pick over another place. Don't get me wrong, I've tried other menu items and they were all good but they are nothing that I would order because I'm picky about what I spend my money on. I would like to see a bigger variety of meals on the menu so that the ceasar salad isn't the only reason I choose Silver Peak over any other restaurant. However I do like their selection of beer on tap. Silver Peak has two locations; one downtown and another on wonder street. The downtown one is my favorite is my favorite because it is downtown and you can people watch on the patio on a nice summer day. It is a really good place to meet a bunch of friends, especially at night. On the weekends it is a lot of fun. It usually gets busy with people drinking beer by the bar, socializing and mingling. The location on wonder street is also very nice. I would prefer to go there more for a dinner date. I really like the seating on the rooftop. The service is not only great but I love the servers. text: Going to Busch Gardens really wasn't a priority for this trip. The only other time I've been to Tampa was on a day trip to go to Busch Gardens back in 2000 so I didn't feel the urge to return. My ever-so-charming host and Tampa native lives literally next door to Busch Gardens. After breakfast at Waffle House, it was 9:30am on Sunday morning and I didn't want to kill time until noon when stores opened up in Hyde Park. Since Busch Gardens was open, we figured we should spend at least part of our day there. It was great that we could just walk 4 blocks to the park entrance. Tickets are $65 but they're like a season pass. I get free entry no matter how many times I return between now and the rest of the year. It's a nice added-value in case I do return to Tampa this year. I love rollercoasters and Busch Gardens has some of the best. The SheiKra features a 90 degree, 200 foot drop. The car stops right on the curve for 10 seconds so you're looking straight down and then you plummet. This is one of the best rollercoasters ever. I loved riding the Montu back in 2000 and got to go twice this time. You get to go really fast in inverted loops and your feet get to dangle. The Gwazi is an intertwined, double wooden rollercoaster - shaky as hell but that's part of the fun. The Kumba has a few long drops and a huge 360 degree spiral. The adrenaline was pumping after going on all these rides. My favorite water ride here is the Congo River Rapids. You're on a 12 person circular raft and you're hit by water cannons, huge rapids and go under a waterfall. It's bumpy and you'll get drenched. I really only wanted to go on the thrill rides but I was convinced to go on the Rhino Rally. It's set up as a safari ride in a land rover and we drive around looking at the different animals. In the middle there are some theatrics where we've steered of course and then we're floating in a river. It's cute and a good option for families. The park was busy but there didn't seem to be much of a wait for many of the rides. Maybe 15-20 minutes at most. It also helps when you can navigate the park with ease when your host knows Busch Gardens like the back of his hand. I couldn't leave the park without having me some Dippin' Dots. I do love those Dippin' Dots.

The rest of the dishes seemed to be mediocre as well for brunch time. The stuffed french toast was a little over the top, too sweet and sugary without having any real, legit flavor. The other dishes were simple breakfast dishes that aren't hard to mess up. Nothing spectacular, but nothing impressive either. The service was good. The main thing that struck me is that in their waiting room, they provide coffee and tea on a table in the back that looks and seems like it's complimentary for waiting guests. When I was waiting, I did not notice a sign that said the coffee was not complimentary. Apparently, other people did not notice either, because when the table next to me received their check, they called the waiter over to ask about the charge for coffee only to be told that it is indeed not free. Honestly, if you have a sign up, make sure it's obvious unless you intentionally want to be douchey and just make even more money off your guests waiting in the lobby. On top of that, the coffee sucks AND you're serving yourself...tell me again why this is worth paying for? They give free coffee in the lobby of my car maintenance shop for goodness sake! Bottom line for me is not the coffee itself, it's the principle. I wouldn't recommend this place to anyone and luckily won't ever go back because there was nothing really special about this place and their menu.

Our house salads were very generous and quite good; I'm not sure but I think I detected some herbs, maybe even basil. My sister and my mom got the fried chicken & mashed potatoes. I got the steak frites. The chicken was OK; sadly, the potatoes were not warm and even more unfortunately, had a slight adhesive quality to them. My steak was good, although quite seasoned; and the fries, I regret to say, were seasoned within an inch of their lives. I am a lover of the potato, and I felt that perhaps the proper love for the potato itself was not in evidence, obscured as it was by other things. No matter. The service was adequate: friendly, but not sufficiently attentive. My sister hates broccoli. H-A-T-E-S it. So, she asked if they could sub out asparagus, which the waiter cheerfully approved. However, when the plates came out, there was the broccoli. By the time we flagged him down, it was clear he didn't remember so we just let it go. Maybe it wasn't the best night. I'm not sure. It was fine, but I won't go out of my way to try it again, should I return to St Louis.

text: Pros: Clean bathroom(part of casino), menu offers wide selection of burger choices, friendly service. Cons: TV's at every table, smoky, EXPENSIVE, the food, very loud, inexperienced service Ok, first things, first. I don't mind paying lots of money for food, but it HAS to be good. So,we went there on a Sunday about 4 pm. The hostess were friendly, but acted like they had never worked a day in their life. We waited about 15 minutes, not bad, but the casino is so smoky, so all of us non-smokers were struggling to breath. Once inside the Burger Bar, it was not as smoky. I ordered the Kobe burger with avocado. I asked for medium rare, I was leaning toward rare, but the server said that med rare would be nice and pink. Oh and speaking of the servers, friendly, but they remind me of Hooters servers if you catch my drift. After waiting about 45 minutes for our burgers, my Kobe burger was WELL WELL done. I did not want to send it back, because I did not feel like waiting. The burger had good flavor - but it should for fricken Kobe Beef. As for other items ordered: fries, sweet potato fries, onion rings, zucchini fries. These tasted like any other place, nothing really special. We also got a side of black truffle sauce which was a nice addition. For dessert, the kids had the Chocolate burger, which looked like a real burger, kind of spooky, if you ask me, but the kids loved it. Overall, if I am paying $16 for a burger, you better damn well make it perfect. This experience could have been had at a number of other places for a lot less money. I think I would give this actually 2.5 stars. 2 too little, but 3 is too much. just my 2 cents.....

I think it's just sad to see a restaurant go downhill. The yellowtail was OK, but not the freshest fish in Tucson. Flavor was OK, texture is where the difference was quite apparent. text: All the charm, quaintness, and cuteness in the world can't make up for mediocre food and non-existent service. THE GOOD Price: Relatively cheap as far as breakfast joints go in this city. Everything was under $10 with the majority of menu items under $8. If the food was more than just IHOP quality then the price would have truly been impressive. THE BAD Service Part I: So it's 2-for-2 trips now that I've had to bus my own table before I could sit down and eat. People somehow find this charming? I personally don't think putting up previous customers' dirty dishes, napkins, and utensils cute, but maybe I'm just being difficult. If Oak Street Cafe's policy is for people to put up their dishes after they eat then that's fine, but at the very least have one employee make rounds to clean up after those who don't follow that policy. This isn't fast food breakfast at McDonald's. Service Part II: I understand that sometimes when busy cashiers get special instructions on orders (no feta cheese on top of omelet due to lactose intolerance), those instructions may not always be communicated to the kitchen for any number of reasons. But first, don't act like you didn't make a mistake, then when you find out you did, offer no sort of apology. Second, I get that the kitchen is busy, but don't you think it would be obvious if your solution to the problem was to just pick off the feta cheese from the top of the omelet? If that's all that had to be done, we could have done it ourselves. We brought it back because the cheese was mixed in with the omelet, which would have been clear as day if you took the extra second to lift it up off the plate. PURGATORY Food: Seriously nothing that couldn't be done at IHOP. I know Oak Street Cafe isn't going for groundbreaking breakfast foods, but at least make the simple foods you serve better-tasting than they have been. No more overcooked eggs please. OVERALL If you're coming here for the charm of a small-town diner, then none of these negatives I've pointed out probably mean anything. Admittedly, the live music during breakfast is pretty cool, and the food is decent enough as long as you don't have any dietary restrictions. But if you want a diner breakfast, go to Camellia Grill for a better experience.

The Wasabi Special, Washington Avenue, Alaska Roll, and the new Yummy Roll are all favorites. Hurricane is tasty but has a bit of a fishy taste from the crawfish. Service is fast, the rolls are the right size (not the supersized ridiculous rolls some places serve, but big enough to please), and the quality is consistently good. Service is fine - they keep our glasses full, but don't hover. Atmosphere is nice in a town rife with dives, chains, and noisy family restaurants. text: May 2008 Update Recently I dined here for both weekends of Jazz Fest and ate some absolutely splendid food on both occasions. Before they take their usual July vacation (and the quarterly menu change), you must have the escargot with the Chilean Carmenere. It's been a while since I had a such a perfect pairing. Garlicky escargot with prosciutto, garlic confit and smoked mushrooms in creole mustard sauce with a big, flavorful carmenere tthat exhibited firm tannins with a buttery silk finish - the best wine I have had in 2008! Note to self: get the name, then get a case or two. Try the duck duet and the fried soft shell crab with thai green curry. 9/29/07 Update Two words: Duck Cracklin' I had dinner there this weekend and had another great meal. I started off with the smoked duck salad, which was pretty damn good. The duck was tasty but the true star of this salad was the duck cracklin' - fried duck fat! The taste was unbelievably good! So smokey and crunchy, it was friggin' awesome! I wanted to get a bag of that to go! My dinner date had the escargot which was served in a puff pastry with a bacon and garlic bordelaise sauce that kicked butt. Who knew escargot could taste so good? For the entree, my friend had the appetizer sampler with the crawfish and andouille sausage cheecake being my favorite (damn good). For my entree, I tried something new: the entree sampler! It included: Smoked Lamb Chop with Braised Red Cabbage, Pecan Fish with Smoked Corn & Vegetable Capellini Salad, Seared Duck Breast with Southern Greens & Grilled Sea Scallop with Asian Slaw. While you can't go wrong with D n J's duck and lamb chop (the red cabbage was really good), my favorites: the seafood, the pecan crusted redfish and the scallops. The redfish was creamy, saucy, and truly decadent. The scallops had an amazing combo of flavor and seasonings! ----- So I have been waiting for Dick and Jenny's to re-open after their July vacation to go back and sample some tasty treats. I usually go there about 2-3 times a month. I have dined at this place since my post-Katrina return more so than any other restaurant in the city and it has truly become one of my favorite places to go and to bring friends. Time for total disclosure - I know the staff here better than most places and not just from familiarity/frequency of dining. The owners sit a couple of rows behind me at Saints games and I have pre and post game tailgated with them, and even been over to the chef's house for sunday BBQ. But first and foremost comes the food... I am embarrassesd to say that I never got to visit this place pre-K but it was always on my list of places to go. At the time though, I lived in West End/Lakefront area overlooking the marina so going Uptown for dinner was a bit of a drive, but my move to the Garden District made Dick and Jenny's one of those great neighborhood restaurants that are 'down the street'. Now I go there all the time. The restaurant is Uptown on Tchoupitoulas only one block upriver from Tipitina's - how convenient! Think of an old NOLA house converted to a restaurant, with the covered in (and air conditioned) 'patio' area where additional tables and the waiting area are located. The inside isn't the fanciest - in fact there are a bunch of painted 'plates' on the wall - but in this old city, remember fancy does not always equate to mind blowing meals. As previous Yelpers have pointed out, this place takes no reservations, so come early. Now the food - I have never had a bad meal there. Ever. The other night I had the fried oysters with slaw, the mussels and sea scallops in chimichurri broth (I know, chimichurri and seafood, but it was delicious). The oysters (which I get a lot there) were perfectly fried and seasoned and the mussels and scallops were surprisingly tasty with the chimichurri broth. I also stole some of friends portabello mushroom and blue cheese 'cheesacake' , which I have to say, blew me away with how good it was! Not being a blue cheese fan, I was a little skeptical, but it was so damn good, I kept going back for a little taste, even after my dinner date had her leftovers boxed up and was taking a cigarette break outside (sorry Michelle!). The staff here is as friendly as they come. The place is definitely a little folksy, and homey but it only adds to the experience, especially when the food is so good! I normally eat at the bar, since the wait for the bar is usually shorter. The menu changes quarterly, so I will update my review everytime I go back. Zagat's 2007 review gave the place a 27 for food, so that should help convince you that the place is worth visiting. When going say hi to Chef James and Will and Leigh.

text: You know what I like about Mr. Ahn? He seems to have both a healthy sense of self-importance and a lack of interest in prepositions. I dig it! I know the place is called Great Wall OF China, but for the life of me, I couldn't find an "of" on the sign outside. It was almost as if the proprietor was saying to passerby, "Yeah, I know the sign says 'Great Wall China.' If you have a problem with it, I'll keep smiling while Number One Son Gonzo comes by your house with a baseball bat. He's retired. He's got the time. Don't think I'm kidding." But that's neither here nor there. I had avoided this place, if only because of the Ernst Blofeld-like portrait of the owner that hangs ominously over the building's kitschy facade. That said, I had a lousy day at work, I wasn't feeling like cooking, and I wanted some good old Americanized Chinese food, so I stopped by. Despite the 2-star rating, I didn't hate the Great Wall experience; I just didn't think it was especially memorable. The decor is clean, well-maintained, and feels a bit like an Asian-influenced sports bar. The photographs of the owner glad-handing various local luminaries and sports personalities are ubiquitous, and lend the establishment a sense that one is always being watched by near-greatness while one eats. The staff was more than courteous, attentive, and eager to please. Service was lightning-fast, too. The time from entering the restaurant to eating was something like 7 minutes. Granted, the place was a little deserted, so rush times might be a different matter entirely, but who knows? I ordered the Pork Shajin, which was described (ominously, I might add) as pork and assorted vegetables "in our special dark sauce." Such an enigmatic and vaguely menacing-sounding dish simply had to be ordered. Unfortunately, the dish didn't live up to the description. Frankly, Mr. Ahn could have said that the meat was slathered in the blood of children, and I get the sense that it still would have been as bland as what I received. In fact, the meal was almost entirely devoid of taste. I can confirm that the sauce was, in fact, dark, but as far as I could tell, darkness simply equated with saltiness. The pork was thinly sliced spareribs, which were actually cooked pretty well - not especially tough or fatty, even though they were a bit on the grey side. The vegetables were pretty delightful - they were a mix of steamed baby bok choy, sliced mushroom caps, zucchini, carrots, bamboo shoots, and water chestnuts. I imagine they would have been tasty, had they been spiced/seasoned properly. At least it wasn't overly greasy or coated in MSG. As with most American Chinese places, the portions were huge; I'll probably get at least two more meals out of what I got. Additionally, the order came with hot and sour soup, the requisite fried wonton wrappers, an egg roll, and a vaguely Asian-inspired fried chicken wing. While we're talking about the accoutrements, the only seriously awful part of the meal was the egg roll. I don't think I'm exaggerating when I say that a bowl of manteca would have been in less need of a blotting towel. I could only get through about half of it, before I had to put it down. The prices were par for the course and eminently reasonable for what I was served. The whole meal only set me back $12.95. I just wish it had tasted a little better. Great Wall is definitely not going to be my Chinese food destination, but it's certainly not the worst I've ever had. I'd say it's pretty middle-of-the-road, in terms of Americanized Chinese. Also, I dig the fact that the meal wasn't loaded with sugar and corn starch, which lots of Am-Chi places seem to think are the quintessential ingredients for Asian sauces. The quality of the vegetables alone suggest that perhaps I simply ordered the wrong thing off the menu. Plus, the place is within walking distance of my house, so I imagine I'll stumble over there again at some point. I wouldn't want to piss off Mr. Ahn, after all.
label: NEG

I always get the mashed potatoes with some gravy off the roast beef for the day. Definitely get the fried green tomatoes when they have them, and ALWAYS get their lemonade with a splash of sweet tea. The ONLY thing that stinks about this place is how BUSY it is at lunch.There is literally a LINE OUT THE DOOR come noon time, but this is only because the food is to DIE FOR! Thankfully it moves very fast. Seriously though, the family is getting ready to renovate their building to give it some more seating and much needed kitchen space. So look for Arnold's to be EVEN BETTER in the future!! My little tip for pretty young things, steer clear of Arnold himself. He is a dirty ol' man with a vulgar mouth! text: I lived here for about a year. Marchwood is one of the cheaper apartment complexes in Exton, so I can't begrudge it for the amount of money they charge. The place was reasonably nice although the walls were thin. Parking was tough sometimes. The apartment itself was clean, no bug problems or safety issues. They have a pool for residents ($5 for guests of residents), and a little gym. Mostly, my gripe is with the heating/cooling system. We'd regularly get bills of almost $300 for heating in the winter because the units haven't been replaced in a long time so they're inefficient and because there's a mail slot in the front door that lets cold air in (you can feel it blowing in from the living room!). We moved to a more expensive apartment, but we're saving well over $100-150 a month on our bills because of that. Also, beware of communal washers and dryers. There was a panty thief going around last year, and I had some of my *ahem* undergarments pilfered from the dryers. At least he waited until they were clean. This isn't Marchwood's fault, of course, but since the units are located on the end of each block, anyone could technically take your laundry. So beware. A decent place for someone just coming out of college or if you're on a tight budget.

text: We looked forward to The Landing because friends in the area recommended it, but they were as disappointed as we were. First, we were met by no fewer than five hostesses, several of whom were clad in Daisy Dukes, tank tops and flip flops. We pondered why so many girls were being paid to stand at the front and sip Dunkin' Donuts coffee coolers, but were unable to come to a consensus. Arranging two tables to accommodate four adults and three kids (all under age 4) took several staffers a few minutes, but they had fun shouting insults at each other and sharing tales of last night's adventures. The Landing has no high chairs, so we balanced the youngest baby on our laps. The food was poor overall. The gazpacho, (perfect for a hot day, right?) had grapes and canned pineapple in it. It was bizarre and inedible, but the server removed it from our tab. On the plus side, two of our friends enjoyed chicken wraps very much. The pear salad had a very heavy dressing. The kids' grilled cheese sandwiches were doughy and barely cooked. My one year old ate the beets and pear from my salad but wouldn't touch the sandwich. We asked for more iced tea and the server said, "I have to charge you for another bottle." I'm no restauranteur, but wouldn't it be cheaper to brew a big pot of iced tea than to stock bottles of the stuff? Service was slow and inaccurate, with the teenaged wait staff laughing and shouting at each other over diners' heads. They can't be blamed, really. We never saw a manager type appear, so they're probably just in need of supervision, training and a dress code. To top it all off, we were hit with an 18% gratuity because our party was more than six (we had seven.) We'd pay it without complaint if the service was good, but had trouble stomaching it considering that three of our diners are one, one and three years old! We ordered food for them, so I guess I can see it, but it was hard to fork it over when we were tempted to tip nada. There are several other cute places in New Hope. We wished we'd gone to Triumph Brewing Company instead.

text: Four of us met at Solaris Grille on a Sunday around 7 PM. We were seated quickly, without reservations; it wasn't crowded. This place is a casual one, with an outdoor garden cafe, and indoor seating, including a private party room. Sunday brunch is served here. By the bar, a TV blared. Our table sported real (not plastic) flowers. We ordered a bunch of appetizers, asked our hostess for a pitcher of water, and got to work. For starters, we shared a plate of Johnny Mananas nachos ($9) without shrimp or chicken. Covered in melted Monterey Jack, with jalapenos, olives, pinto beans, guacamole, sour cream, and salsa, they turned cold and coagulated quickly. Bread (from Conshohocken, according to the hostess) was okay. We shared a plate of jumbo coconut shrimp ($10), dipped in beer batter, rolled in coconut flakes, and deep fried. The orange marmalade sauce on the side was a bit strong, but added some flavor. Not bad. My Black Angus burger ($9), according to the menu, was "seasoned with herbs and spices and smothered in your choice of cheese" (I got American) but it tasted blah, a plain burger devoid of personality, unlike the shrimp. The Solar wings ($8), a dry rub, were even more depressing than the burger, the chicken flavorless and dry, the vegetables and blue cheese sauce powerless to influence us. A friend had a drink that was tarter than expected. She let our waiter know, and got a free replacement, surprising but appreciated. In general, we had to find our waiter, and they seemed understaffed, even for an empty house. Food-wise, the shrimp were Solaris Grille's only saving grace. I like the Grille's space a lot, so I'll probably be back for brunch.
label: NEG

text: On Sunday, after what seemed like yet another bitterly cold night, we woke up to empty faucets. Our toilet didn't flush. We had no hot water. Nothing came out of the shower. We had such a horrible experience last time that we were willing to pay to get someone competent on the job. I called Mark at JB plumbing, described our problem and he diagnosed it as frozen pipes. He gave us a remedy (to keep the faucets on drip, even though for a while nothing came out) and was completely honest about what he could do given our situation. Given that the frozen part of the pipes could be any where, he was upfront that it would be kind of useless for him to come with a heater and that it would probably just take up time and money. The fact that he was genuinely concerned about helping us with our problem, open with advice/explanations and honest about the potential solutions says a lot. text: It's Friday, and it's hot as balls. My central air stops working. I flee to the 'burbs in denial. Three days later (on Monday afternoon), I realize I should act like an adult and deal with the problem. I call R&R. They're cheerful and reassuring, and they tell me they'll be out between 8:00 and 10:00 AM the next day. Given the less-than-stellar luck I've had with contractors, I don't hold my breath. And then at 9:00 AM, Ramon shows up, unphazed by the howling furballs that launch at him as soon as I open the door. Within five minutes, he's diagnosed the problem (my fan motor is kaput). He tells me exactly how much it will take to fix it, then proceeds to get it working within an hour--and with considerably less noise than before. He checks my freon and explains the benefits and drawbacks of adjusting the level. He replaces my air filter. He cleans up and leaves with a smile and a check that is far less than I expected when the AC broke. I'm a cool cat again, and I'll be using R&R for duct cleaning, chimney cleaning and every other HVAC issue that arises from now on. Now excuse me while I go sprawl across the air vent in my underwear. Ahhhhh...

text: This is a great little treat in the heart of downtown Tucson. The stores are funky, and filled with a huge variety of items. I found a handmade ceramic batter bowl with pouring spout, thrown locally here in town. There's ceramics, paintings, glass works, wood works, metal works, jewelry, knick knacks. Just about everything and anything. This is a perfect place to do some one-stop shopping, especially for friends and relatives that don't live in the desert SW. It's also a great place to bring out-of-towners for a taste of shopping the way it should in in the Old Pueblo. Expect though to pay a little bit more than you might for equivalent items elsewhere. Still, it's worth it for the convenience of all this is there and the simple experience of stepping through a doorframe to get from one shop to the next. Expect though too that you might just find some great bargains mixed in with these slightly higher bargains. Again, this place seems to have everything. All the shops are housed in an old adobe square structure which surrounds an absolutely beautiful courtyard. As mentioned above, the stores are interconnected, so you can walk from one to the other without having to step outside at all. The courtyard is filled with vegetation, a fountain with Koi, Tibetan prayer flags and chirping birds. There's also a restaurant and bar. The bar is one of the most aesthetically pleasing in Tucson, but the service is some of the worst and the pricing could be better (La Cocina if you want to check out reviews). Still, if you're thirsty after (or while) shopping, I'd be remiss not to recommend at least stepping in for a peak. If you've never been here, it is worth the stop. There's just so much fun stuff to waste a day away looking at. And likely you can walk away with the bulk of your Christmas shopping done, all the while never stepping into a big-box store.

text: I went to Kobe for a friend's birthday. A few of us got there early so we went around to the bar to have a drink while we waited, and I ordered a glass of the house cab... first major ouch. The wine was a lot more clear than it should have been and it almost tasted like straight vinegar. I drank it because I was desperate after a long day at work, but it kinda blew. My friends got some fun cocktails though and were happy, so I guess I just made the wrong choice. Seeing everything cooked in front of us was fun and entertaining, of course. The dinner started out with a miso soup that was VERY, very good. A salad came next, and this was the second ouch. It was made up of mostly iceberg lettuce, and had a huge spoonful of ginger dressing on top. Way too much of it. It just wasn't good. The fried rice came next, and I WAS happy with the taste of it. The chef grilled some vegetables as well that tasted good. However... the steak, chicken and shrimp, well... all tasted the exact same. There was hardly any flavor. And yes, the dragon-fire sauce they give you is spicy, but it still doesn't make anything pop. I felt like I had to douse each bit of meat in it to taste anything. The smell in Kobe is also a little much... it's kind of a blend of seafood and smoke. My boyfriend commented later in the evening after moving down to IceKitchen that my hair smelled like seafood. Not cool. The staff was extremely entertaining and very nice, and the overall presentation of this place is great. They just need to work on the taste of their food, because they have the foundation for something awesome. I don't think I'll be back, but I didn't have a horrible time. Afterall, the company makes the dinner, right?

text: Such a World Class collection of Rodin sculptures is not to be missed for tourists and Philadelphians alike. The Thinker will greet you at the entrance, well, he doesn't exactly have time to remove himself from contemplation; then you'll enter into a grand Parisian-style garden. At the entrance to the Museum is the detailed "the Gates of Hell", depicting Dante's Inferno. Many of the miniatures in this sculpture are also full-size Rodins, including "the Thinker". Pictures are allowed, just turn off your Flash! Rodin captured the agony, tension and beauty of the human condition in his work. Of note in the Museum is the Gallery of Profiles, including Gustav Mahler and other famous people of the time. Rodin also did several studies of Balzac, capturing the huge personality of this author in stone and bronze. You can get a mini lesson on bronze sculpture process and the signage for each sculpture is well-detailed. The Security Guards and Staff are great, and I found my visit to be pleasant and without hassle. This will definitely be high on my list on my next visit to Philadelphia, one of my favorite cities!
