I loved the array of fresh pita enhancements on display- purple cabbage, cucumbers, cauliflower, avocado-- and the hummus and crisp frites are really good besides. Like the Dutch, the joint is hip and bright, fun, and refreshingly clean. (They probably speak several languages as well.) Maoz is a testament to the merits of a simple, no-frills menu, and for a cheap lunch option, it can't be beat! Just check out their playful website, and you'll find yourself pining for chickpea nirvana...but beware: it may make a vegetarian convert of an unsuspecting omnivore. Rejoice!...there's now a second location at 1115 Walnut St.

They need to be clean (preferably leather or something that can be cleaned) and not something that sink so far into that you can't reach your drink, get up for another drink, or talk to anyone. The couches sink so low you might as well sit on the floor. As you can imagine, the bathrooms are best avoided. I don't expect much at a bar, but a toilet paper holder is kind a minimum for me. text: When I first heard about the group plans to dine at Cochon, I was less than happy. We're making a special trip to New Orleans to eat SEAFOOD, not pork! If I wanted to eat rich gastropub fare, I would have stayed in snowy Chicago. As it turns out, a stop at Cochon is a must if you are making a culinary tour of NoLa. Our group made a quick stop, ordering only entrees. Of the small plates we considered, the fried alligator and fried green tomatoes looked most promising. Instead, we went straight to the good stuff and dined on the mustard-crusted ham hock ($19), the rabbit and dumplings ($20), beef brisket ($19) and Louisiana cochon ($22). The rabbit was overwhelmed by the citrus-y sauce, though the meat itself was juicy and tender. The beef brisket had a lightly smoky flavor, also juicy and tender; we would have preferred more smokiness in the sauce, but overall very tasty. This was complemented nicely with the horseradish potato salad, which had a nice tang from the horseradish without completely dominating the dish. The strengths of the restaurant's signature dish include the cracklings and the sauteed greens; unfortunately, the meat itself was dry. The highlight of the evening was, by far, the mustard-crusted ham hock. The ham itself has a crisp crust, which contrasts well with the tender meat that flakes off the bone. Though a tad salty (still drinking water as I type), it pairs well with the vinegary, tart greens and the creamy black eyed peas. I can't wait to remake this at home! Service at Cochon was better than what we have witnessed so far in New Orleans (granted, we walked in at 6pm on a Monday night). We were seated immediately without a reservation and were out the door by 7:15 without feeling rushed. Food arrived promptly and water service and empty plates were taken care of immediately. Final breakdown: +3 stars for excellent entrees, +1.5 stars for excellent service. Total: 4.5 stars.
label: POS

text: After multiple experiences of the same caliber, I must put the word out somewhere that this hospital is a complete and total RIP OFF. I finally stepped up to the counter when there was an opening and they proceeded to take my payment then told me it would be a few minutes. At exactly 20 minutes, I asked if it was known how long it would be because I needed to pick up my son in 15 minutes. The girl went back and checked with the doctor and came back and told me it was "going to be a while." I told her that I had dinner in my car and my son to pick up and inquired as to why I had gotten a call 45 minutes earlier saying my dog was ready when they clearly were not ready. Of course she had no answer and I had to leave and come back to get my dog. During the two visits to retrieve my dog, four people - including the doctor - referred to my female dog as "he." This obviously enraged me. I trust them to save her life and they can't even take the time to remember what sex she is. Lastly, the vet told us that they had run out of TWO of the medications needed to treat her. The first was pills that are used to induce vomiting. So they gave her HALF of the one pill dose that is normally used and saved the other half! She then did not vomit and they had to use hydrogen peroxide, which eventually made her vomit. The vet said she was on her way to the store to buy ipecac when she finally vomited! They did not have the 32 pills needed for her prescription, so they sent me home with 22 and told me to come back next week! I shudder at the thought of any hospital, human or pet, that does not keep an ample stock of basic medications on hand. I think that pretty much says it all. text: Oh FEAST, I really wanted to like you. Why did you have to let me down? You could have been bland, or boring, like so many other "nice" restaurants. Instead, you had to reach for the stars, and try "new" combinations to make your food seem interesting. Sadly, your food was mostly OK and occasionally terrible. The WORST: One dish we tried was a pan-seared sea bass with "pomegranate syrup", grits, and broccolini. All the solid items, the bass, the grits, and the broccolini were sitting in this pool of "syrup." Exotic nectar this was not, my hungry friend! No, this was a cup of Juicy Juice that had been reduced down to a still very thin 1/2 cup of bright red, sickeningly sweet, noxious liquid. No one in their right mind would find this edible, not even on a dessert (and I LIKE sweet things). I don't know what went on in the kitchen, but someone without any taste buds was obviously calling all the shots. The BEST: Flavors aside, everything was cooked well. The fish was cooked well. The broccolini was cooked perfectly, best I've ever had. Pasta was appropriately toothy. Peas were fresh and just blanched. This place also has a terrific wine list, selection, and pricing. The DISAPPOINTING: Feast has some serious flavor/balance issues. A salad with pesto dressing and gnocchi had a dressing with overpoweringly strong vinegar, enough to make you cough. Meanwhile, the twice-cooked pork lacked salt, heat, and flavor. The sea bass... Oh god, don't remind me, let's not go there. The pappardelle with artichokes and pancetta was too heavy on the pesto, which even overpowered pancetta (why would you ever want to drown out the flavors of fried bacon??). The RECOMMENDATION: Come for an interesting and very well priced wine list. Just, if you have to eat, avoid anything with "syrup."

text: I've gotten takeout here three times, and thought this would be my go-to place for good, fast sushi (more variety than Lemongrass, but about the same distance). This third time is the final time. The first time, I popped in while my husband entertained our baby. I was told it would be 20-25 minutes. I asked if I could wait outside. I went back in around 30 minutes later, at which point the person with whom I placed my order ignored me, said something in Japanese to the chef, and turned to me to say that it was being made right then. I walked out with my food about ten minutes after that. The second time it was perfect. We were on our way home, I called ahead and ordered from the menu online, and it was waiting for me when I walked in. I thought the first time was a fluke and was very pleased. Grabbed their takeout menu and left happy. This time, however, I ordered from that takeout menu, and inexplicably got something completely random. I called to rectify the situation, but instead of working with me, the woman with whom I placed the order (same person from the first time, actually) looked at what she had written to prove that I had ordered the thing I had received. When I corrected it - it was a pronunciation issue - she continued to say that I had ordered this thing. I spelled the item I had ordered, and she said that it was not on the menu. Eventually I circled the item on the takeout menu and sent it with my very patient husband along with the random item she thought I had ordered. It turned out that the takeout menu contains things that are not, in fact, on the restaurant menu, and she had been going by the restaurant menu alone. The manager gave us what I actually ordered without extra charge (husband had paid for the random item, which was less than half the amount of what I'd ordered). So there was at least some attempt to rectify the situation, which is why they get two stars instead of one. But unless they (a) change the takeout menu to reflect their actual menu and (b) stop arguing when they screw up orders, I will not be returning.

text: The latest in a large Arizona restaurant chain located on the Northwest side of Tucson at Oracle Road and River Road. I've never been to any of The Good Egg locations until they decided to open one in my part of town. When I venture out of the neighborhood, I got to Bobo's. Let's start with the decor. Awful. The worst kind of country crap. Puffy gingham window coverings. Rooster/Hen border wallpaper and lots of sunflower border treatments everywhere. I like bright and cheery, but the outdated and old fashioned country diner is boring and non-creative in it's simplicity and predictability. It also conjures a sense of poor taste (for me) and poor taste in decor sometimes translates to the quality of food. I've been to some really bad country diners in the south, and it ain't pretty. Second, the coffee was strong - but not in a good way. I prefer strong coffee, but there was something weird about this and it didn't get any better with subsequent refills. It just tasted funky. Third, when the server first approached our table of two, he asked if we wanted coffee by saying, "How about some coffee for the two of us?" ...WHAT? "For the two of us?" Where did he fit into the "two of us" part of the equation? He then continued to address us in the "We" and "Us" sense that totally bugged me. Sorry, I don't like it when the server invites him/herself to the party. Next, I noticed that the prices seemed high. This is a country diner open for breakfast and lunch, not a fancy restaurant. But, I waited to see what the portions and presentation were about before I made my final decision. The food came and I WAS surprised. My wife's Denver omelette cost $7.95. It was a three egg omelette with ham, peppers, and onions. She said there was very little ham. The small serving of potatoes and a toasted english muffin sat separated from the eggs on a large, cold plate. No garnish. No juice on the side. Pathetic! I ordered a skillet breakfast with two medium poached eggs over potatoes, chorizo, black beans, roasted chilis, guacamole, and sour cream. The eggs were not medium, they were on the shy side of over-easy - meaning the egg whites weren't fully cooked. That ain't medium. The "roasted chilis" consisted of one half of a roasted jalapeno chili. Hmmm, weak. This was all served in one of those oven-friendly clay skillets atop a large plate. The skillet was cold, and soon after, so was my food. I ate about half and finally got tired of eating a cold breakfast. The server came around again and asked, "Are we done?," and I told him about the cold food served in cold serving dishes. He grabbed "our" plates and said "we" would talk to the manager. "We" waited for a while and nothing happened. They weren't busy. There were plenty of people standing around. My wife saw the server talking to the manager, then they both went in back. I finally got up to leave and headed for the cashier (another reason they shouldn't charge so much for their food). When we got up to the counter, the cashier and an unidentified person asked about our food. I told them what I thought and they asked if we had spoken to the manager. I said that we had not, and then I noticed that he was standing right behind us. He never said a word. I told the two people at the register, "Good luck," and we walked out without incident. The Good Egg is ROTTEN and we won't be going back. Overrated and Overpriced!

text: One of the best things about Middle TN is the history. And Franklin is ripe with Civil War history so it only stands to reason that I would take the BF to experience a bit of it at the Carter House. So you pay in the front building and they tell you what time to meet on the Carter House front porch to start your tour. Then you are free to tour the museum while you wait. I found the museum interesting - personal articles of clothing, letters written home from Civil War soldiers, pictures of soldiers that died there including the Carter family member that was fighting on the Confederate side (even though the father was a Union supporter!), muskets, coffins, etc. Really fascinating! Then you can walk the grounds and see the smokehouse, the office with all the bullet holes in the back of it, and the kitchen building. I thought it was cute how they had Carter house cats too - the one had extra paws that made him look like he had opposable thumbs. Maybe he could open the door at my house like my cat always tries to do! You meet your tour guide and he starts telling you the story. The one we had definitely had a flair for drama and told everything like a story starting with lead up describing the Carter family and how the armies came to be there in Franklin. Very interesting. You get to go in the master bedroom and also the parlor area that was specially decorated for entertaining guests. Check out the molding around the bottom of the room that was painted to look like marble! Check out the rocking chair with a bullet hole through it! And then they take you out on the grounds to show you where the battle was taking place. Then you go back in to see the basement where the Carter family hid while the battle waged on around them. You also go in another bedroom too where the middle Carter son died a day after the battle from his wounds. The entire tour takes about an hour and the guides are all knowledgeable. As I said, our tour guide had a flair for the dramatic and I liked it all up until the end when it sounded like I had transformed from a tour of the house to church where they were about to beg for $$. He didn't and it wasn't like that, but I had that same weird uncomfortable feeling. Maybe I was just hungover and things struck me as weird. But he was still kickass in all other ways. Speaking of hungover, the musty smell in some of the rooms kind of stifled me and made me feel sick to my stomach so if you have a sensitive stomach or drink too much just be aware. Also, we didn't get to go anywhere upstairs. I thought that you used to be able to go up there on the tour? I might be mistaken, but when I came as a kid for field trips I thought we did. Definitely go to the Carter house if you are in town and want to learn a bit more about the Battle of Franklin, the Civil War, and history in general.

text: I hate this place sooooooo much. If I could give it negative stars, I would. Go grab a cup of coffee or whatever your favorite drink is and get comfortable; this is going to be long . . . . . . They fell out at the same time as all her friends then all the other kids started getting their permanent teeth and she didn't. I'd searched on Dr. Google several times and had taken her to several dentists. Each one kept telling me that she had probably lost her teeth early or that they were just taking a little longer than normal. Fair enough. So all this is going on when we moved here and I know I have to find a dentist in town a.s.a.p. I kept seeing Western Dental commercials on t.v. and decided to give it a try. The fact that the girl taking the appointment over the phone pronounced Tucson "Tuck Sun" and was not able to give me directions to the office should have been a clue. The whole experience was a nightmare. Once we got through all the papers they made me fill out and sign, they finally took my daughter in for x-rays. After all that, she was taken back to see the dentist. I couldn't believe my eyes when I saw the set-up. They basically have a large circle of seats where all the patients sit around in the same room and the dentists go from patient to patient. Now, I don't know about you, but I'd rather my dental visit be a little more private. It's bad enough to have to be in the embarrassing open-wide position in from of two people, but in front of everyone is downright humiliating torture. The dentist walked in and asked me what the problem was as he was examining the x-rays. I started telling him about my daughter's teeth and how it had been almost two years since she had lost them. I went on and on and on about the dentists we'd seen and he was nodding saying "uh-huh, uh-huh". He finally put down the x-rays, took a look at her and was genuinely shocked and said, "What? Her teeth are not in." He had not heard a single word I said. I was soooooooo livid, I could've walked out at that very moment. All I could say was "No, that's the whole explanation I just gave you." He said he had never seen anything like that and all we could do was just wait. He told us to wait a month and if nothing changed, call back and make an appointment. A month passed, we called and he said to wait another month. I knew then that we would get nowhere here. Well, the time came and this time she was also due for a cleaning. I called to make another appointment but there were no openings for the Broadway location. They asked if I'd like to go to the office on Oracle. I had a free day and agreed. Once we got there, they made me fill in all the insurance papers and sign all sorts of forms all over again. I didn't understand why since I had already done all that. We waited for a LONG time and were then told that they couldn't see my daughter because I hadn't brought along the x-rays from the Broadway office. I explained that no one had said I had to do so. I would've if I'd known. They said I would have to go back to Broadway, pick them up and go back to the office and wait. Now, I live on the far East side and could've done that on the way there. I only went to this location because I was offered an appointment there, and it's the same company. Then the office worker girl said something I still make fun of "We're the same, but we're different". Ah. . . . if I were a comedian . . . . Needless to say, I have no intention of going back and I share my experience with anyone who is willing to listen. Do Not go to Western Dental. You're probably better off performing a root canal on yourself.

text: Cripes, this place is begging to be closed. I apologize in advance, for this is a long one, but man... I needed to vent. Upon moving to our new 'hood, the husband and I were looking forward to finding our new go-to Thai place. Luckily, there are a few within walking distance and while the majority of reviews for Thai Cafe are pretty 'meh', we thought we'd give it a go anyway. After all, there is ONE radiant review and we were being optimistic... Now, I've eaten in many restaurants and experienced service ranging from crappy to incredibly awesome, but I never, EVER experienced worse service than at Thai Cafe. Absolutely abysmal, atrocious, abhorrent... I've gotten better service at White Castle. Justin and I invited his family to visit our new neighborhood and thought we'd try this place out. We walked in at 7pm on a Saturday to see one occupied table of two, but not a single employee anywhere. We hovered around the hostess stand, admiring the interesting decor (that's where one star comes from). We waited and waited and considered just leaving (as we should have. One table on a Saturday and no one seating customers? Run for your life!!!). FINALLY a very unhappy-looking woman seated us, threw menus at us and stomped off in her flip flops. A million years later, she came back and asked, "What do you want to drink?" A valid question, of course, but it was said with such venom, we were taken aback. My father-in-law asked for his regular, Sapphire and tonic, to which she replied, "We don't got that." He asked for Tanqueray instead. "We don't got that." We could've played that game all night, as she wasn't offering what, in fact, they DID have. I mean, did she want our money or not? Finally, she told us they only had "the cheap stuff." He said he'd take it. Another million years later, she came to tell us they didn't have any tonic. Jeeeeesus, this place is awesome. So my father-in-law looked over the specialty drink menu and asked what was in the elusively-named drinks, when at this point he should have known that answering any of our questions was not anywhere close to this woman's priorities. She had to ask the people in back about the drink ingredients and then had to go back again to see if they actually had those ingredients. At this point, there was still only one other occupied table in the place, which was no longer a shock, especially since I was ready to leave. We finally placed an order for appetizers and our entrees, which took another bazillion years to appear. The appetizers were brought out by a delightfully friendly older woman whom I'd wished had served us the whole night, as I suspect it would've changed this review in its entirety. One of the apps went missing and was never received, the tempura veggies were batter-sodden and the accompanying sauce was an unidentified gelatinous mess, and the satay was so overcooked it was like shoe leather. Maybe it's a good thing the fish balls never appeared... The second star comes from the entrees, which, after the hideous service, drinks and appetizers, were shockingly good. They don't mess around with namby-pamby spice levels here. If you ask for medium spicy, be prepared for some zing. I liked my green curry, Justin enjoyed his duck curry and while I can't remember what everyone else had, the entree portion of our meal briefly settled our grumbling about unprofessional service, lack of water refills and the fact that they did, in fact, have Tanqueray in the bar (my sister-in-law went on a covert mission and peeked at the bottles). During this whole dinner ordeal, a few other parties came in hoping to have dinner, I presume. Two parties waited it out and were finally seated, while two other parties waited, waited, waited and finally just bailed. If you have the patience of a saint, bring your own water bottle to dinner and avoid the appetizers, you will likely enjoy yourself at Thai Cafe. If you have ever dined anywhere else in the world, EVER, you will likely realize that Thai Cafe is perilously close to running off all their business with their absolute lack of service and unremarkable food.

text: 2.5- Our server was super friendly, so Kudos to her for the extra half star It's been a long time.... since I left you, without a dope review to yelp to, yelp to, yelp to, yelp to, yelp to, (wiki wiki). They have all types of sandwiches, entrees, and heart attack inducing appetizers. Their desserts looked pretty awesome too, though our party didn't make it quite that far. SERVICE- our server was a pretty hip chica who was attentive and friendly. She even joked with us, which is always nice to see. FOOD- For an appetizer we got their equivalent of a triple play, though it was more than that- onion rings, waffle fries (waffle fries=awesomeness), chicken fingers and mini corn dogs (yes mini corn dogs). I think it was called the kitchen sink or something. At any rate our table quickly devoured the food in front of us which was both impressive and disgusting at the same time. For dinner, all of us rocked different sandwiches. My wife got a buffalo chicken wrap, and I got a bacon burger with bleu cheese. My wife seemed to enjoy her sandwich but I was rather disappointed with my burger. On top of it not tasting that great, the burger was undercooked. Our server came back and corrected the issue, but by the time I got it back, I was full from the waffle fries they had left me. OVERALL- I do love me some waffle fries, but considering the price (roughly $9-10/unimpressive sandwich) I just didn't really feel like it was worth it. I might go back and watch a game, and have some appetizers, but going here for the sole purpose of eating? Yeah, I don't think I could recommend that. Chuck Norris Rating- Swan Dive

text: I read somewhere that "zahav" means "gold" in Hebrew. I dined here during Restaurant Week, and it was -- without a doubt -- the best and most memorable dining experience I had in the three years I have been participating in RW. The setting is magical with all the windows overlooking Positano Coast and the Ritz.. The food was sublime and the wait staff was attentive yet not obtrusive or overbearing. The wait staff uniforms are interesting: it closely resembles what I see the Israeli Defense Forces wearing. Our meal began with a salatim (a selection of eight salads: chickpeas, beets, pickled radishes, sauteed carrots, etc), a huge plate of humus and an oversized just-out-of-the-oven laffa. First course consisted of two dishes each person: we ordered fried Cypriotic sheeps milk cheese, fried cauliflower (featured in Esquire magazine; with chive, dill, mint, and garlic), burmuelos (leek and mint fritters/croquettes), and roasted chicken freeka. For the main course, I ordered "The Bulgarian" (a small plate of ground beef, lamb, cumin, rice and beans) and my friend ordered "The Sabra" (young chicken, soumac onions, and Israeli cous cous). For dessert, I had cashew baklavah with argan ice cream (argan is a nut from Morroco) and he ordered "New School" Konafi (chocolate, pistachhios, and lebaneh -- yogurt -- ice cream). We decided to splurge and order drinks with our meals: I had a lemonnana (bourbon, muddled mint, lemon, and verbena) -- my amateur taste buds registered it as an Israeli mojito substitutting the rum for bourbon. Again, it was a sublime experience -- probably the best Restaurant Week experience in my three years here. For the amount of food we had, it was certainly a good value!

text: Dooky Chase Restaurant. What can you say about a staple of NOLA's history. Established in 1941, Dooky Chase's survived not only hurricanes Katrina and Rita, but they survived Camile as well. Whatever hardships have been thrown at Dooky's, they have always come back. The tour books and some of the reviews here say the neighborhood is "iffy" or 'has been slow to come back after Katrina". Well I was there 4 days ago (as of this posting) and I can tell you that there are a dozen new houses being constructed across the street and down the block, a rebuild on the street is currently on going and the restaurant itself looks great. Maybe the neighborhood is 'sketch' at night if you aren't a local but in the immediate area there is vibrancy, but you'll have to judge for yourself. Our part consisted of five, one of which was a professional chef. We order several main stays of the menu such as fried chicken, stewed chicken, baked mac and cheese, greens, etc. Everything was fabulous, except for the fact that the item ordered by the chef, stuffed crab cakes was sold out. The chef in our party sent word back to their chef to "send me whatever he'd like to make me that's off menu". The chef did not disappoint. He sent out a deep friend, herb encrusted crab dish that was fantastic.. The fried chicken was well received, the stewed chicken practically fell apart in your mouth it was so tender. The food was the classic 'home cooking' style you would expect from the south. The dessert menu is limited but according to our party, when the peach cobbler is that good, you don't need a larger menu. the cobbler was fresh, sweet and most certainly home made. We also had a rare occasion to meet Ms. Leah Chase, owner and operator of the restaurant. She is 87 years old and is the quintessential southern black lady with sass. She is pleasant, interesting and very engaging. Has stories to spare and has basically seen, heard and done it all. If she is there when you go, let her bend your ear for 20 minutes, you won't be sorry. Portion sizes are good, bordering on huge for both lunch and dessert. Currently they do not have enough staff for dinner but if you eat there for lunch, you won't need dinner. If you want a great food experience in NOLA, you can't go wrong with Dooky Chase's.

text: I am a huge fan of Riverchase. Before every municipality in St. Louis started building super pools, Fenton did it first. They created a great little outdoor and indoor pool space with an amazing recreational center for the residents of Fenton to use as well as residents of, well, everywhere else for just a little more money. Riverchase's pools are always immaculate. They have the huge water slides and a great lap pool and diving area that many of the newer establishments do not have outdoors. Also, the indoor pool is great and has slides and lap lanes, as well as a huge hot tub that is open year round. This place is much more than a pool though. There are a ton of sports teams you can join, both as a child and as an adult to stay fit, they have great work out rooms, and a ton of classes from arts and crafts to aerobics. The dressing rooms are pristine and the staff is incredibly friendly. As neighborhood rec centers go, this is one of the older ones around now, which is sad considering it's only about 10 years old. They have really kept it up, though and it's a very nice place to go and work out. If you live in Fenton, it's a cheap membership and if you don't, well, it's a little more, but maybe you will find it worth it. You can always try to finagle a guest pass out of a friend that does live in Fenton....that's what I always do.

text: Dingy, dark and small--the East Side knows how to cultivate its dive bars. FooBar isn't bad. In fact, I'd have to say I like it. FooBar is owned by the same fellow that runs the Rosepepper, which means one thing: margaritas! The Rosepepper's margaritas have been voted best in the city on multiple occasions, and FooBar's are identical. Plus, you can get them for just $4 on Mondays. Two-for-ones all day Sunday, and happy hour is every day from 5:00 to 9:00. Unfortunately, FooBar is located in a slightly sketchy part of Gallatin Pike, and the place is probably one of the smallest bars in town (excluding Dino's). FooBar has live music many nights, and, while I'd typically be into that, the place is so small and the acts are so loud that the volume borders on unbearable. If you go on a night when there's live music, don't expect to be able to talk to anyone or look anywhere other than directly at the band.

The local folks confirmed that there used to be a Mexican restaurant there with different name/decor etc. All agreed that whatever had been there before, the lunch we had was superb. I highly recommend it.

text: After just returning from NYC, where I ended up having disappointing cupcakes from both Magnolia and Crumbs, I was skeptical to say the least when I happened upon Philly Cupcake. I happened upon the bakery while heading home from a trip to Macy's, as the cute decor lured me in. However, I told the owner (i assume) and 2 other workers that since I'm a self-proclaimed cupcake aficionado, I had to check this place out and determine it's worthiness. I even offered to taste it out in front of them, and give them my honest opinion (i feel constructive criticism is imperative- esp. when dealing w/ a new bakery), and they eagerly accepted. I took my first bite and the cupcake (I kept with the basics and had vanilla w/ Choc) and was pleasantly surprised. It was delightful, in fact! The cake actually had a caramelized, crunchy top and a moist, dense cake. Less dense than Brown Betty though. The icing was creamy and not overly sweet, and I thought the ratio of cupcake to icing was spot on. It was unlike any other cupcake I had ever tried, and that's nearly impossible to achieve since we're talking about cupcakes here. Though they are smaller that the average cupcake, they are so delicious and filling, you only need a few bites. I felt the $3 price is a bit too steep for Philly, however, and would make more sense to charge no more than $2.75. The high price is probably a good thing though, as I will make less visits. I tried taking my nieces there, as they were in town for the holidays, but we were greatly disappointed to find them closed on a Monday, with no hours of operation sign posted. All my nieces talked about all day was getting a "Philly Cupcake" :-( Hoping they hire more staff soon so they can be open daily. This place is a fantastic new addition to the city and I wish them well!

text: I am so happy that this was my first experience with a New Orleans classic: the praline! While they don't make any of the pralines right in the shop, you walk in and it just smells of sugar. I ran around frantically picking up every praline flavor because I can't decide which I want to try. Out of the several flavors they had, I ended up picking a chocolate one that was just wrapped in saran wrap. I felt that might be better than the pre-packaged ones, and boy was I right! I hadn't even finished paying for it before I already had it unwrapped. It was fudgy, nutty, buttery and everything that an authentic praline should be. It also seemed to be a lot thicker than the paper thin ones everyone else seemed to be selling. Throughout my stay I probably tried 4 other places, but nothing was as good as this. Skip the busier Southern Candy Makers and come here instead for the ones wrapped in saran wrap. You won't be disappointed.

text: Usually at 11 AM I'm in the middle of my REM cycle, but when in Philadelphia and awake for brunch, I dine at XIX. This prix fixe lunch is all you could ask for, and features a fabulous buffet of "things" for people who eat. Since I don't, I just like to stare at the food and imagine what it would taste like in my mouth. The first time I saw the sign for XIX outside the Bellevue on Walnut and South, I thought it was a help group for cross-eyed drunks with huge noses. And since I was looking for a Jewish husband, the first word out of my mouth was "oh my God!" When I got up to the 19th floor, sat down at a random table, and started to pour out my life story of drugs, booze, and my celebrity boxing tragedy against Judge Judy, I'd caused a whole table of 90-year old socialites to go into cardiac arrest. And that is how I became the single-most mass murderer in American history. My fave thing about XIX is that not only is the name in Roman, but the food is also Roman. How do I know it's Roman? Because one time in Milan I had a really bad trip, and found myself surrounded by towel-wearing men, manchego cheese, and cold cuts that looked surprisingly like the ones in the XIX buffet. Or maybe that was just my last trip to the bath house. I forget. I can't keep track of my sex life any more than I can keep track of my social security number. Hence why I'm always making up a new one every time AmEx cancels one of my cards. If you're scared of heights, XIX is enclosed by walls and windows, and has the most fabulous views of the downtown. The architects basically designed the view so you can't see any poor people, which is perfect for me. Poor people make me lose my appetite. I have a whole slideshow of street bums that I'll look at to control weight gain. hEllO, it's like the new thing in dieting. Competition for the brunch/lunch scene is fierce on Walnut Street, and if anyone knows anything about the word fiErcE, it's me. XIX is high-end, sexy, and aside from being a wonderful lunch spot it's also a cute place for drinks and date nights. Also, if your date is going less-than-perfect (i.e. he suggests you "split the bill"), you should know that there are no bathrooms on the same floor as XIX, which means you need to take the elevator; hint hint, hitting that Lobby button is far too easy after "excusing yourself" to the ladies room. For a trendy lunch spot and some delish Roman food, try XIX. And ladies/gay men: don't forget about the elevator. This restaurant is totally designed for bailing on a bad date. If I were you, I'd schedule a bad date just to experience the architectural bail-out masterpiece. Speaking of which, I'm on EHarmony right now... This has been a Review by Fulgencio

text: This is what I have been waiting for. A place where a man can get a man's sandwich. And a place where the sandwiches are affordable. And a place where the sandwiches are delicious. I was dying to try Fozzie's ever since they opened, and upon viewing the menu, I know I will become a regular within no time. My first visit I opted to go with The Big Bend Mafia. A delectable mix of spicy italian beef and salsiccia suasage covered with peppers, onions and cheese and smashed between two hoagie buns. We got our meal to go, and by the time I got home the juices from my sandwich were seeping through the paper my sandwich was wrapped in - a true sign of a great sandwich. The Mafia was bursting with spices and flavor - and the meat had some kick to it. My wife had the falafel sandwich, which was pretty good but didn't compare to mine. The falafel came on a bun in 3 round "pucks" along with a bunch of other more healthy toppings than my Big Bend Mafia. It still tasted good. We both had the home-made chips which were surprisingly crunchy and delicious, cut very thin and cooked to a good crisp. Most home made chips are too thick and soggy and covered in grease, these had a good crunch - quite the opposite. She also ordered the Carmel milkshake - another big hit. Sweet and creamy delight! I liked this place so much I brought my brother back the next day and he had rave reviews for it as well (he had the classic italian sandwich). I would recommend ordering ahead by calling - we did have to wait awhile for our food when we just walked in to order. But, everything is made fresh, which partially explains the wait. It was worth it. I can't wait to go back and try some of the extensive menu Fozzie's has to offer.

text: Call me the Grinch or rather "The childless Grinch who abhors mass commercialism that occurs at a rampant pace during the holidays." Linvilla is a torrent of Xmas commercialism gone bad. Perhaps I would be singing a different tune if I had kids and brought them here for Halloween and the holidays to do what kids do at these things - like pet animals, or eat caramel apples, go on a hayride or go and cut down the Griswold family Xmas tree. But I don't, so bah-humbug. Don't get me wrong, I love the holidays - the whole bit - trimming the tree, snow, carols, the whole nine yards - I just hate how commercialized it can all get and quick - and Linvilla is feeding into that holiday frenzy, appealing to the kiddies, and getting a mad pay-off for it. Huge parking area, a bevy of stores with all sorts of trinkets, and tzotchkes, with, almost as an afterthought, some greenery, some sad looking pre-cut trees (at $50- $90 a pop- why not just buy a tree in the city?) and the "go and cut down your own tree' experience (for $60, and you must get on a hayride - which isn't really - to get there and back - the whole thing can take an hour and a half at the very least)- which really isn't as fun or idyllic as it sounds. I was anticipating the kiddies, yes, I suppose, but I wasn't anticipating that I'd feel like I was shopping at a mall when I decided to go to a place whose name includes "orchards" in it. There was nothing outdoors-y, intimate or Christmas-esque about the experience or the place at all, save the fact, that it was indeed, located in the outdoors. It was crowded, kind of a mad-house and I felt like I was being price-gouged left and right. After assessing the whole scene, I understood that it was to be expected - it's not like Linvilla is out in the country, it's smack dab in between suburbs, and thus resulting in creating Suburban Orchards with a suburban shopping mall feel. Don't come here for the atmosphere, or to get you in the holiday spirit. It's probably good for kids, but in the only way it can be good for kids, like Disney. Xmas trees here are no better nor cheaper than where you would find them elsewhere.

text: Ok. Two things first - I'm really soft on service industry people because I've been in the trenches before, so I'm usually very understanding and I don't freak out about much when it comes to service. Also, I don't expect much from this place, as it is a terribly tacky Copeland's joint, I knew what I was getting into. Or so I thought. My family went to dinner here, (there was a gift certificate involved) we were a party of 6, and were quickly seated, so I knew it wasn't a super busy night. Our server was very softspoken, which isn't very effective in such a loud place, we worked through it though. We ordered our drinks, which included a lot of unsweetened iced teas. Ordering our food was fairly incident-less, so maybe this experience will take a better turn. We ordered the spinach and artichoke dip, which is pretty standard. It came out quickly (pro) and with extra chips (pro) but the extra chips on the separate dish were stale, when the chips with the spindip platter were fresh, crispy and warm (con) eh. Sidenote: I'm still mourning over the fact that they don't serve the spin dip with the fried bowtie pasta anymore. It's a true tragedy. The spin-dip was good, I do like that it comes with a side of sour cream and salsa. Then it really started to go downhill. Here's the breakdown of what we ordred, so that you can see exactly how deep the food confusion was: Me and my sister: salmon with mashed tatoes Dad: Mahi Mahi with sweet tato fries and mac n cheese. Also ordred french onion soup Mom: gumbo Bro-in-law: Herb Roasted Rotisserie Chicken w broccoli Bro 1: sasusage, chicken and shrimp pasta Bro 2: crawfish ravioli Ok, not too heinous, right? My mom is always a bit difficult, b/c she doesn't eat much, and always bogarts Dad's sides. but whatever, nothing CRAZY. A random person comes out from the kitchen with what she called a salmon dish. Me and my sister look, and it looks nothing like salmon and it's with fries. My mom asks if that's the Mahi Mahi, but kitchen person says it's not. And proceeded to put it down in front of Bro-in-law. Who ordered the CHICKEN. She left us with this random dish in bewilderment. Then our server came with 6 extra side plates and put them on the table. wat? We had long been done with our appetizer, what are these mystery plates for? Then our dishes start staggering out. We send back the mystery dish, and my sister gets her salmon, my brother gets his crawfish ravioli, and bro in law gets his chicken. My brother's pasta dish is completely wrong, it's just chicken, so we have to send that back. I don't have my salmon, and the mystery dish turned out to be my dad's mahi-mahi. (It's worrisome that the kitchen staff doesn't know the diff between rotisserie chicken and mahi mahi) so we have to chase it back down. So I'm waiting in dinner limbo, not knowing where my dish is, and feeling odd, b/c my sister got the exact same dish, so why is mine MIA? A good 10 min later, when our server comes back around, we ask about it, and oddly, he produces it right away. I fear he snatched it off another table behind us. It was like that. My brother gets his pasta dish finally, and apparently, the sauce was so weak that he didn't even eat it. I'm like, how can you mess up pasta sauce? We tasted it and it was pretty weak. not bad, but quite bland. Also, my bro-in-law's chicken wasn't the kind he ordred, they gave him the lemon chicken instead of the herb roasted chicken. The sweet potato fries were burned. We had to order another serving. The amount of errors with our entrees was extraordinary, and of course, there was no offer to comp or rectify the situations. The only upside to all this? It all happened very quickly. At least there were no long drawn out waiting spaces between mistakes. This is probably a case of speed=errors. so, SIGH. Being the local equivalent of a chain restaurant that has been in operation for decades, operations should be much more solid. I can't really give a reason to ever come back. If you get a gift certificate to here, I'd strongly recommend seeing if you can trade it with someone.

text: My boyfriend and I booked a room at this casino for our two night stay in Reno. We were lured in by the price - $39.99/night, but after reading reviews on Yelp and other travel sites were concerned that we were going to be staying in a dump. We were impressed walking through the lobby of the casino, which is luxurious and quite grand, but held our breath until we got to our room. It was a 25th floor smoking room, but was very, very clean, and smelled only faintly of cigarette smoke (important for me, the non-smoker in our relationship). The king bed was extremely comfortable, and we had a nice view of downtown Reno and the mountains in the distance. We had our first night's dinner at Smokin' Gecko's BBQ, which is technically part of the Circus Circus casino. The food was fantastic--love that cornbread with honey butter. We had breakfast and lunch the next day at Flavors! buffet, which is a lot better than most of the buffets I've ever gone to. Only complaint about the food would be the scrambled eggs at breakfast--college dining halls do a better job than they did. We spent a lot of money in the casino (of course), but had a blast losing it all. No complaints about the parking garage, which was narrow, but we were able to find a spot for our Mustang and didn't suffer any dings. Minus one star for the high price for wireless internet--$9.99/day is just ridiculous. For a trip that's closer (and thus cheaper) than Las Vegas, I really don't think you can go wrong with the Silver Legacy.

text: I gave Mi Lah another shot for dinner with decidedly mixed results. On a cool fall evening, I appreciated a hot cup of tea to start. We had the green (nice and toasty) and white (sweeter, flowery). My corn chowder was the high point of the meal, with a rich, implausibly creamy texture, chewy bits of seitan, and just the right amount of red pepper to add a little depth. My companion did not fare so well with his seitan and tomato on toast (it doesn't even sound good, does it?) The "marinated seitan" looked and tasted suspiciously like what you can buy frozen in a Morningstar bag, and the out-of-season tomatoes and cold grocery store toast didn't help matters any. That crumbled seitan showed up again in my grilled zucchini, which was cooked perfectly and seasoned simply. With the celery and seitan stuffing and a light, maybe unnecessary tomato sauce, this was tasty, if a little basic. Again, my poor date got the short end of the stick with bland, gummy seitan and zucchini cakes. I liked the mustard sauce on them, but the plain steamed vegetables and underpowered mashed potatoes would have been right at home in a suburban catering hall somewhere. When the bill came, I was bummed - this is 3 star (at best) cooking at 4+ star prices. When I was reminded that Horizons' heavenly seitan steak cost the same as those sad zucchini cakes, I felt a pang deep in my heart, knowing that we had surely chosen the wrong vegan restaurant that night.

text: We'd read good reviews of this place on Tripadvisor.com and thought it would be a good place to eat dinner, since we both love tapas. What a mistake! We were the only people in the restaurant on a Saturday night, which should have told us something, considering that other restaurants in the area had full parking lots. It actually reminded us a lot of the show Kitchen Nightmares, where the restaurant was deserted and the standards had slowly slipped over time (we're giving them the benefit of the doubt that they weren't always this awful). We arrived during "happy hour," which ostensibly should have entitled us to $5 tapas. After we were given the check, with full priced tapas on it, we overheard another server (not ours) tell the second group in the dining room that the $5 tapas was tapas that was not on the menu. Unfortunately, our server did NOT tell us this. He was very nice and friendly, but seemed quite callow, given the absence of his notification about the tapas specials and the fact that he didn't offer us dessert or to order more tapas, even though we said that we'd start with 3 and would probably order more. There were other strange things about the service like, with an entirely empty dining room, they gave us the table next to the bathroom. The woman who seated us didn't pull out our chairs or spread out our napkins, which was another indication of the unpolished service that we received here. The food, though, was the big problem. We wanted to start with three different tapas, but they were out of the one that sounded most appealing to us, the fried green tomatoes with crab meat. We ordered the ceviche, four crab croquettes, and the shrimp al ajillo. The ceviche turned out to be a garden salal with precisely TWO shrimp, sliced lengthwise, and a half of a bay scallop, which was cut into two pieces. Not exactly what is usually indicated by the term "ceviche," especially for $7.50. The crab croquettes, which were described as "filled with crab and cheese," turned out to be plain potato croquettes. Neither crab nor cheese was in evidence here. The shrimp al ajillo, at $7.95, was a giant rip off. This, of the three dishes, turned out to be the only one that was what it said it was: shrimp with garlic sauce. However, $7.95 at Tapas Garden buys you 6 medium-sized (26-30/lb) shrimp. Woo hoo! I'm posting a photo, though it's only got 5 shrimp, since I forgot that we were photographing the food and had eaten one of the shrimp before I remembered this. I was so irritated at this point by the misinformation and misleading descriptions that we just paid the check and left. I didn't even finish my glass of wine because I was so irked. I would definitely advise avoiding this restaurant unless you would like to pay too much for mediocre food with either excessively small portion sizes or misleading ingredients like "ceviche" or "crab" croquettes.
label: NEG

text: Hey, if you're feeling the need to lay down some serious bucks on nothing but atmosphere, then you're sure to love the tragic experience known as El Vez. Honey pie and I tried this joint out after considering it for a while; in fact, she may have tried it prior to our trip, but I can't recall if this actually happened or not. No matter. Hey look, there's a goofy bicycle rotating in the center of the restaurant! Check it out! There's a photo booth where you can go in and make nauseated faces after realizing how much you spent and how satisfying the food wasn't! But you say you enjoyed their one of a kind cocktails and margaritas? Get outta town! What they're serving here isn't anything you can't get anywhere else, save for maybe that frozen blood orange margarita, but having tried it, I can safely say you're not missing a thing. So then, be prepared to pay out the wazoo for the "special guacamole" they have here (many different varieties; nothing exciting that I haven't had at other eatieries for a fraction of the price) as well as your entree. What? You don't want to spend between 15 and 25 bucks for each thing? Well then, you have no business being here! Actually, how this place stays open based on getting what you pay for is a mystery. What El Vez serves is nothing exciting, with no major crazy variation on anything that justifies the prices paid. I suppose it's good if you want trendy, "new" Mexican bullshit, but for what it's worth, you can do a lot better by going to one of the more authentic hole in the wall joints in town. It might not be flashy and the music might not be as obnoxiously intrusive, but your wallet and stomach will be much happier, plus you won't have to deal with hipster servers who put on the fake smiles and couldn't care less who they're dealing with. El Vez is cookie cutter nonsense with a colorful high gloss finish, that, unless you're just of that sort of crowd who doesn't care what they waste money on, doesn't leave any positive impression once your visit is over.
label: NEG

text: I don't ever plan on writing reviews for franchises because essentially, you get the same experience as far as food/drink quality and service goes, especially when the aforementioned franchise is Starbucks. It's kind of impressive and scary how all Starbucks employees (regardless of their make, model, size, shape, sex, skin tone, etc etc) are almost Stepford-ish in how nice, considerate and generally chipper they are. A secret (well not so secret anymore) way to test the general amiability of a Starbucks barista is to walk in, look stupefied, and then say the following words: "I... don't know what to get. Do you have any suggestions?" If they're good, they'll smile and give you some suggestions based on your tastes. If they're great, they'll do the same, but then offer to make you something else for free if you don't like what you bought. This is why I love Starbucks and am annoyed by people who hate it. Yes, they're a big faceless corporation, blah de blah, but they got so big because they make their customers feel like they're the only ones that matter for those brief two minutes. But I'm soapboxing now, so I'll cut it short. This location rocks because I love how it feels like a library with a Starbucks attached. It reminds me of my undergrad days, and even simple things like the bricks in the ceiling, or how there is never a shortage of desks to lay out my books/laptop, or how all of the patrons are considerate and quiet, or even how this location is kind of set a little bit below ground making it feel all... cave-like; all these things just make me love spending time in here. Say hi if you see me. I'm the brown guy with the iDevice headphones on. There aren't many Indians in that location, I mean it's not like there's a really nice private university nearby with Indians all running amok. Oh wait... Ok fine, I'm the Indian guy always wearing flip flops; I know most Indians have an aversion to flip flops.

I understand great food takes time, and I have no issue with that. I am extremely disappointed in the level of customer service we received from our waiter. As he only had 2 tables the entire 2 1/2 hours we were there, I expect that our drinks would always be full and that he would be attentive to all our needs. I do not believe I will be returning to this restaurant, and I strongly urge anyone else not to waste their money also.

text: I walked in about five minutes before my appointment time and walked up to the desk. A woman saw me walk in and walked over the the desk and smiled and said hello. "Can I help you?" she said. "I have a one o'clock appointment for a pedicure." I said. She asked me name and my address. Then she told me to pick out a polish color as she pointed to the polish rack. I went over to pick from what seemed a limited collection of colors. I wanted a bright pink but the closest they had was coral or magenta. The salon was well decorated with muted earth tones. Nothing very eye catching but not at all dull. There was good quality furniture all throughout the salon and the occasional retro touch with an old book on hairstyling or an circa 1920's wall art piece. The salon looked very clean but I was very hard to tell if the technician had cleaned her implements before or after using them on me. The implements and products were places on a bamboo place mat that is impossible to sanitize. The pedicure chair had light on it to indicate if it had been sanitized but the light was not on. The chair had internal jetting, which always makes me nervous. And the chair next to me that was not being used had water spots and streaks on it. Could have been cleaner or could have been from the previous pedicure water. There was a bottle of bleach cleaner in the pedicure room. Sandy was the manicurist doing the service. She was very nice and well dressed with a cute zebra print skirt. I followed her to the pedicure room and the pedicure tub was already filled and jets running. She had me start by putting my feet into the water. After a very short soak, she took one foot out removed old polish, shortened filed toes nails. She then pushed back my cuticles and smoothed out the nails with a buffer then applied a "sugar scrub". After that she applied a lotion and did a foot massage. Her movements were fast and although I did enjoy the massage it was mediocre at best. Next was polish...I had chosen a shimmery coral color. She applied base coat, two coats of color and then top coat. Then without missing a beat applied cuticle oil. Now, as a manicurist myself I know that polish drys through evaporation. Polish cannot dry when covered with oil. There was so much oil my flip flops were all oily when I got home. Plus when she was applying the oil she put her finger into the polish on my big toe and then reapplied more polish after the oil was on the nail. That nail is now very thick with polish. But the worst was the lotion. I think it was Hempz and I just hate the smell of that stuff. I gives me a headache. But most people love it. The one thing that defines a pedicure is a good polish job. This was not. My feet were slipping around in my flip flops from all the lotion. I had to walk very gingerly. I would recommend bringing your own polish with you since their selection is not the best. I paid $46 for a 30 minute pedicure. This is a little on the high side. For the money, go somewhere else.

text: I expected better of this place. Ordered the duck dinner for two substituting duck, wonton, noodle soup for the standard soup. The clear broth was flavorful but lukewarm. One of my pet peeves is lukewarm soup. There's really no excuse for it. The server can tell because hot soup has steam coming out. If it doesn't have steam coming out of it, the soup is not going to be hot. Simple. Turning to the duck itself, I'm a traditionalist. There was a thick visible layer of fat between the skin and the meat. Not a good sign. The key to Peking duck is the days ahead prep which results in the fat layer being minimized. When I see a thick layer of fat between the skin and the meat, it is a sign t o me that the restaurant is short-cutting the drying process. Under the circumstances, there is no way that the duck cannot be greasy, and it was. The pancakes that accompanied the duck were dry and cracking. Why can so few restaurants figure out that the pancakes need to be moist so the Peking duck can be properly wrapped so the hoisin sauce stays inside rather than on the diner's hands? The second duck course served stir fried with string beans was delicious and not greasy. The meat was not overcooked and the balance of textures between the crisp beans and toothsome duck meat was what makes Chinese food great. The fried rice that accompanied this course was tasty with sweet peas and abundant shrimp. I gave the restaurant two stars instead of three because the duck is supposed to be the star of the show and the Peking duck did not live up to star billing.

text: Wow. Where to start? If you don't know, this hotel is in its own zip code - about the size of the community college I attended. Luckily, I was pre-warned of its labyrinthine layout and sprawling floor plan far in advance by a colleague - who mentioned that she never set foot outside in her week of staying here, because, simply, you don't have to. Bars, restaurants, convention center, shopping, coffee, hotel rooms are all on site, encapsulated in a Biodome-like atrium with a glass ceiling. An entire ecosystem exists indoors, including a winding shallow river (complete with river boat tours) and real plants, trees and various flora throughout. Sunshine streams in from the ceiling and it's pretty cool in that way. But that floor plan. My (and just about anyone's) biggest complaint would have to be that you must do a series of maneuvers to get from A to B, even if you can see B from A directly in front of you. Shorts sets of stairs, ramps, elevators, bridges, rivers, etc. block the most direct path to anywhere from anywhere. Fine if you're a family on vacation and in no particular rush - but if you're there for a conference (as I'm sure 80 percent of the people here are) that is a huge pain in the ass, which only pisses you off more the longer you're there. P.s. there are shortcuts that I discovered on my fifth day...FIFTH day. Another warning: Cascades Terrace Lounge (the open bar right at the Cascades entrance) *moves.* Yeah, it spins, ever so slightly. It's made up of two circles - the inner being the circular bar with belly-up seating, the outer being lounge tables and sofa chairs for sharing a more intimate drink. The outer circle spins slowly - a fact I noticed when having a drink by myself the first night at the inner circle bar. It's hard to explain the dizzying, disorienting effect this had on me: have you ever been in a car a stop light, and the car next to you starts rolling forward? You see it in your peripheral vision and for a split second think your car is moving and it makes you confused and slightly sick? Imagine that split second lasting about a full minute as you go "Am I moving? Where's a stationary object? No, we're not moving in here, but outside the bar is moving? Are we rocking because the bar is like a barge on this fake river? No, we're definitely moving in a circle... but not everyone is moving. Hmmm...am I about to have a stroke?" This, of course, is exacerbated by booze, no less. Cascade Terrace, you can take your novelty spinning and shove it. What else... the shopping is nothing special - a "book store" that was actually a stationary store with a few novelty coffee table books inside. Who wants to read a coffee table book while traveling?? A few more boutiques that cater to grandmothers looking for clothes for themselves or gifts for their 6-year-old grandchildren. A toy store. The convention center. I feel unfair having just been to the awesomely re-done Phoenix Convention Center, with its updated color scheme and prints. This was probably last done in the early 90s. Gold, orange and green are the themes, including heavy, metal and cushion chairs that rank a "could be worse" on the comfort scale. Carpet had a loud print that reminded me of a Vegas casino in need of an update. Sound system worked alright and no issues with AV in any of my sessions. Kudos to the water at the back of the rooms in one of those big jugs that gets chilled so I can fill up the one plastic water bottle I bought that lasted me the entire trip over and over.

text: Full review in the blog. Settling into what may be the most comfortable chairs in dining history and placing the thick linen napkin on my lap I was greeted by a young man who inquired as to whether I preferred tap or bottled water - selecting tap my glass was filled and remained well above half-full throughout the meal's two hour duration. Three knives, three forks - all silver, a potted plant, and salt and pepper shakers decorated the well padded table and I'd shortly be greeted by my server, a pleasant and jovial man who admitted to being new to the Perrier family, but never failed to have the (right) answer to any question or request. Presented with the menu it was explained that there was an a la carte, a 3-course business lunch, or the tasting menu - I was also told of three specials and given suggestions as to the restaurant's signatures. When my server asked if I was ready to order, indeed I was. "I'll have the tasting menu and I'd like to add a couple of courses." "Sir, I must warn you that will be a lot of food." "I'm sure I'll be fine." After a few jokes I inquired about the cheese and dessert cart and was informed they are not operated during lunch, but that any/all selections from either could be done as a composed plate. My first course of the afternoon would be course one of the tasting. Served in a small sauté dish which was uncapped tableside the Escargots Cassolette with Hazelnut, Champagne, Garlic Butter smelled like a dream come true - a very pungent dream. Featuring shelled and plump snails, at least ten to my tongue, plus tiny bits of chopped nuts in an aromatic broth with the bite of champagne but the base of pure butter and finely pressed garlic the dish wowed. While perhaps not something you'd want to order on a date night, the contrasting textures and rich aromatics were profound and well balanced...I soaked up every drop with a slice of baguette - my server agreed this was "the only way to do it." Course number two would be titled Diver Sea Scallop, Charred Watermelon, Tomato, Rosewater Emulsion the dish did not really look all that interesting with a single scallop sitting in a cloud of foam, but looks are often time deceiving. Regarding the scallop - it was perfect, fresh, nearly brulee crisp on the exterior and practically raw within. More interesting than the scallop, however, was its bed - a texture I can only describe as finely chopped salsa with hints of smoke, sweetness, and acid all nicely balanced. My third course would be one of my supplement courses - it would also be the best dish of the afternoon and every bit worth the title "signature." Described in French as a Galette the Signature Crab Cake with French Green Beans and Whole Grain Mustard Sauce sat tall, proud, and without a bit of filler. More a crab burger than cake in shape/size and more a sweet crab omelet than cake in flavor the dish was topped tableside with a pour of buttery mustard speckled béarnaise that did not overpower but instead served to enhance. Hitting a nice pace with a dish arriving every 15 minutes my next course would be the other supplement - Seared Hudson Valley Foie Gras, Port poached cherries, and French toast in a maple foie gras reduction. Flawlessly seared, perfectly clean, a little sweet, a lot savory - not a novel presentation, but a classic done classically. For my main course, Domestic Lamb Loin with Purple Cauliflower, Crunchy Oats, Marcona Almond, and Golden Raisin Reduction the dish was remarkable. Served medium rare and so tender that they opted against presenting it with a knife the lamb itself was a fine piece, slightly gamey as expected but well met with the sweet raisin reduction. Presented beautifully with the pureed purple cauliflower as a base and topped with a granola textured compote of oats and almonds the dish was a sight and flavor to behold. Waiting approximately 20 minutes while the desserts were plated in the kitchen the restaurant was now bustling. Enjoying my coffee and its subsequent refills the plates that would arrive yet were unfortunately not from a trolley or carte, but they certainly were beautiful. Arriving with ample description, two plates and easily a pound in weight - all nine of Le Bec Fin's signature desserts - to the shock of my server I would clean these plates as well. While some may call Le Bec Fin's style dated and the food boring, I found the word's classy and classic much more applicable. No stranger to hyper-modern cooking (Alinea) or loud uncomfortable seating in jeans and a T-shirt (Ko) for greater than $150pp I found Le Bec Fin to be a flashback to the way fine dining used to be. Sure, there will still be refined and high quality service, sourcing, seating, and food once Le Bec Fin closes its doors for good, but even then I'll be glad to have experienced Chef Perrier's gem while I had the chance.

text: This is one of the first places I went to after I moved to the city. I've had several items from the menu and liked everything but the crab soup. My favorite is probably the blackened burger with hand cut french fries. They have several beers on tap, including two of my favorites, Guinness and Blue Moon. As far as liquor selection they seem to have just about anything you could possibly drink. What's really cool about this place is that it doesn't matter where you are from. If you hang out here and talk to people, they will talk back to you. You won't be ignored or made to feel uncomfortable. Its a real nice atmosphere. There are a couple of regulars in just about every day if not every day on the weekend so you always end up knowing someone there. And if you are really lucky you'll get to see the crazy Trinidadian do his dance(he's really good).

text: As a newcomer to the East Coast and Delaware, I was excited to try something original to Delaware. Unfortunately, I would say my meal was forgettable at best. I had sirloin steak, the special for the night, ordered at medium rare. It came out much rarer than that, leaving pools of blood everywhere on my plate (though I am not too picky, and ate it anyways). The major disappointment for the night was the house-made root beer, which our server highly recommended. I am not sure if I got a bad batch or not, but it tasted more like water with a hint of root beer than anything else. Imagine 1/5 root beer to 4/5 water. Aside from the lackluster food and drink, the staff was friendly and attentive, though perhaps there is a misplaced light switch because the lights in our section kept going on, off and fluctuating in intensity. I will probably try Iron Hill a few more times just to make sure I haven't judged it too hastily.

text: The pizza here is not much better than a frozen one from the grocery store. The crust does not appear to be handmade, but one from a Joe Corbi's pizza kit. Bad: it appeared as if they took a pre-made plain pizza and threw on canned mushrooms and frozen spinach (onions and green peppers are fresh, as I could tell). text: If you want a hoagie that is not laden with enough cholesteral to choke an ox, a Vietnamese hoagie from Cafe Huong Lan is worth a shot. With seasoned tofu, fresh cilantro, some sort of buttery mayo and jalapeno peppers on a very fresh French baguette, it is so deliciously light and perfect. If you really want to reduce the fat, get it without the buttery stuff. It's still good. I'm also a big fan of their tapioca-like plantain pudding dealie. text: I like this place. It has good food for not bad prices, fun drinks, and a nice atmosphere that isn't too over-the-top for a Starr place. Fun, because you can pick everything that you like in a salad for only $12 (a few things like steak, etc. are extra). A few of my friends got the tilapia and it was incredibly delish, especially the sauce (not sure what it was but it tasted like autumn). The drink menu is where it's at: fun cocktails and martinis. I had a chai-tini which tastes like it sounds, and they had one of my favorite beers (Three Philosophers by Ommegang) so that was a huge plus. And $8 for a martini is pretty darn good. The service was great as well. We had a party of 8 at 9:00 on a saturday night, and they seated us quickly and provided quick, attentive and friendly service. Our appetizers came out within 10 minutes and the food arrived as soon as we were finsihed with the apps. And the place was by no means empty. So all in all, not the absolute best food I've ever had, but a great fun night out. I'm sure I'll be back.

text: Terrain at Styer's is so quaint, it hurts. The food, the ambience and the service are all fantastic. The beautiful, mismatched tableware, mason jar drinking glasses, simple cloth table napkins all add to the experience. I ordered the iced vanilla mint au lait. It was so incredibly delicious and a wonderful way to start a very warn day. My friend and I were then served the bread pot accompanied with honey and lavender (?) sea salt drizzled butter. For our entrees, my friend ordered the egg white omlet served with applewood smoked bacon. I oredered the blueberry pancakes. The portions are perfect so that you leave the table feeling very satisfied. I wish I had more room for one of the many delicious pastries. Throughout our meal, I found myself staring at the decor - it was unique and complete perfection. The service was prompt, courteous and the server very nice. I can't wait to go back and try their dinner! Make sure that you have enough time to browse the grounds (and enough money to pick up some one of the kind goodies).

Subsequently, my Aunt compared the atmosphere and food to an old-timey New Orleans eatery. Coming from her, that's about as good as it gets! I highly recommend the fried green tomatoes, hush puppies, soups (especially the borscht if you're into it), and the homemade deserts (Try the carrot cake!). One of my favorite dishes of all time resides here; Honey's version of Mexican corn. They serve it during the late summer/fall, and it's one of the most amazing things I've ever tasted! The buffet is very cheap and very low quality. If you want good food just walk over to Silver Legacy or Eldorado. The casino itself feels a little claustrophobic as it's not laid out well. It's also kind of dark. Most dealers and coin attendants seem like they're not very happy with their jobs, not a lot of smiling faces. text: While I am still searching for my favorite po-boy shop (through literally a hundred or so places that offer them here in the city), I visit the Magazine Po-Boy and Sandwich shop often on off-days. It is a *very* tiring 3 block walk, but is worth it. There are some tables and chairs in the main area of the shop and there is a second dining area for overflow lunch crowd (and a table or two on the sidewalk). The menu is written on the wall to the left the counter, behind which a bevy of people seem to be constantly busy. I usually get the veal cutlet sandwich, oyster/shrimp combo po-boy, the spaghetti, and the Italian salad. They offer nearly every kind of po-boy and sandwich you can think of (I think soft shell crabs too!)... It is a very nice little neighborhood place to grab a cheap eat. And the food is pretty good. Not that it is a bad thing, but you can't get liquor or a beer there and they close at 6pm. Though for me, it's all about the FOOD...check it out.

text: I have been going to Healing Wizdom and Creative Colours for years and have always received wonderful, friendly, skilled treatments and services. I have honestly never had a bad experience and I have received treatments from most of the staff. This is kind of amazing for a small business. Waxing, facials, massages, hair cuts- all excellent. After receiving a massage from Annie the other day, I finally decided to post a review of the place- it really deserves the great praise it gets. This is definitely a 'mom and pop' type of place and is unique in its decor and vibe. This is not a sterile medical spa experience or a corporate spa. This is a place where everyone will get to know you and you will feel welcome. This is a place run by real people, for real people and the service is gentle and warm. But again, what is most amazing about Healing Wizdom is the quality of the therapists. From the moment you walk in and throughout the whole service, you are completely taken care of and given options in your service, which I really appreciate. How many times have I received a massage and never been asked the most basic of questions: what kind of pressure do you like? I like strong pressure and I have had to tolerate more than one massage that felt more like a rub (never at HW) and I get tired of having to ask the therapist to increase pressure. Annie was very thorough in her massage- asking me about my problem areas, what kind of massage oils I like, pressure, focus, etc. Then she continued to check in with me throughout my massage to make sure that the pressure was appropriate. And man, was it appropriate! I felt like there was no place in my body that was ignored, although there was the proper focus on the back, just as I like it. Not only was the pressure excellent, but the pace was perfect. I hadn't really thought much about massage pacing before this massage, but her rhythm was so slow and steady that I couldn't help but notice how spot-on it felt. Nothing in this massage felt rushed or sloppy. This was an amazing massage and for the price it is really a no-brainer. I highly recommend Annie and Healing Wizdom in general. Go.
label: POS

text: Their menu is mostly Chinese, with a few Thai items. I had the Chicken Pad Thai, and I was blown away. You can specify level of spicyness, and I had the mild. The flavors really came through, and the noodles were perfect. This was a different recipe than what I've had at any other Thai restaurant, and I loved it. Ambience is what is to be expected at a strip-mall walk-up. You can carry-out, or eat-in in the dining area. There was a steady stream of customers during the dinner hour. Owners are a handsome young-looking mom-and-pop Asian couple with three adorable little children, plus a teenager. The teen even helps out at the counter. Chopsticks, plastic utensils and soda are self-serve. Two separate restrooms for men and women. They are located on the South side of Indy, on South Emerson Avenue, about 2 blocks North of I-465, on the West side of the Street, in a little strip-mall building. I haven't tried the Chinese cuisine items, but for the Pad Thai, I'll have to say this is worth the trip. Ambience isn't going to impress the boss/wife/gf/inlaws, but the food definitely impresses. This is indeed a gem. They can also prepare large quantities for catering with advance notice. There is a different combo Chinese/Thai restaurant further South on Emerson, on the South side of I-465, so don't confuse the two. I liked this one much better.

text: I have received the most horrible hair cut of my entire life at Aveda Salon. I love Aveda products and buy them often, so getting a hair cut at Aveda salon seemed like the next logical step. Little did I know that my stylist would prefer to ignore my requests and concerns, and cut my hair the way she saw fit. This stylist was not recommended to me by any friends; I chose her by chance, based solely on the fact that she was a senior stylist. After I walked into the salon, was greeted by a friendly sales associate, admired the décor and beautiful scents in the air, and sipped a cup of Aveda tea, I was asked to get into the chair in order to receive the consultation. My stylist was a beautiful lady, who listened to what I had to say very intently. Apparently, the words did not sink in because 15 minutes later I was looking in the mirror with the sense of utter horror. I asked the stylist to keep the length - she chopped my hair 4 inches shorter. I asked for long layers -she made mine short, which caused the hair to look curly and frizzy. I was so busy chatting with my lovely stylist that I didn't notice all the atrocities that were going on north of my neck. By the time I realized the seriousness of the situation, it was too late to fix anything. I chose to stay calm, keep a brave face and not say anything. But believe me- growing out a bad hair cut is no easy task. I had to wear a ponytail every day of the week for two months. I am sure it's just my luck that I chose an unsuitable stylist; and I am sure that there are many young talented hairdressers at Aveda Academy. But for now, Aveda salon is for purchasing hair care only. I'll take my hair cutting needs someplace else.
