FIRST IMPRESSIONS: For some reason, this place is always relatively full, while other places just can't seem to get a turnout...I'm thinking it's got something to do with the porn. Most Yelpers here will wonder why the hell they are here, but they will realize it's probably got more to do with their friends wanting to stick around, which is what always happens to me when I'm there. THE ATMOSPHERE: This place is so cliche Olde City it's sickening...wet couches along the wall, bar on the other side manned by unattentive bartenders who try to get slutty girls to do slutty things on the bar for all to see. The dance floor is always packed, but unless you have a drunken dance partner to accompany you, don't count on being able to go out there and find someone because they are all taken or just total creepsters. Upstairs is Otium, which one letter away from Opium, which is what Otium reminds me of-- an Opium den. THE CLIENTELLE: Hilarious...absolutely the most amusing crowd around, you've got your middle eastern guys trying to be jersey boy italians, whose haircuts and beards make them look like Osama bin Jagerbomb. You've got your fat chicks who love to try and strike up a conversation despite you showing very obvious signs that you're not interested, or in the case of girls, douchebag epitomes that think they're God's gift to Olde City, thank God they only prey on spots like this and stay away from the good ones. You've got your underagers who somehow manage to get in because they know the doorman. It's great. And by great, I mean horrendous. THE DRINKS: Nothing special, typical club drinks, just order your goddamn Vodka Redbull and be happy with it... THE MUSIC: Uninspired DJ plays the same kind of crap you hear at any other club, transitions and continuity between songs is virtually non-existant, like most of the other DJs in Philly's suffering club scene, he might as well have just been playing off his iPod. In fact, I usually get so annoyed by the above mentioned atmosphere and clientelle that I don't want to dance. The dancefloor itself is pretty good, but there are other aspects that take way from it-- for some reason, the area in between the bar and the dancefloor is always crowded, and people feel the need to be especially rude here, it's like paying a toll of patience. THE BOTTOM LINE: Really nothing special, I'm surprised Moda has been around as long as it has, but I don't see much of a future for this place, seeing as how the only thing that sets it apart from the rest of the area's attractions is the porn, and even that isn't appropriate. This place isn't much a disappointment because I never saw much potential, but it's not a place that I'd recommend to anyone I'd seek to please or impress with my knowledge of the city...in fact I'd probably do the opposite to demonstrate that knowledge. Noisy, busy, rough around the edges, but always fun, fast, and satisfying. Sadly, none of that seems to ring true in its new locale up on Chapala. text: "More Like a Poly-Cotton Blend" Tweed, you're new, so I'm going to give you some tough love in the hopes that you improve. Because you have the potential to shine. I was squealing with joy at the prospect of trying Tweed. Perhaps I expected too much so soon after launch. The big sell is local ingredients. I like this, so I'll sprinkle some stars. The space itself is quite handsome and the location can't be beat. More stars. My appetizer, yellowtail sashimi with various sauces, was just OK. The fish was tasty. The fish-to-sauce ratio however was perplexing. Four pieces of fish, five sauces. That leaves one sauce in the lonely. Cutting the sashimi pieces into even smaller pieces was not an intuitive solve. The sauces, ranging from squid ink to cayenne, wasabi and creme fraiche, were too heavy and at times, a bit nauseating. The squid ink sauce in particular: it has the consistency and interest of tar. My lamb entree with a smidge of kale was fine, but not notable in any way. It was attractively sliced. It was nicely plated. It was a bit undercooked. It was neither delicious nor undelicious. It simply lacked oomph. The kale provided no contrast or texture and seemed besides the point. One nice touch: I was served cucumber water. But then, it was topped off with un-cucumbered water. In other words, diluted cucumber water. Something to fix. My dining companion had the soup of the day (a gazpacho, I think) and the chicken. Both were pretty but not necessarily tasty. And now, some star-smashers: - The service - Rule #1: Know your menu. If your menu says the yellowtail sashimi appetizer is plated with "a painter's palate of colors and flavors," be prepared to tell me what that means. (It was blots of different-colored/flavored sauces.) And if I ask you what panna cotta is, please don't try to bluster through and fake it. It breaks the illusion of feeling like you're somewhere special. Rule #2: Pace yourselves. Allow people to be fully seated before you start asking what they want to drink. My lap had barely formed. And give me literally more than one second from the time my fork hits the plate before you pounce the table and clear it. Rule #3: If you don't like the gays, maybe don't wait tables in the Gayborhood. From the moment we were seated, I got the feeling that the waiter was uncomfortable serving two men. (Other servers were great.) It's not something he said, it's not something he did. My friend put it this way: "He didn't say one more word to us than he had to." Now, I don't need to be draped in a rainbow flag or fed a dildo lolly to feel I'm welcome. But do try to manage your bro tone. It might hurt a little. That's OK. - The dessert - The carrot cake roulade was blah. It's two Hostess Ho Ho-type roll-ups dressed fancy. The cake component was faint on flavor. The filling, goat and cream cheese, lent none of the freshness that goat cheese should. The butter pecan ice cream was frozen, rough, inadequately emulsified, and in a nose-thumbing to science, curiously dry. The dish was finished with praline-type crumbles, which did not provide the hoped-for save. Rather they had the panache of gravel. Good coffee helped balance things out. - A note on design - Should you wish to use the bathroom, you will need to pass behind the grand center staircase. Good luck. Clearance is tight and the lighting is low; consequently I nearly clonked my head on the back of the stairs. Overall Tweed has the right idea. Outstanding menu, if not outstandingly executed and served. I'll give it some more time as it merits a second glance.

text: "Dedicated to art and free to all." I had lived in Saint Louis for over 4 years before I set aside the time to go to the Art Museum. A co-worker and I had gone to the St. Louis Symphony concert on Art Hill, which was a part of the race weekend events. When he learned that I had not been to the museum yet, we made plans to meet there on Sunday. Having had the fortune to live in Paris, Moscow, New York City and the Twin Cities, I did not know how well Saint Louis would fare by comparison. I was thrilled to discover that my new home town has a museum with an impressive collection of art and artifacts (from the Egyptian mummies) to a very rare painting from the 17th century female painter, Artemisia Gentileschi. Add to this discovery, my delight in their modern art collection, especially one of the rarer Van Gogh pieces from his northern paintings, and the St. Louis Art Museum is a place that I visit as often as I can. Just this past New Year, my boyfriend and I spend a lovely afternoon strolling through the galleries. He was equally impressed. I am thrilled that they have completed groundbreaking on the new wings and eagerly anticipate their opening in 2012. Until then, there are so many exhibits that I have to explore in depth. That should take me a few more visits.

text: No other place like it on Earth. If you haven't been, go. Now. If you have been, please come back. Now, more than ever New Orleans needs to be seen, be felt, be heard by the multitudes. Any American who calls themself one has an obligation to hajj down dirty south, more south than south, into the swamps past the hillbilies and indeed back in time. There is something for Everone in New Orleans. Especially if you enjoy to eat. Especially if you enjoy to drink. There are three gods here. New Orleans is a Catholic town, sure, everyone knows that. But Bachus still still has a heavy foothold what with the inumerable olefactory pleasures available. And Hecate, looking both way across the expanse of spacetime, forward and back, keeps our souls firmly nestled among one another. New Orleans is very karmic, much like its spiritual sister San Francisco: It gives you exactly what you give it. That's why rednecks always end up in fights on Bourbon St. It's also why your grandmother had the best time ever and that fat uncle bought a condo in the Quarter. There are many things which might perhaps be a better sumation of the Crescent City, but this is what i think of when i think of my home: In New Orleans, we kiss hello and hug goodbye, ask about your mother and talk to your dog. And knowing your name is not a requirement for any of it.

text: I've had lots of mediocre sushi in Tampa. From SB in Ybor City to CB near the stadium, there's a lot of just average... or restaurants trying too hard to be fusion. I grew up near Tampa, and every time I come back, there's only one requirement as far as dining -- I have to get in to see Ryo at Kaisen Sushi. Kaisen is a little known secret that Tampa has been hiding for years. Ryo initially opened over by Harpos, further south on Dale Mabry than their current location. I went in for the first time in 1999, and have been a repeat customer ever since, dining there sometimes twice a week. In all my years of eating at Kaisen, I've never once been disappointed. In fact, they know me by name now and I get that personal of service that keeps me coming back. Here are my highlights: Appetizer: Calamari -- I can't say enough about this stuff. It's not your typical frozen rings, this stuff is FRESH. They saute large chunks octopus, not just rings or tentacles, in a delicious sauce that has a mild tangy flavor to it. It's then topped with bonito flake, green onion, and a lemon. I could eat calamari appetizers as a meal and walk away satisfied... Stuffed Mushrooms -- Forget everything you know about stuffed mushrooms. Ryo takes large mushrooms, stuffs them with crab meat, tempura batters, and deep fries them. They're then coated with what I think is ponzu sauce for a delicious creation. Nigiri: One of my personal favorites is the zuke tuna. Ryo takes the best cuts of Tuna and marinates them in what I believe to be sesame oil, rice vinegar, and soy sauce, for about three days. The fish changes consistency and flavor, and becomes just ridiculously good. You have to try it. Ryo's fish selection and cuts are the absolute best in Tampa, in my opinion. He hand-selects everything, and he's committed to culinary excellence. You really can't go wrong. Rolls: My personal favorite, although not containing raw fish, is the Cynthia's Vegetable Tempura roll. The kitchen takes asparagus and sweet potatoes, tempura batters, then deep fries them. These scrumptious veggies are then rolled up and served with a side of ponzu sauce. It's HEAVENLY. The spicy tuna is by far the best I've ever had as well. Most restaurants pulverize the tuna or use shoddier quality of fish. Ryo takes his sushi tuna, cubes it, and mixes it with spicy sauce. You don't feel like you're eating some strange mush -- it has consistency, texture, and above all, great flavor. Dessert: I love the green tea ice cream. It's that simple. They also carry "Red Bean" ice cream, but I tend to stay away from that. It's a little too weird for me. For all you non-sushi lovers, they do a delicious cooked salmon and chicken teriyaki. I can't recommend Kaisen Sushi enough, that's plain and simple. If you're a first time sushi-er, or a seasoned expert, stop into Kaisen and prepare to be wowed. They also organize a yearly fishing trip, and I hear a lot of people have had a really good time on these excursions. You'll always see Ryo making sushi, and his Dad and sometimes his wife are there working to keep the place running smoothly. GO! NOW (unless it's Sunday or Monday)! DO IT! :-)

text: I have to agree with another reviewer who requested negative or zero stars. US Airways sucks. Conversely, I have to agree with another 'nother reviewer who compliments them on First Class -- it's the only way I'll ever fly US Air again. I'm switching to Southwest for FF points, where the people actually like their jobs. In a 10 day period in February, I boarded US Air flights 4 times, carrying the same suitcase everytime (when you fly in and out of PHL, you learn to carry on -- baggage handling is a clusterfuck.) The fourth flight, from MCO to PHL, was delayed two hours on the runway (this is when they were still charging $2 for softdrinks), while they searched MCO for a circuit breaker - I am not making this up. You might think a circuit breaker is a basic maintenance item, but no, turned out they had to fly one in from Charlotte! When they started pulling passengers with connecting flights off the plane, I called customer service from my seat and booked a flight for the following morning. I have no idea if that plane ever left MCO that day. Next morning, I arrive for my rescheduled flight to PHL and the surly gate attendant tells me my bag is too big. "Gosh, Mr. Poopy-Pants-underpaid- unhappy-with-life gate attendant," I say, "it fits in the overhead and I've carried it on 4 flights in the past 10 days." "I don't care, it's too big and you're going to have to check it." Mind you, I am extremely sensitive to people carrying oversized bags onto planes -- my BF has a skinny bag that's too tall to fit "wheels in," and takes up 1.5 times the space of my bag in the overhead, but they let him on because it's not more than 9" deep. And what the hell is up with 9"? The overhead opening is at least 14" high. So why the new rule? Duh, so they can charge you for checked bags, of course! But, I digress. I say, "Okay, can I gate-check it down the gangway?" (Remember, I'm flying to the baggage black hole of America, PHL.) "NO," the asshole yells at me, "you'll have to pick it up in the baggage terminal." Yeah, no. So he straps a claim check on it and sends me on my way. Just before boarding, I rip off the claim check, carry my bag onboard and stow it, wheels in, no squishing necessary, tidily in the overhead bin directly above my seat, and we took off 45 minutes late. SO THEN, when we land in PHL (late, BTW) our gate isn't available. Huh? Didn't the pilot tell you we were coming? Weren't we in flight for the past two hours and in radio communication the whole time? Oh, geez, sorry, this other plane is still at the gate, you'll have to find somewhere else to offload your passengers. That added another 40 minutes to the travel time. I wrote a letter to US Air's ombudsman (aka teflonman) who defended both the lack of basic maintenance items and the 9" luggage limitation (he said it's an FAA rule, which, hello, it's not.) And the gate thing, well, he basically gave me the customer service version of "shit happens." So last Thursday, I flew to PHX on business (BTW, packed an even smaller bag than before to avoid any more unpleasantness), a flight I had booked with Amex points on February 6. I couldn't select seats when I booked, but figured I'd do it when I checked-in online. On Wednesday, I checked in and selected a seat. Sunday morning, when I went online to check-in for the return trip, seat selection was not available, so I'd have to do it at the airport. I honestly didn't think anything of it. When I got to the airport and went to the gate, I told the pseudo-cheery (but, I suspect, equally unhappy-with-life) gate attendant that I needed a seat assignment on the flight. Guess what she said? "This flight is oversold, you don't have a seat." WTF? Yeah, apparently, even though your ticket is issued and you have a confirmation number and a ticket number, YOU ARE NOT GUARANTEED A SEAT ON THE FLIGHT! Chirpy-psycho-killer gate attendant helpfully informed me that hardly anybody reads the fine print but it's in there! I did my level best to remain calm until she opened the flight on her Fred Flintstone computer and allowed as how she could give me a middle seat, and I should feel damn lucky with it. That flight took off 30 minutes late, landed on time and, wait for it, the gate wasn't available AGAIN! How do they get away with it? How do they charge your credit card (or in my case, Amex Points account) and not guarantee you a seat? Isn't there a Customer Bill of Rights these assholes have to honor? And you know the ultimate irony? US Airways has the best ontime rating of any airline in PHL or some such nonsense. I can only assume that they're self-reporting, because I haven't left on time on a US Airways flight in 3 years. They build so much fat into their schedule that you sometimes arrive on time, but I've still missed meetings, appointments and social events thanks to their incompetence. And no, it's rarely weather related. I hate US Air.

text: This was a bit of a disappointment. I'd heard good reviews of this place from a couple different travel books, and some friends suggested I try it out, so when I was driving through Santa Barbara I decided to stop in. It's conveniently located right next to the train tracks, so there's plenty of free parking and a lot to do in the vicinity, so that's a bit of a plus. We ordered some of their fresh Alaskan Halibut, served over a bed of ginger rice with a side of veggies, as well as some Miso Sea Bass from their new economy-friendly menu (an entree, soup/salad, and dessert all for a lower price. This was served with a crab cake and some more vegetables. We opted to get soup (clam chowder) and added a baked potato on the side. Dessert was Panna Cotta. The clam chowder came out first, and that was a bad start. I don't know if I've ever had a worse clam chowder...even the canned stuff tastes better. They packed a ton of corn into ours (clam chowder, not corn chowder, chef - there's a big difference), and it didn't taste very much like clams at all. We each had a couple bites before giving up and leaving half of it to waste. The main dishes came out soon after, and while the fish was cooked decently well, the side dishes were really lacking. They were bland, and a lot of the vegetables were overcooked. Really, the best part of the meal was the crab cake, and that's pretty sad. Finally, the Panna Cotta itself was okay, but it was served with strawberries (which looked a bit old) and a balsamic reduction that really didn't go well with it. That being said, the wait staff is friendly and fast, so a positive star for that, but I won't be returning to this restaurant next time I'm in the area.

text: Whenever I travel and hear of a restaurant that's a can't-miss/landmark institution/best [fill in the blank] ever, I get equally optimistic and skeptical - excited that it may indeed be an amazing experience and also concerned that I may be setting myself up for disappointment with unrealistic standards. In the case of Bern's, the experience blew away my expectations. Reservations were made a month before heading to Tampa and despite some initial fears that they may have lost our reservation (since we didn't receive a customary confirmatory phone call a few days before), we were promptly seated without a glitch. (Btw, dress code is semi-formal so a button shirt with slacks is the way to go). Upon entering the foyer, you're struck by the decor - the red lights and walls suggested a bordello but the intricate carvings and details gave it a refined feel. There are separate dining rooms with slightly different decor (we were seated in the "Bronze Room" by the large mirror). The first thing I noticed upon seating was the wine list. Only 181 pages and 1-2" thick. I'm not much of a wine guy but it was a no brainer that I would have to order at least a glass (went with the waiter recommended 2--6 Terra Valentine Cab ($14), which went really well with the steak. The steaks are priced based on cut, thickness and weight and having read earlier reviews, my friend and I were eager to try the 20 oz. Special Chateaubriand for two. Surprisingly, the waiter reported that he would have to check if that was available (and unfortunately he came back and said only 9 oz. cuts were available). So we ordered two separate orders of those ($35 each, which ended up being an incredible bargain). That's because the steak entrees come with french onion soup (delicious), organic salad, baked potato (good, but really way too much), and sides of onion rings and veggies. For good measure, we also ordered a (huge) side of the white truffle mac & cheese (which he emphatically recommended over the foie gras ... wow). OMG, the Special Chateaubriand was perhaps the best piece of steak I've ever had! The Special is dry-aged on the loin for longer than the regular Chateaubriand, resulting in a exterior that's almost resembled jerky but with a juicy, almost buttery interior that just melted. The waiter actually thought we were regulars because apparently not many people order the Special (I have no idea why not ... do they just not read the entire menu and order the first thing?!). We were so completely stuffed (hardly had the baked potato, onion rings and only half of the truffled mac&cheese) that we thought we couldn't possibly eat anymore and were sadly convinced we couldn't check out the separate Harry Waugh Dessert Room. But the waiter suggested he put our name down while we rested and had a tour of the kitchen (huge staff that's like a well-oiled machine) and the amazing wine cellar (~150,000 bottles on site with another MILLION in the nearby warehouse)!! After that, we miraculously discovered we had a little bit of room for at least some cafe con leche ... and the signature macademia nut sundae with hot fudge. I don't have a sweet tooth but this may have been one of the best desserts I've ever had. So yes, I had ridiculously high expectations ... and they were surpassed beyond belief. Put another way, I figured one trip to Tampa in a lifetime is probably more than sufficient. But now, if I happen to find myself anywhere within a two-hour radius from the greater Tampa Bay area, I will not hesitate to go back to Bern's.
label: POS

text: First of all I applaud Joe Edwards for his efforts to continue and make Delmar the best street in all of St Louis to visit. Without his vision and efforts the street and U city would be a dilapidated rundown area and not the the engaging, diverse, and profitable place that it has become over the last 30 years. From Blueberry Hill, the Pageant, Tivoli, Bowling Alley and now Eclipse/Moonlight in addition to the Trolley cars coming soon; the man has pursued his wonderful, funky, eclectic vision for U City to it's fullest. That being said, there is no way that this restaurant deserved any of the awards recently won in the Riverfront Times and Sauce magazine. I give the Eclipse high marks for its interior, but the food is very average. I appreciate the efforts of the Chef to bring in some items that you can't find on most StL menus (bone marrow as example) but the food is lacking in layered levels of flavor. The bone marrow was disappointing, the Trout needed some acidity, the Caesar you could get at any Applebees, and most everything was on the cold side. The service was marginal at best. I did think that the Eclipse bar and the Moonrise bar were both being ran by a mixologist with a subtle but loving hand. I wish I would've enjoyed the food more, but much like the other reviewers I will still return to the Moonrise but I will skip the Eclipse and make my way to the bar. I do hope that it improves because I will always support Joe Edwards and his efforts to grow U-City

text: A great place for an extended stay. In fact, I'm here for 7 more weeks. Its like living at home... but with maid service. My room is HUGE. Its practically a small house. Do note however that there are two sizes of rooms, so get the big one. If you don't, make sure you never see the larger room and you'll probably be happy. Now the room looks a little worn. The staff treats you like their family. Tonight I realized my kitchen was missing the chef's knife that my friend's room had. I called the front desk at 11 PM and together the desk agent and I raided empty rooms until we found the knife I needed to finish dinner. All the hotel rooms are accessible from the three story courtyard pool area, but only after you enter through a heavily fortified, securely locked gate, which is quite reassuring in this hotel-commercial-light industrial (a term I learned from Sim City) area. Not ideal for vacationers for several reasons but mainly because it is in METAIRIE, LA which is just like the suburb you came from - Applebees, Target, Barnes and Noble, etc. Also, you won't find high end sheets or fancy toiletries here. text: I like this venue quite a bit...while it can't free itself from the shackles of Ticketbastard, it does a better job than anybody else in town in similar circumstances. But, there is nothing beer in a giant, novelty guitar-shaped plastic jug can't cure, and I hope they still have those. I don't know how much they cost, and frankly I don't care to know. I recall finding a bathroom easy enough, and other than getting out of the parking garage, I had no real hassles. The venue is a bit of a classic, but like other classic venues (The Troc) it coasts on its own glory (though not as much). Let me put it this way...if a band I liked was coming to town, and I could choose between The Tower, The Troc, The TLA, and The Electric Factory, I'd choose the Tower every single time. text: After a co-worker raved about the all-you-can-eat crab, I decided that I had to check this place out. I went ahead and got the Comps+ card so I could get the deal for $7.77 and headed out on a Friday night. (Without the member's card, the buffet is about $16.) The boyfriend and I got into line about 6:15 PM, and despite the number of people ahead of us, still managed to get into the buffet fairly quickly. The cashier who greeted us was a fun and vibrant lady, but the girl who seated us was dour and tired-looking. She barely said two words to us. While the BF waited on our server (I asked for a glass of water), I went ahead and checked out the food. To say that it was disappointing would be a bit of an understatement. Each "station" only has one or two offerings, and none of them looked particularly appealing. I decided to start with the crab and shrimp, which was the reason why I came in the first place. Unlike the Atlantis, the snow crab was sort of piled haphazardly next to the shrimp under a strange plastic dome. There was a scary, fishy smell coming from under there which almost made me turn away. Still, I didn't want to leave empty handed, so I grabbed a little of both, some cocktail sauce, and returned to the table. While I'd been gone, the waiter brought me iced tea instead of water, which was okay, I guess. The shrimp was warm and rubbery, but didn't taste too bad. The crab legs were thin and wimpy, not the large, robust legs I've seen at other buffets. The meat was also rather dry and salty, so I get the impression that they were overcooked. The boyfriend tried the chicken madeira, which looked appetizing enough. To hear him describe the flavor, however, "It's bland and salty at the same time." After trying a bite, I had to agree. There were no exceptional tastes jumping out at me, and it seemed like the chef thought dumping a whole lot of salt would make up for that. The Mexican station was a near bust; the only decent thing was the Spanish rice, and it still would have been better with the addition of some fresh salsas. The Chinese station was pathetic; undercooked egg rolls, bland fried rice, and I didn't bother with the steamed rice or the chicken stir-fry. There were a couple of cold noodle dishes at the salad station that were okay, and the boyfriend said the pizza slices were edible, if doughy. The linguine with clam sauce tasted like watered down alfredo sauce, the clam chowder was extremely thin but surprisingly tasty, and the seafood dish with penne pasta was all right, but I found a bone in one of the fish chunks. (Though, I guess that's bound to happen, sometimes.) The supposed "steamed" veggies were drowning in butter, and the roasted red potatoes were too salty. By the time we were finished wading through that nonsense, neither of us really felt like dessert. (In fact, I got an upset stomach a little after eating the crab and shrimp. It wasn't bad enough for me to think of it as food poisoning, or anything, but it does make me a little leery to go back.) For $7.77, I guess it's not so bad, but I wouldn't pay a dollar more for this fare. Charging $16 for it normally is a rip-off! For shame, Grand Sierra.

text: Yes, it's a bit of a haul. Every time I head out west to Wiethop, I feel like I'm in the country. But even though it's certainly out of my way, it's a fabulous place to visit if you're up for some gardening. I've made the trip to Wiethop six or seven times since mid-April. That first trip, I was astounded by the size of the greenhouses, just filled to the brim with colorful flowering annuals, hanging baskets and overflowing prearranged pots. Wiethop also has another greenhouse devoted completely to perennials. After the cold, grey winter months, just stepping into the greenhouses' riot of color was restorative to my soul and inspiring. I helped my mother-in-law plant her flowers. I helped her sister. I moved on to Justin's offices. And then finally, FINALLY, we bought our house and had our own yard to plant. Unfortunately, buying a house meant I was also out of money, so I had to exercise extreme restraint on my last trip out to Wiethop. Luckily, their prices aren't exorbitant and if you're willing to forgo some blooms this year, you can buy starter perennials for far less than the grown up flowering ones. So I had to exercise restraint AND have patience. This home-owning stuff is really turning me into a grown up... If you're looking for trees and shrubs, you won't find them here, but for your annuals, perennials and vegetables, Wiethop is a great choice. You can always head next door to Sherwood Gardens for the shrubs and such afterward. Parking can be rough, especially on nice sunny afternoons, but Wiethop opens up early--take advantage of their hours if you don't feel like waiting for a spot and standing in line at check out!

text: In honor of Thanksgiving it's time to review a turkey. And this is a turkey that commits complete and utter sacrilege to BBQ! My First Friday crew and I chose Q as our after gathering because it Olde City was so packed to the brim that it was the only spot that we could find a place to sit down for drinks and food. the wooden decor looked promising, it had a decent TV setup for watching sports, and the thought of eating some delectable barbecue became quite enticing. But in the end it was just plain awful food wise. When it comes to ordering BBQ, pulled pork and mac & cheese are usually the go to staple for me. I generally find that you can tell a lot about how a BBQ joint prepares their food by the effort that they put into their pulled pork (a good pulled pork recipe involves some serious preparation after all!). And when it came down to it Q's pulled pork sandwich was just complete and total blasphemy! When I wasn't biting into bland and overcooked pieces of pork, I was biting into fat and gristle. Rather than bring out the BBQ flavor that usually screams epic taste, it felt like they were liberally using the sauce to cover up the horrible quality of the pork. And for the extra kicker, they put coleslaw on top to add another disaster onto the mess. Who does that? I'd comment further on the mac & cheese, but honestly it was just pretty uninspiring. I'm tempted to give one star for the shameful disgrace of BBQ. but it did have well rounded drink selection. They had a seasonal Flying Fish on tap, and a good selection of Tequila (at least they got part of their name right!). and the margarita selection did look pretty delectable and reasonably priced. But while it did have some pluses, I do have a hard time taking a places that horribly butchers half of it's namesake seriously.

text: Disgusting, reasonably priced sushi. The fuku fries saved them from a one star. So a friend of mine who goes to the university in Tucson recommended this place to me a while back. We decided to share an order of Fuku Fries (shoe string fries that had a hint of wasabi and sriachi ketchup). We also shared the las vegas roll (imitation crab meat, salmon, cream cheese that is deep fried and drizzled with ell sauce), fried california roll, spicy tuna roll (spicy tuna with cucumber), and the spider roll (cucumber, avocado, crab mix, lettuce, and soft shell crab). We also ordered the green tea. The tea was nice and fragrant. Then apparently the order came with a bowl of miso soup and a salad with some type of thick and tart homemade dressing. Both were ok and the fries came soon after. We barely tasted the wasabi on the fries but we definitely tasted the sriachi. This was possibly the best thing we ordered. Then the food arrived. Every roll was pleasing to the eye and smelled just as good...and every bite was just as gross. First, fuku doesn't know how to prepare proper sushi rice. It was too soggy and not very flavorful which confused the hell out of me. The las vegas roll was unappealing but then again I don't normally enjoy cream cheese in my sushi. The spicy tuna didn't taste very fresh. Furthermore, the deep fried california left an aftertaste that aroused a desire to brush my teeth. The spider roll was the best roll of the night. The atmosphere was great. The black and white interior translated to an elegant yet modern vibe. I love the shirts that they have too. The service was ok. The food either arrived quickly or rather slowly. In short: The sushi was beyond disappointing, the fries are a must, the service and atmosphere were great, The price would have been reasonable had the sushi been decent, I'm not going to return and advise that you do likewise.

text: We ran across this place while looking for a bar to start off our weekend. All the bars in the area seem to be closed at 11 (WTH). But we were wondering what's the big fuss going on with a big group of ppl at this burrito joint (since I'm a sucker for mexican food), so we decided to be noisey and walked in. The only thing that caught my eye was their guacamole and huge nachos. We decided to try it even though we weren't hungry. The line was pretty long but it moves hella fast, so fast that I couldn't even get my order together before they called NEXT!!! The prices are a little pricier then most mexican joints but I personally think its worth it because their stuff is pretty fresh. I don't feel grossed out eating such a heavy meal at 11 at night. It wasn't as greasy as most places. They serve beer there on tap but stop serving at 11. That's just wrong!!! Anyways, beaware of all the drunken college kids at night though. Apparently its a place to go when you get the munchies. 90% of them are drunk. It was pretty hilarious seeing these girls trying to eat while being extremely intoxicated. Good food but don't care for the crowd.

text: My girlfriends and I tried Van Goghz for the first time last weekend and had a pretty nice time. The bartender was nice and the martinis were delicious. So we decided to go back this past weekend and take some other friends with us. WORST. IDEA. EVER. Although the waitress was pleasant and polite, she was terrible at the actual "service" part of the job. Drinks took forever and she didn't seem to feel the least bit apologetic that they were short on ingredients in the kitchen to make about half of the items on the menu. The food came out one person at a time (we had 8 people) and the drinks were 20-30 minute waits each. Then she lost my debit card - and probably out of fear for her job, denied ever getting my card and accused me of lying about giving it to her in the first place. I had no other form of payment so I was trying to work something out with the bar manager. She was nice, by the way, although at a complete loss as to how to help me. The owner would not come out from her office or the kitchen or wherever she was and told the manager to just deal with me. I was surprisingly calm despite the terrible service and just wanted my card to be found so I could pay and be on my way to another place. After trying to work things out for well over an hour (after waiting an hour to get our tabs in the first place), I decided to just leave - something the bar manager said ok to, not something I just did to skip out on my tab. Turns out the owner who was hiding in the back called the police and tried to have me arrested over my $80 tab. The cops were super friendly and probably quite relieved to realize their "problem" was a 29 year old professional, sober woman and not some drunk bar fly. The owner might have known this if she had ever come out of her hiding spot. They obviously let me go with the promise that I would come back and pay my tab within three days. I will go back to avoid having a warrant out for my arrest, however this is the absolute worst $80 I've EVER spent. Word of mouth can make or break a business...and I have a big mouth. This bar lost a lot of business Saturday night. UPDATE: Two days later I had a conversation with the other bar owner when I want back to pay my outstanding tab and avoid being arrested for theft. She was truly pleasant, sincerely apologetic, comped my tab from Saturday and offered very good incentives for me to give the bar another chance. That has still not been decided because any business I give them puts money in the "silent" partner's pocket, but I appreciated the kindess from Ginger, the free pizza she sent me home with and the genuine apology. She seems to understand how to run a business as did her bartenders. If only the other owner were the same...
label: NEG

text: The hostess was very friendly. That was the high point. First, contrary to folk rumor, Ted Nugent is not the owner. I ordered a chicken cordon bleu sandwich in keeping with the rich French culinary tradition of the Montanic people. The chicken, cheese, and ham were tasty. However the bun was coated with an ambiguous oil. While this did make swallowing easier, it rendered the sandwich too slippery to handle with anything but a knife and fork. A friend ordered the pot roast which I tried and found to be tender but a bit bland. I also sampled a few bison dishes: pretty good! Verdict: unless you have some vendetta against bison save the trip to Ted's for when they have one of these tucked in between the Macaroni Grill and the Olive Garden (I'd give it 6 to 12 months). text: A couple years ago, I went to see ON THE RECORD at the Academy of Music. At the time, it was the new Disney musical featuring eight cast members who, throughout one recording session during which they only sing Disney songs, - note: no dialogue - they fall in love, are jilted and reconcile by the curtain's fall. Let the "record" show hat I received comp tickets and originally had no intention of seeing this production. So, the four sordid lovers enter the recording studio. Singer 1 and 2, the mature actors, seemingly share a romantic past, the epicenter of which I can only imagine is that they lost a child together and their relationship couldn't handle the strain of mourning thereafter as both 1 and 2 got teary-eyed at "Baby Mine" from Dumbo. Maybe that's too deep. Maybe there was a freak circus accident. Lovers 3 and 4, young starry-eyed idiot girl and motorcycle riding leather-clad boy meet, fall in love, have a fight, and fall back in love. No dialogue, people. You can't imagine how many melodramatic gestures, "thumbs up" and glaring looks flew across that stage. There are four other characters in the show. Let's call them the back-up singers. The back-up singers generally move the set and dance while doing it to make it look like they are having fun. They are not having fun. Moving the set is never fun. So, our back-up singers, like the four lovers, are clad entirely in black. Everyone in the show is decently covered in pants, or even a knee-length skirt... ...all except for our two female back-up singers who have knee-high high-heel vinyl boots and pleated skirts that barely cover their backsides. It was Disney does Dallas up there. Here I am, thinking of all of the children in the audience who so idolize these women on stage - and the women are dressed like high-end street walkers. No. Not even high end. If there were a pole onstage, I would've been confused about my surroundings: S&M club or Academy of Music? There was no reason for it. The skirts could have easily been six inches longer and still been above the knee. So, my question to Disney: what are you trying to sell? Isn't it enough that you kill off every mother of a princess so that she grows up in a single parent home? Or that all the princesses up until say, Belle, were fairly vapid and let's face it, illiterate? Isn' t it enough that any female Disney character over thirty is automatically the villain? Or that every princess' proportions are absolutely ludicrous - riiiiight, Pocohontas..... Apparently not. "'Someday my prince will come' and he'll assume I'm available and up for anything with this skirt that reveals my ass when I bend over." So ends my rant. I have no problem with high boots. I own my fair share, but do we need them onstage in a "children's" musical? My mission this week: educate my students on the objectification of women.
label: NEG

text: Ventured to New Hope last night to check out the new Vegan restaurant. Really enjoyed it. Jeez, if someone cooked for me like that ALL the time I could easily become vegan or at least vegetarian - until the grips of a steak or bacon craving got to me of course! In any case, even as a Carnivore one can totally enjoy the food at Sprig & Vine. Please check out the photos I posted - you're going to want to come try these dishes for yourself (since you can't scratch & sniff the pictures). Tried something from each course & the only thing I wasn't wild about were the side of greens. They were good, just not for me, but my friend liked them. Liked the artichokes A LOT - kind of wanted to lick the plate (for real, but I didn't). Enjoyed the risotto cakes too. The Olive Oil cake sounds kinda of weird but DOES NOT taste kinda of weird. It was yummy. The atmosphere was comfortable & the service was impeccable. Colin was friendly & knowledgeable & gave us lots of time to enjoy our meal. Get there NOW before it gets too crowded. Soon, as more people discover Sprig & Vine, this place is going to be booked solid.

text: Pat's apparently is well known across ... well, everywhere. If you want to experience a touristy steak, feel free. If you want a great steak, stay far away. The meat itself is fine, if mass produced. Unlike quite a few other places, Pat's has a huge hunk of meat cooking at any time. The problem I found is that the steaks sure seem mass produced. If I get a provolone wit, I'm going to get decent meat, but unmelted cheese and rather sad onions on a rather small roll. For the same price, I can go to John's (or even Tony Luke's) and get a much more appetizing, and more bigger, steak. The choice for me was simple.
label: NEG

text: Seriously, who needs therapy when there are pralines this good in the world? Depressed? Down? Need a little cheer in your life? Then get down to Butler's Run on Second Avenue and add some sugared sunshine to your day. The gooey goodness comes in many varieties at Leon's. Of course, there are your traditional nut-based pralines, like almond, cashew and pecan. Then there are some more of the unique flavors owner Leon Vlahos invented himself, such as the Jack Daniel's, Kentucky Bourbon and Amaretto praline varieties. And the candy contentment extends beyond pralines, such as chocolate turtles, English toffees and caramel pecan rolls thrown into the mix. Need an extra large helping of treat therapy? Try one of Leon's Mix Tins with a little bit of everything thrown in. Trust me - this is one of the few times it's ok to medicate on your own.

The sandwiches, burgers, etc. were nothing special. They had a small and rather expensive list of beers. However, it does also have some historical significance,as the Inn has been there since the early 1900s and has been visited by some famous people. Overall, the food was decent and seemed like a fun, sports bar minded and family friendly environment as well. So if you're in the area, I would give it a try but would not necessarily go out of my way to find it.

text: So... I went to St. Petersburg for a best-friend's wedding this past weekend. We spent three consecutive nights partying at the Undertow. Why such a bad review? Lets get into it. Thursday - Things were awesome on the first night, very efficient bar tenders, reasonably priced drinks, and the location was superb, it's right on the beach. I also saw one of the drunkest drunks I have seen in years. A cowboyish weirdo stumbled into a wall heading towards the bathroom, then he turned around and headed back towards the direction he came from and projectile vomited in a plant. BTW, projectile vomiting is real (I thought it was just an exaggerated joke). Thursday night verdict, two thumbs up. Friday - We were invited to crash the bride's bachelorette party, and after some debate, we decided that if the bachelorette's needed the groomsmen to entertain, it was our duty to ensure entertainment mayhem. We showed up, full-throttle, danced, partied hard, and made a few local friends. The ladies enjoyed themselves immensely; I on the other hand had a peculiar event take place. It started with me ordering a red-bull, just a red-bull, and no vodka. As I loving drank from sweet can of energy, I was summoned to the dance floor to make some moves, so I rested the can on a nearby bar. A couple vigorous dance moves later, I felt parched. I returned my half-full can of red-bull and took a large draw. As the sweet sweet nectar of the Gods fell down my throat pipe, I sensed something was wrong, then it hit me like a cow, someone tossed a cigarette in my drink. I quickly ran towards the only place I knew I could make a mess, the plant my cowboyish friend vomited in the previous night. I spewed. Projectile vomiting is indeed real, and it was re-confirmed in a flowing celebration of red-bull, cigarette butts, and my massive seafood dinner. Needless to say, we had a decent time. Saturday - After being a groomsmen for the first time for the most bangingest beach wedding ever, we happily returned, yet again, to the Undertow. A flurry of sexiness showed up at the bar ready to kick it, hard, wearing wedding clothes, funny hats, and sunglasses, and of course we were toting around a newly wed couple in mildly formal clothing. Although I was flamboyantly accessorized, I felt it was my duty as member of the groom's party, to bring along one necessary item... the remains of the newly wed's three-tiered wedding cake. I proudly walked to our area of the bar, wedding cake in hand, and within moments, as expected, the cake-fight began. Soon enough, after security had us surrender the remaining bits of cake, we returned to a somber evening of raging dirty dancing. We closed the place down for the third night in a row, but it was not by on our own accord, we were thrown out by the assholeiest bouncer in the history of the bouncing world. I don't know where this guy got his bachelors degree in bouncing, but it most likely was not a reputable bouncing academy. Anyways, the next few events lead to my 1 star review for the Undertow. It was the end of the night and we were settling up our tabs for our departure. As we were ready to leave, the bouncer came over to us and tells the groom that we need to leave and the bar is closing, to which the groom replied, "okay, just give us a second." Then, as if the bouncer had eaten a hot tamale or been bitten by rattle snake, he turns red, and in a matter of milliseconds, totally looses his cool and barks at the top of his lungs, "I TOLD YOU TO GET THE F-CK OUT OF HERE." Side note, I have never heard anyone scream as loud as this dude. He was not only extremely heated, but he was super vocal and animated with his ejection techniques. It was like an albino gorilla flinging poop around while screaming vivaciously. This screaming in the groom's face was not taken lightly by our wolf pack, and so our military friend jumped in and said, "chill out." Which only fueled his extreme grumpiness. Within minutes, all of the other bouncers, management, and bar tenders surrounded us. They all told us to get the hell out. Both armies faced. We rounded up our party, screamed back some choice obscenities, and explained that they should not treat "good" customers such as ourselves with such disrespect, especially after throwing tons of money at them for 3 consecutive days. Anyways, I threatened them that I would yelp about it. In conclusion, place is great, but everyone that works there sucks.
label: NEG

text: First impression: we were packed in like sardines, so my neighbor was practically in my lap. At one point she actually leaned over and commented on my partner's dish, which I think was just an effort to diffuse the awkwardness of our seating situation. The chips and salsa were good (as confirmed by my Mexican partner) but only the first basket is complimentary so don't get too carried away. My house margarita was unusually orange but very good--I think they use fresh juices. For dinner it looked like they had some good veggie options, and I was going to go with the burrito but then saw "chorizo salsa". I asked the waitress to leave that off, and she told me that the rice is made with chicken stock. Rather than stick with a salsa-less, rice-less burrito I switched to a veggie quesadilla. I was surprised at the portion size, the quesadilla was actually made from two taco-sized tortillas quartered. This was OK for me but I would expect more (especially considering it was over $10). The veggies were perfectly done. My partner got tilapia and shrimp over angel-hair pasta, which was HUGE. He said the fish was well-seasoned but the shrimp, not so much. I don't know, I'm just not that impressed. I know Mexican is difficult to find in this city but you're better off looking elsewhere... unless maybe you already payed for parking.
label: NEG

text: This is my husband's and my favorite restaurant. We even had our wedding catering based off of their menu. Great food at a good price. If you love Garlic & Garlic bread, this is it. You get unlimited bread and it's not the kind of bread that you would think would be unlimited, it's San Luis sourdough and it's loaded with parm and garlic. The meals are all a good portioned size and exactly what they promise on the menu, as well as the desserts. We love the Tri Formaggio, Cortina, and Genoa. For dessert my favorites are Chocolate flour-less cake with Raspberry sauce and creme brulee, nothing is super special about these desserts but they are both well done. If you want upper-level casual and fun on any given night this is the place to go.

text: I went to Smith's yesterday and I'm convinced that it is the worst place ever. EVER. Ok, granted everyone and their mother was there watching the Phillies playoff game. But I have been in much busier bars where the bartenders and waitstaff hustle to get done what needs to be done as quickly as they can. I walked into the place and went straight to the bar to order a drink for my fiance and I. Simple stuff --- a lager and a Bud Light bottle. I was standing in a sea of Phillies fans, but only about one person back from the bar. The bartender could clearly see me at the time, but was too busy serving about 20 beers to some dude who was passing them back to his friends. Ok, FINE. Thing is, though, she was serving them with the quickness of a sloth on valium. Finally, 20-beers guy gets all of his beers to all of his friends and I start to have high hopes that I'm next to be served. She completely turned away from me and sauntered over to the other part of the bar to wait on some other guy... and then another guy... and then ANOTHER guy. I finally gave up and one of my fiance's friends sucked it up and waited in the cluster of people and got us drinks from the slowest bartender on the planet. After that first beer, I wanted another so I decided to attempt the whole song and dance again. Same deal, only I stood on the other side of the bar right in front of the cash register. I figured, "Hey. She's gotta put the money in the thing so she HAS to see me." Same deal all over again. She completely passed over me and waited on guy after guy after guy with the motivation of a tree slug on heroin until finally, I got fed up and I needed my booze and had to resort to getting her attention by yelling, "HEY! I have been standing here FOREVER and all I need is a lager and a Bud Light bottle." To which she responded after she looked up at me with the attentiveness of a turtle on 50 vicodan and a whiskey chaser, "A lager and a whaaaaaaaaat????????" ARGH. *NEVER AGAIN*

text: The IMA's collection rests on its chief benefactors, namely the Clowes, Lilly, Marmon and Pantzer families and their differing collecting tastes. While Indianapolis is a relatively old Midwestern city, the IMA's history is recent; it was known as the "Art Association" until 1969. The recent multi-year renovation, redevelopment and expansion of the Museum and grounds created an entirely new experience for art patrons. Let's all say our condolences to the Krannert Pavilion's Brutalist architecture of the 1970s and hello to a somewhat uninspired series of camera-ready atria that will no doubt allow some very impressive parties. The collection itself is conservative and unprovoking. Highlights include Robert Indiana's iconic masterwork (and trademark-infringed) "LOVE" painting and sculpture, a beautifully painted though incredibly ill-placed Rembrandt, a decent Hopper, an encyclopedic Asian art collection that is one of the best in the country, and the largest collection of JMW Turner drawings outside of Great Britain (although quantity does not trump quality). I thought the gift shop was as poorly stocked as the previous one. Not a single postcard of the new museum's exterior, yet there were plenty of old postcards showing the now-demolished Krannert Pavilion. And for an artwork that's been copied, dubiously appropriated and downright stolen, why was there not one postcard available of Robert Indiana's outdoor "LOVE" sculpture? And what about museum merchandise based off its own artwork: scarves with motif from the museum's Tiffany piece, jewelry pieces mimicking something from the Asian galleries or pop-up note cards laser-cut with the new museum facade? Sure, all the "LOVE" stuff is nice, but capitalize on other museum strengths. This is a wonderful museum that has a decent collection. The parking is free, the new eating options are terrific, and there are other fun attractions on the museum grounds, most notably the Lilly estate, Oldfields.

text: I finally got out here after missing the UYE get together. Now I wished I'd gone. I"m sure it would have been a blast. Sweet Lucy's is situated in the middle of a bunch of warehouses/industrial type area in NE Philly. It has a nice wide open space with plenty of seating and I believe if memory serves a fair amount of brick. There are several plasma/flat screens on the wall for your TV viewing pleasure. And they had some newer type country/western playing on the stereo while I was there. I ordered the 2 meat combo platter with pulled pork and beef brisket. I got the mac and cheese and the garlic mashed potatoes as my sides. I barely had time to fill up my cup with lemonade before my order popped out. The pulled pork was as several others have alluded to, really really really really good. It didn't need any sauce on it at all. The beef brisket was nice and tender and had a nice vinegar tang to it. Unfortunately I couldn't taste a lot of smoke/hickory in it. A little BBQ sauce paired with it well and gave it added flavor. The BBQ sauce was tangy and sweet, which i liked. The mac and cheese was nice and creamy but it had some nice crunchy bits in it too. The garlic mashed potatoes were pretty decent, though some of it wasn't as mashed as it should have been. The gravy was a little watery for my taste however. It didn't taste bad, but I didn't like the consistency. The coleslaw that came with it had some crunch to it, but had no bite to it. It needed some more pepper and/or some onions. While I can't say this was the best BBQ I've ever had, it was definitely good overall. I'll be back to try the pulled BBQ chicken and kielbasa. BTW Lulu, I do have possession of my wits, thank you very much.

text: So, I woke in January of 2009 weighing in at 240 pounds and being miserable. I moved back to Philly for a month to focus on getting healthy while I found my next job after working on a successful Presidential campaign. I almost signed up for a month of hot yoga but at the last emailed Lauren and decided to take the Feb 2009 immersion class. From the moment I walked into the studio, I knew I was in the right place. No one made be feel bad for how I looked or that I was awfully out of shape. Quite the opposite. It was like the whole team cheered me on as I went from immersion to full on classes. When I started, my body was in shock. I hadn't worked out since college sports and I hid in oversized campaign shirts during my workouts. But, as one month turned into another, I began to come to Lithe almost everyday, and sometimes twice. My body began to love me, and next thing I knew the weight began falling off my body. Because of Lithe, I have lost 80 pounds, and what's better- I don't have any saggy skin or other things that happen when you lose weight. I have muscle tone, a high metabolism, and a love for working out. If you need to get in shape, stay in shape, lose a lot of weight, or just a little- come to Lithe. text: The Arch is quite an experience. It just looks kinda cool from afar, but when you get up close it's really impressive. You just don't see the magnitude until you're at the base. A warning: the tram you ride up in is very small and a bit rickety. Once you get to the top, though, the ride is worth it. The St. Louis skyline itself itsn't all that exciting to look at (unless you've lived there & know what all the buildings are) nor is East St. Louis, but it's just cool to be 630 feet up in the air looking down at everything. One time I went up in the Arch, it had snowed outside so everything was covered in white - it was quite pretty. The most recent time I went up, it was a very clear day with blue skies and we had a great aerial view of the brand-new Busch Stadium. The museum underneath the Arch is kind of neat, and it's free, so check it out while you're there. You can also get tickets to a movie about the Arch construction and for a riverboat ride down the Mississippi, but I haven't experienced either of those attractions yet. If you're visiting St. Louis, the Arch should be on your agenda. You won't forget it.

It has a corporate-esque look but it is complemented by tons of soft natural light and a cozy fire place. They also have a nice patio in front and in back. I spent almost $12 for a Capri breakfast panini and latte, which is too much. But, it was fresh and yummy (diced tomatoes, scrambled eggs, pesto, and mozzarella on an absolutely delicious rosemary olive bread). Overall, the menu is limited and pricey. They have fresh and yummy sandwich and salad choices and they are known for their beignets (overrated). They also serve handcrafted beers for $4 and PBR $2 and happy hours with $1 off bottled beer. They serve up a variety of nightly entertainment, including live music, Tenacious Trivia, etc. I won't be a regular because I know I can get so much more for so much less elsewhere, but I will be back.

text: Oh, SEPTA. I ride you all the time. The pee smell and messy stations, I don't care about. That's just something you get when you ride the subway. What really drives me up the wall is the two-tiered fare system, where you pay more or less depending on your access to tokens. This is just WRONG, especially since token machines are present in tourist areas and near universities but absent in stations where the majority of people actually live in the city full-time. I know in theory you can get tokens at stores around the city, but I lived near Broad and Snyder for three years, and was able to buy tokens at the Rite Aid at that corner not more than ten times. At one point I asked when they got tokens in, and the manager said SEPTA delivered them at random times, and they never knew when they were going to get more. Really, SEPTA? Really? Someone below mentioned that SEPTA is not too bad because it has extensive service to the suburbs. Well, the vast majority of people who ride SEPTA are using it to get around in the city, but the suburban transit (in my experience, I don't usually go out there) is better, more efficient and reliable than intra-city transit. This is a flaw in the system, not a plus. SEPTA needs to serve the majority of its patrons better, not a few of its patrons really well. A few more things: 1) Why can't the people in the booth give me change or sell me a god damn token? What do they do except roll their eyes and go on strike every few years? 2) Sometimes buses just don't stop. For no apparent reason. At Olney. When there are twenty people waiting. 3) The signage in all the stations is horrible. This is true of all subway and surface lines and regional rail 4) "we're getting there": most appropriate and hilarious slogan ever.

Will definitely be back to try some more of the many suggestions he gave me. For food, the best (only?) vegetarian option is the Fried Green Tomato and Burrata Po Boy. We started with the hush puppies which were flavorful and perfectly done. (Oddly, the savory hush puppies were served with a blueberry jam. Both were good, but they did not go together well.) text: Mixed feelings re: this hotel. Positives: great location - you can walk to food, shopping, beach, etc. nice extras - nice free breakfast in the morning and free tea in the afternoon and free coffee in the evening. the breakfast pastries are not great, but hey, it's free. the waffle maker is a plus. Negatives: very noisy - we were in a room perpendicular to state street but it was SO loud we could hear everything. and the noise did not stop until around 2am each night. if you're looking for a relaxing hotel, this is not it. it's great if you want to be part of the drinking/partying action. even with ear plugs in, I could hear the drumming and music from the street. small rooms - we got the standard queen bed and it was a very very small room. just enough space for the bed and table. very small for $189/night on the weekend. but perhaps that's the going rate in SB. potentially not clean rooms- this is one of the reason's I'm giving this place a 2. I noticed that each night I was there, I'd wake up with really red eyes, which would go away when I left the room during they day, but would inevitably reappear after spending a night in the room. I'm certain I'm allergic to something in the room. I asked the front desk if they had pets or smoking in the room in the past, or if they don't clean their comforters for each guest. They told me no pets, no smoking, and that the comforter was cleaned before we got the room. They didn't offer to do anything about it. Perhaps it is true, but I know I've never had an allergic reaction to any other hotels I've stayed at, and the worn quality of the comforter made me question its cleanliness (worrying if I'm reacting to dust mites, etc.). This is not a complaint against the cleaning ladies - they did a great job cleaning the place every day. Just a little irritated with the lack of attention received from the front desk regarding this complaint (i.e., they did nothing). Also surprised that the hotel doesn't provide lotion in the bathrooms. Perhaps I've been too pampered at other hotels, but I just expect hotels to make you feel comfortable, rather than concerned about its potential lack of cleanliness. So overall, location is a 5, but noise, small rooms, and lack of cleanliness brought it down to a 3. and lack of care from the front desk re: my complaint bring it down to a 2.

text: In a word, our experience at Koo Zee Doo was "bizarre." Like other people we were recommended to go there and heard that it is "family style." Apparently the waitress is not familiar with what family style actually is. It is a common practice all around the world, except of course in the grand U.S. of A., where a table of lets say 4 people order 1 or 2 entrees which is then shared amongst the people at the table (think Maggiano's). At Koo Zee Doo however, at least according to our waitress, family style just means you share everything but it is expected that each person order their own dish. You see, when the three of us arrived (one average build male and two slender females) the waitress warned/suggested to us several times (when I say several it was at least 4 times) that for the 3 of us will need to order at least 2 appetizers as well as 2-3 entrees. When we then ordered 2 soups and a salad for appetizers and 1 entree she again warned us that it won't be enough food and the chef does not like having to cook at different times if we were to decide to order a second entree later. Also, when she went over the menu she told us that soups are individual, but salads and entradas are shared. When the soup was brought to the table we only received 1 even though we said that we were ordering one for each of the women. You might think that this pushy ordering was an effort to get us out, but it was only 8pm and when we were ready to leave the waitress asked us 5 times if we wanted dessert...each time we politely asked just for the bill. The other strange thing...I was warned that it was a BYOB, however I did not realize it is actually a byo-any beverage. They only have water and a single flavor Portuguese orange/tangerine soda. PS: the entree with our appetizers was more than enough for the three of us. The food was decent, but not worth a trip back to be bossed around. PSS: As if all the bizarre treatment wasnt' enough...we also had to send our bread back because there was a nice long black hair dancing between our rolls.

text: I cannot believe I am giving a restaurant one star, but here it is. We were visiting Nola for the holidays, and got a recommendation for Luke from our concierge. This is the unfortunate story of our dinner there. First, we had reservations, and were seated promptly. Our server took a few minutes to get to us, but ok - they were full. No problem. We ordered drinks, then he ducked away as we were going to ask questions about the menu. Ok, again, it was busy. The drinks arrived promptly, and we got water, and were able to ask a few questions about the menu, which is honestly pretty poorly explained. For example, the menu lists an item called "shrimp en cocotte" - we asked what that meant, and he didn't answer - just repeated what the menu said. We ordered said shrimp dish, and I ordered the "entrecote" (ribeye), and a bowl of soup. The soup came immediately, Matzo ball chicken, and it was great - peppery, not too salty, nice texture to the Matzo ball. So far, so good. At this point, looking around, I realized that our server had all the tables in the front two thirds of the place. He was running his butt off, admittedly, but virtually no one else was helping him out. There were a couple of food runners, but they were only coming out of the kitchen to bring food to tables - nothing else. So then our entrees arrive. My steak looked delicious, but there were no fries. And clearly, the dish is "entrecote and frites" on the menu. The food runner disappeared so fast, though, that he didn't hear me calling after him. I also had only the butter knife, and try though I might, it didn't get through the steak well. My guy started in on his shrimp right away, and it was great. Shrimp were tender, perfectly cooked, and the grits were phenomenal. It was literally three or four minutes before ANY server, of any variety, passed anywhere near our table, and I could ask for fries and a steak knife. I did get both, at last, and the fries were tasty, but not freshly cooked. For a $25 entree, you have got to be kidding me. The steak was very flavorful, though, and prepared medium rare as requested. And this is when it got bad. I can forgive errors in the kitchen, or a food runner bringing out the wrong thing. But we sat for over 20 minutes after we had finished our dishes, napkins on the plates, empty water glasses too, without seeing our server. Or actually, we saw him plenty. He was hustling, even took the orders of tables right next to us, and pointedly avoided looking at our table so he wouldn't have to deal with our empty dishes and need for further service. All the time waiting, with nothing to eat or drink, gave me the opportunity to look around. At some point, I noticed that the tables in the front third of the restaurant had bread rolls and butter, but NONE of the tables in the second third (where we were seated) did. Odd. Maybe bread rolls are only provided to half of the patrons. I never figured it out, but literally the whole time we were there, all five tables that I could see in our section didn't get bread. But I saw it being taken to the front tables. Finally, finally, the guy came over and apologized for neglecting us, and actually said he had been stuck with a table. Only, he hadn't, because I had been watching him for the past 15 minutes. Yes, our server was moving, but the place was ridiculously understaffed. Except for the three, yes THREE, hosts who they had on duty. What restaurant needs three hosts? It was so frustrating to see them literally standing around doing nothing while things were not getting done in the restaurant. Anyway, no matter how good the food is, terrible service ruins a meal. I really had been looking forward to dessert, but there was no way I was giving them more of my money, or spending more time there. This place is so horribly mismanaged that no one should waste there money there, even if the chef is a James Beard award winner. He clearly has nothing to do with this place anymore. And yes, we still tipped over 15%. We just can't ever short-change someone in the service industry. But this place does not deserve your money. Don't go.

text: After my harsh writeup, and taking another jab during my Old Granite Street Eatery review, I realized I haven't been fair to 275 Hill, a restaurant. Sure, the food on the brunch visit was disgusting and a solid indication of what the rest of the menu had in store, but before I completely dismissed the place shouldn't I try dinner? According to some, that's when 275 Hill really shines. Besides, brunch is for amateurs and nursing hangovers. If you're going to evaluate a restaurant, you ought to do it during their prime time. So, I went to 275 Hill for dinner. I'll spare you the suspense: it was just as terrible as brunch. In fact, it was worse, and further showcased everything wrong with 275 Hill. Let's start with the chef. In each convoluted, adjective-loaded summary on the "chef driven" menu, it's made painfully clear he's in charge. The chef chooses the vegetables; the chef blends the wild mushrooms and goat cheese; the chef offers a prix fixe menu without calling it a prix fixe menu (because that might intimidate us simple Reno folk, right?), instead dubbing it "Chef's Table". Chef, chef, chef, chef, chef. Oh, you mean the guy in the denim coat, strutting around the dining room with a bluetooth headset in his ear? You mean the guy sitting in the back lot during service, smoking a cigarette for would-be customers to see and later recognize as he undoubtedly parades through the dining room again? You mean the guy who sent out that undercooked risotto and those beef-and-cheese filled shells of disappointment? Yeah; I don't like that guy. I don't like the chef at 275 Hill because, judging from his food and demeanor, he could care less about me or anyone else who makes the mistake of eating in his establishment. From the plating to the flavor, it's clear the chef doesn't like you. In the kitchen, as he chats on his bluetooth, feigning enthusiasm over his "craft", he probably thinks you're unworthy of his offerings, and as he scowls past you (while you're trying to make sense of the dish in front of you), he probably wants you to leave. Two insipid cocktails, a faux elk dish, empanadas that truly are madness (Who would serve or charge nearly ten dollars for those things? Only a mad man.), and fifty dollars later, I obliged him. Everything about 275 Hill -- from the plastic 3M hangers on the bathroom doors to the mismatched plates to the cheap glass-wear -- is a joke. When considering the quality of the food and drinks, the prices are offensive. The food itself, made by a domineering chef, well, I wouldn't wish it upon my worst enemy. If you consider 275 Hill to be a worthwhile place to spend your time and money I pity you. I won't be going back.

text: Some suburban shopping centers are chock full of C-list chains that boast dumb names and list franchising information as a featured link on their websites. The food court area of the Goleta Marketplace fits right into this trap, so you might justifiably step into Gina's Pizza with some trepidation. But don't let the pictures of Italy and a bevy of healthy houseplants trick you into letting your guard down, man! This pizza is flat-out bad. It hurt my feelings. The crust is thick and hard, presumably pre-made off-site, and clearly inferior to if they had put the toppings onto French bread or a Boboli. The cheese is rubbery and not particularly flavorful, and though I'd like to provide an assessment of the sauce, there was not much sauce to speak of on my pie. Places you can find better pizza: *Any major or somewhat major city in the United States or Canada, except Pittsburgh *Bars *Stadiums and arenas *Little Caesar's at the Luxor Hotel and Casino *From those kids that sell mini frozen pizzas as a fundraiser for their t-ball team *Your microwave *Your friend's microwave *On English muffins *The Costco food court *Gina's Pizza if you're drunk Not to mention that the girl at the counter thought it would be okay to casually toss my receipt in my direction instead of handing it to me. I'm no Miss Manners, but that was bullshit. If they had some pizza worth eating, that would be one thing, but they don't have pizza that's worth eating. Honestly, if you live within 0.2 miles and you're desperate for somewhere to get a beer and watch a game, I understand. Otherwise, do yourself a service and pick up a DiGiorno.

text: City Diner is another old established eatery in South St. Louis just one block south of Tower Grove Park. The atmosphere is definitely from the '50s & '60s, and the background music proves it. But when it comes right down to the food...nothing special. Today (4-3-2009) was my first trip there for breakfast. They did offer an "Early Bird Special" available from 7 to 9 AM. I had 2 eggs, hash browns, sausage, wheat toast & of course coffee. All of this for a mere $5.40 not including the tip. CHEAP. However, I asked for my eggs "over-easy" and they came out next to "over-hard". I sent them back. On the other hand, the server was always there to top off the coffee. Friday & Saturday they are open 24 hours. Normal hours are Mon. - Thur. 7 AM to 11 PM. Tuesday evenings feature 1950s prices from 5 PM to 9 PM. How does $3.99 for dinner sound? Naturally, non-specials run quite a bit higher, but not outrageous. For example: City Diner Meatloaf, $8.50 served with home-made mashed potatoes, gravy and choice of vegetable. Or, 1/2 Smoked Chicken $9.50 smoked in-house to a rosy hue, served with your choice of potato and vegetable. All-in-all, I'll probably go there again. But it did not live up to the high expectations I've read in other reviews.
label: NEG

text: This is probably the creepiest pool hall I've visited in Nashville. I didn't even stay long enough to play a game of pool here I was that creeped out. And its not like I'm some prissy girl who hangs out at trendy clubs, I'm all about the dive bar scene. I initially came here (even though it is quite a bit out of my way) because I heard how many tables they had. And to be fair, they probably have the largest number of pool tables I've seen thus far in Nashville. They have three separate large rooms of tables but weirdly enough they only have 3 or 4 full sized tables. I don't really understand the purpose of having so many small tables but hey what do I know. They even do all sorts of tournaments here which is evident by all the wooden pull out bleachers they have. Its kind of funny seeing so many gym sized bleachers in a pool hall. In one of the rooms they also have a bunch of poker tables so I'm assuming they have poker tournaments as well. JOB is dimly lit and smells weird in a way I couldn't describe efficiently enough other than to say its unpleasant. The people playing pool were some of the creepiest and openly hostile people I've encountered at a pool hall and I'm not exactly sure what causes them to be this way. I don't know if its just territorial behavior or what, but as we were walking around checking the place out I kept feeling extremely self conscious from all the staring. The staff were way unfriendly and stand-offish. We stood at the counter for over 10 minutes waiting for the bartender to walk over so we could ask her a question. It wasn't like she was doing anything either, we were blatantly being ignored. We didn't even get to ask about what kind of drinks they had, she was that rude, but I did spy a fridge full with bottled domestics. I don't know maybe this place would be cool if you were a pool hustler or just liked being glared at by unkempt rednecks. I know its kind of far outside downtown but give me a break its in a freaking strip mall.
label: NEG

text: This place is definitely my favourite nighborhood coffeehouse. It's huge, has a nice back area with huge windows to look out of (with a view of a garden not more buildings and trash!) Or you can sit up front and hang out on the bar seats and stare out to the city sidewalk life moving by, or in the darker middle of the coffeehouse area, with cozy couches candles and whatnot. The free wi-fi is bonus for those dark winter days when you need your computer, but need some people around you too. Music soundtrack is good too, I nice mix of electronica, chill and alternative rock tracks, if you didn't BYOM. I just wish they had a frequent coffee buyers club because I spend way too much money in here!
label: POS

text: I'm yelping for my husband who doesn't feel like yelping. He got there at 6:45am and the place doesn't open until 7am.
