text: Two parts to this review, the station and Amtrak itself. Station: 1.5 stars. Amtrak Train travel in general: 3.5 stars. I really enjoy taking the train now. It is a new thing for me. Flying for years visiting relatives, although fun when I get there, is almost always torture. Squished together, the lines, check in, re-check in, security check, and now pat down/shoes off/power up laptop, take off jewelery etc.. ad nauseam... Amtrak has none of that nonsense. Advice: I always recommend the business class as it is only 20 bucks more, with the same lousy food naturally (hehe) but the seating is more spacious and comfortable with a lower noise volume which makes the comfort level goes up the scale to 100% in comparing to just regular fare. I have tried coach (LOUD and sometimes Greyhound-sque) & I have tried the lowest level of 2 person suite for travel (less leg room,) and I still prefer the business class. Perks: Business class you have 2 foot rests... one in front of you that you can rest your feet on and a leg/foot rest that props up like a lazyboy chair. You can lean back in your chair without disturbing who is behind you. There are 120V electrical plugs (for coach also) for every seat pairing. Pros/Cons: It is a longer way to travel, by train, but not that much longer if you are going to Chicago or Michigan. Sleeping our way to Michigan, rather then driving through the ice and snow is a blessing. Your luggage does not get searched, you can pack liquids and breakables as you choose, you don't have to take off your shoes, in business class you sit in a different (A LOT less crowded) waiting room. For $20 it is beyond worth the cost. Pros: Your luggage is always with you. You don't have to pack like someone might go through your stuff and you don't have to worry about your lip gloss causing an international incident etc.. If you pack something your big suitcase that is your favorite item, you don't have to worry about a luggage handler/sorter/etc.. lifting it off your hands. Carry that hair gel and in your carry on with no worries. This part is a big deal for me. Through many years of flying and the last few years of having to pack everything trying to keep in mind where to pack valuables (on me,) liquids of any sort (sealed in something and pray it doesn't burst in the suitcase.. oh the horrible memory of ruining a beautiful dress from Hair conditioner. :( etc....) .. THANK GOODNESS all I have to do is pack it up and go to take the train! Cons: Your luggage is always with you. Make sure ALL your luggage rolls or your shoulder bag is VERY light. Trust me. Your shoulders/back will NOT like you if you lug your heavy (or soon to feel that way) luggage around everywhere (thinking of Union Station and trading off to go to another hub.) The station itself: I like the location, as it seems a bit removed from the immediate area's traffic. The people who are working the ticket counter have 10 shades of attitude but they get 10 flavors of crazy going through there and not just mine. ;) (Good crazy is ok :p :D ) The fastfood joint is dirty and I couldn't bring myself to eat there. The chairs are horrible and there are no good places to put your luggage nor yourself for that matter. All sorts of characters walking in and out of there. I feel safe enough but I wouldn't have anyone I care about stay there too long waiting for me to pick them up. Always room for improvement. What's up: Take luggage that has wheels. Your shoulders/back/neck will scream at you if you try to carry bags everywhere. Pay the extra 20 bucks for business class for a much better experience. I love trains now. So stress free compared to driving/flying. Don't tarry at the station. Time your rides to be close to pick up time. I have heard many stories of VERY long waits for taxicabs, be warned. As you can call while you are on the train there is no reason to make people wait at the station for you or vise versa. Have fun! :)

text: I really wanted to like Charles Plaza, but was disappointed with most everything. For starters, as others have said, the only basis for being "healthy" is that they offer an extensive vegetarian menu, but anyway that wasn't a selling point for me, and not the basis of my rating. While Charles himself is very nice and friendly, it seemed as though he was the only one who spoke English. Fortunately, there were very few other diners (at one point my boyfriend and I were the only people there at all), so the service was certainly reasonable. Before getting to the food, I should mention some basics that they just plain got wrong, namely the lipstick on my water glass and my mismatched disposable chopsticks that had clearly been used before. Sure, I'm all for recycling, but I don't think that disposable (porous wood) chopsticks should be reused by other customers. While we were not victims of "upselling" per se, we did receive (and ultimately pay for) a couple of items that we didn't order. First, we received (barely hot, bitter) tea as soon as we arrived. At other restaurants, the tea is complimentary if served without being asked for, but when we received the bill we found that we had been charged $2 for it. Later, I ordered egg rolls, which my boyfriend doesn't like. The menu said that there were two per order, but we received four, and were charged $5 for four, despite specifically requesting one order of them. We ordered one of their two specialties, a chicken hot pot, which was average, and contained some sort of extremely bitter, unpleasant root vegetable that had both my boyfriend and I almost gagging. We took most of it home, so later I will try to figure out which vegetable was the culprit. [EDIT: Turns out there were about half a dozen turnip/parsnip/some other root vegetable ends (tops?) in the dish. Who would do such a thing to perfectly mediocre food?!] We also ordered a "beef" (seitan a.k.a. wheat gluten) noodle stir fry, which was pretty decent, although the "beef" tasted more like mushrooms. Our crab and chicken noodle soup was great, except for the eggshell (not crab shell) I found myself chewing on at one point. In short, Charles Plaza isn't horrible at around $20pp (with a lot of leftovers, and probably more like $10pp for a group sharing), but with all the variety that Chinatown has to offer, I don't think we'll be going back.

text: I will respond to two interesting reviews of this city with my own celebration of its mediocrity and hope to inspire others to help me make it better here. Even though this is probably just a say-something-nice-or-dont-say-anything-at-all, the weather is actually convenient, you can do things outside on any day of the year, and there are mountains and therefore parks, trails, etc in every direction. It's a myth that it's too hot to do things outside in the summer in AZ. Other places are hotter. There's the U of A here, which makes things better, and a nearly unlimited diversity in types of places to eat, buy crap, hang out, get drunk, be offended, etc. As a vacation spot Tucson is one of the best places to chill without a beach, especially if you are really old and like to golf, and has some very nice resorts. The only really important tourist stop is the desert museum, which is not like the museums you're thinking of. The one complaint I get most often from people visiting or who have recently moved is that the people at bars are not friendly and even sometimes rude. Tucson, what's your problem? -1 star I also get a lot of complaints that there is a lack of a young professional population which is very true.

text: The Claw may be the best kept secret in Golf. The Claw is the home course for the University of South Florida's Golf team. This course is a 7,000 yard monster from the back tees. The hazards on this course are endless. You will be faced with Sand Traps, waters hazards, snakes and large Alligators. The narrow fairways and endless hazards are mentally exhausting. My most memorable moment at the Claw came on the 516 yard, par 5, Sixth Hole. Long hitters can reach the green in two shots if you can fly the small lake that's right in front of the green. Me, being a total Wuss, I laid up. It turned out to be a bad decision. I thought I hit my ball in the perfect spot about 10 yards short of the water hazard. Little did I know that there was a 9 foot Gator sunning himself five feet from where I hit my ball. Needless to say, I gladly took a drop and the 1 stroke penalty. He was a large reptile and who was I to disturb him. The Claw offers a breathtaking look at the Florida wildlife. Not only is it a beautifully maintained course, it's also a certified, Audubon Animal sanctuary. Other than my Steve Irwin moment, my round was a lot of fun. I practiced at their wonderful driving range, played a fun round, and had a few Brews in the restaurant when I was finished with my day on the Links. The Bottom Line is, the Claw is a hidden Gem located just South of Downtown Tampa. It's a wonderful course and practice facility for Golfers of all levels. My only advice is be careful where you step. If your ball goes out of bounds, or even slightly off the fairway, you may want to take a drop. I would rather take a couple of penalty strokes than get bitten in the ass by a Gator.

As for warmed it was cold in the center. Served on a much too large plate with a pretty candy syrup design the design was the best looking and tasting thing on the whole plate. text: I went out on a late, snowy, cold December night looking for a place just to chill and have a drink. When you're on Mass Ave you kind of expect a certain kind of feel when you go into a venue. Ball and Biscuit delivers. It is a hybrid modern lounge/old school speakeasy. How does that happen you may ask? On the lounge side, the decor consists of a number of classic (very comfortable btw) older style chairs and couches and tables. The exposed brick walls look like the contractor forgot to wipe away the extra filling, but it gives it a texture that you don't see often that is actually pretty cool. The exposed ceilings finish the industrial New York feel. There is low lighting, I can't remember, but there may have been candles too. Either way, it was enough to see who you're talking to without straining at all. On the bar side, you'll find a number of high tables and a small, but comfortable bar space that was very well put together and efficient. I liked the food menus being written in chalk for some reason. I guess it's because that means it changes and you never know what you'll get. I have yet to eat there, but the selections sounded perfect for the venue and looked pretty good from the plates I checked out. Bartenders and waitstaff were all easygoing and friendly. Ball and Biscuit is good for groups (probably no larger than 8) or one on one date spots. I almost forgot the thing that impressed me the most...the music. They played Cody Chestnutt and The Roots! While it's background music and not at a volume that you're going to get up and break it down, the fact they played a diverse range of music was appreciated. Thumbs up!

text: If you're online and researching potential tattoo parlors - as opposed to stumbling half-drunk and off-the-cuff into the first place you pass and ending up with horribly ugly design you'll hate for your entire life - then congratulations! You've made the first step in the right direction. It's obvious to many of us that getting a tattoo is serious business. You are not only receiving a mark that you will bear for a lifetime, but you are taking part in an art form that dates back for millenia. It is a ritual for many, a rite of passage for others, or a statement of individuality. Whatever its purpose, it is to be considered with the utmost sincerity. In other words, try and reconsider getting that band logo you've always wanted; chances are that when you are 60, that same band will be long forgotten - by yourself and the general populace. Also avoid other obvious bad decisions - names of significant others (not counting memorial tattoos), portraits and anything involving unicorns. Not every tattoo shop is appropriate for everyone. Do more research, scope out the place, check out the artists' portfolios. Don't be afraid to visit multiple places, even just to get inspiration. Also check out individual artists; there are many talented people in the industry and they all have something unique to offer. All that said, I can recommend from experience Headlight Tattoo II, located on Clements Bridge Road in Deptford - spitting distance from that dismal pit named the Deptford Mall. Headlight has two other locations - one literally around the corner in Deptford (closer to Westville), and another in Woodstown. However, I can only specifically recommend Headlight II, as that's where I've received all my ink to date. They accept walk-ins, but I'd highly recommend making an appointment - not only to avoid disrupting the artists at work, but to allow the proper time for your tattoo. I'd like to recommend a particular artist, but I would first like to give my general impression of Headlight II. The first thing that struck me when I first entered the parlor was the sanitary smell in the air. A hospital-like cleanliness mingled with that intoxicating smell of fresh ink. I considered this a good sign, as safety and sanitation is integral to the tattoo experience. In general, it's a very laid-back place; no one here is the intimidating sort, as if they are a member of the San Francisco chapter of the Hell's Angels. These are down-to-earth guys who take their art seriously and will do everything they can to deliver the tattoo you've envisioned. There are many samples and portfolios for inspiration, but I'd recommend offering them something unique, whether that's bringing in an image from the web or from a book, or even sketching something yourself. Getting a tattoo can be extremely stressful - which only adds to the pain, in my opinion - so it's a relief when you're able to relax in an environment that is as mellow as Headlight II. Now, as far as specific tattoo artists are concerned, I can only speak of a single artist who has done all of my work so far (and I regard as a something of a hidden gem in their plethora of artists). His name is Lee Cramer, and he is the most down-to-earth, cooperative and downright talented artists I've come across. The guy's got a degree in graphic design, and it shows in his work. He has an amazingly steady hand (with the fine line work of a draftsman), an amazing eye for nuance and detail, and, like most great artists, he is a perfectionist. He will make sure you eventually receive the tattoo that you want. He describes himself accurately on Headlight's website: "If you want a nice clean tattoo from a good young man who isn't on drugs, doesn't drink much, is clean, handsome, polite, and loves his family, his fiance', animals, and his country, ask for Lee Cramer ." I couldn't have said it better myself. And remember - PLEASE TIP YOUR ARTIST!! I can't stress this enough. That's where they make their bread and butter. Tip like you would at a restaurant - 20% is the norm, but feel free to tip above that if you're truly happy with the results. In conclusion, take your tattoo seriously, give Headlight II a look on your search, check out Lee Cramer's portfolio (online and in the parlor), and TIP YOUR ARTIST. And most of all, make your session enjoyable. If you open yourself up to it, getting a tattoo can be an amazingly fulfilling experience. And from personal experience, I can attest that Lee Cramer will make sure it is just that.

text: So, I've been to the Drunken Fish a few times, at each location, and have never been blown away by any of the experiences. However, I've decided I'm not going back based on my last one at the CWE location. I've never gotten poor service at any of the Drunken Fish locations, but I'm usually on a date or otherwise dressed to impress. The last time I went was to grab a bite right before work. I was in scrubs and no make-up. Oh em gee an atrocity. When I went in the hostesses ignored me for a moment while they finished up their conversation. They were all gathered around talking because the place was pretty much dead and acted like I wasn't even standing there. Then looked at me..."Hi........just you?" Yes, just me. "Okay. Sit wherever you want." Okay. I sat at the sushi bar. Sushi was fine, as usual; my actual waitress was sweet. But as people walked in behind me, couples, groups of friends, all dressed up to high CWE style, I kept hearing, "Hi, welcome to Drunken Fish! Would you like to try our happy hour?" Wait, happy hour?! Then I realized their happy hour was 5-7pm upstairs. Cheap drinks and sushi. I came in at 5:30pm. Why the hell wasn't I offered the happy hour? I would have saved about half of my bill. Then I had to think that it was because how I looked. That may seem silly, but that's the kind of place this is. That's how ALL of Munsok's restaurants are. Completely hung up on appearances. Sitting down there by myself paying for overpriced sushi when everyone else was yucking it up upstairs paying only half of what I was paying for the same thing made me feel like the girl in the 1st grade class that didn't get invited to the birthday party everyone else did. By the way, when I left, I didn't get a "bye" or a "thank you" for my business, even though the same group of girls were all standing there not doing anything and just silently watched me walk out. That's cool. I just won't bring my business back. And I'll write scathing reviews on Yelp about it. There are really no redeeming qualities about The Drunken Fish. It's not worth it. This place, and all of the places under this same umbrella, are pretentious and shallow as hell. That's why I don't work for them anymore and that's why I won't be back.

text: Located within an outdoor mall, the Brass Tap is a great find in the Wesley Chapel area. It's a decent sized bar that has a local upscale feel to it. So on to the main event, the menu. Its an expansive menu with about 7 pages front and back of beer, beer and oh ya, more beer (300+ to be exact). It's arranged by category (lager, stout, etc), with a detailed description of each category. Within those are a list of beers, which also come with their own description, including color, taste and region. After going through this text a few times, I felt like I was getting an education as well as a buzz. We tried around 6 beers total and each was unique and tingled the beer senses with diverse flavors. The favorite in the end was the Breckenridge Vanilla Stout, if you like a beer that's not sweet but still tastes like your having some sort of after dinner treat, I definitely recommend. All in all I will be visiting this place many many times in the future and that is what 5 stars is all about.

text: I cannot BELIEVE I am the first to review this fantastic restaurant! Attention, Reno Yelpers: You NEED to go try out Lupita's! We finally made the trip all the way out to Sparks (it's, like, MILES!) on Friday night, and boy, am I glad we splurged on the gallon of gas! Now, we all know that there are a LOT of Mexican places to choose from in Reno/Sparks, and many of them are good. So it gets hard to say what makes one Mexican place stand out above the others. In Lupita's case I can tell you two of those things...beef tongue and raw octopus. Husband ordered the Lengua in Salsa Verde and it was heaven on a plate. For $10. Yes, you read right, $10. And that included rice and beans and tortillas. I had a sopa and two tacos, one lengua and one carnitas. The carnitas were so flavorful and tender. Combo plate total: $8. Along with our ridiculously cheap meals we were given complimentary ceviche that was so good I was ready to order another GALLON of it! This was seriously the most satisfying meal I have had in a long time. Lunch specials are even more reasonable than dinner...starting at around $5. This is just a great, casual, sit down place with great atmosphere and wonderful food. If you don't feel like waiting in line at Beto's or spending a lot of money at Bertha Miranda's, give Lupita's a try next time you're craving Mexican.

text: I try and meet up with my dad once a week for lunch or dinner. If he's pressed for time we meet in the middle, which often means that we dine in St. Charles. This was the case last night. Alexander's is a rehab of an old (old being relative), vacated chain-restaurant shell. Good on them for reusing an existing structure. Having read their history on the back menu I now know that this is one of four local outposts of a small, family-run chain originating in Chicago. Cheers to local, family-run establishments. Beyond that, though, I have to say I've experienced better. An aroma of stale smoke pervading the entire interior was the immediate impression upon entering the door. The decor is kitschy and the colors are a bit harsh. I'd never heard of the place and didn't realize it was Greek until I saw the menu, but as another reviewer mentioned below the offerings are light on the Greek. No dolmades? Spanakopita? Moussaka? No baklava? This is a historically Greek family running a suburban steakhouse. Our server did not know the special, went to ask in the kitchen, then described it differently than it was delivered. That said, my dad thought it tasted great and it was a huge portion. Sue had their pulled pork sandwich with the now-ubiquitous sweet potato fries. Pulled pork sandwich at a Greek joint? I ordered the gyro, which if memory serves was the only Greek "sandwich" on the menu. I ate it - and don't get me wrong, it tasted fine - but I did not find it representative of the cuisine. Service was generally slow, and they were not busy. That said, the owner / manager came by twice to check on our table. As the meal drew to a close, it was clearly an imposition to ask our waitress to split the bill. There are better restaurants in St. Charles, and there are better Greek restaurants in St. Louis. I wish Alexander's all the best, but I will not be back.
label: NEG

text: By the time we ate at Tommy's I was sick and tired of eating out in New Orleans. I just wanted to be home. Combine that with the fact that the acoustics were terrible. There were a gazillion Opthalmologists under one roof all trying to be the loudest one at their table. Conside these things when you read this review. Tommy's started out great (mostly because the service at nearby Emeril's sucked so badly that we acutally left and came here instead). The service was lovely. But, the dining room we were in was beyond loud. The wine was good but the kitchen was back-logged and painfully slow. We tried 3 different types of baked oysters (Tommy's, Bienville & Rockefeller) and they were all only okay. The dressings were really salty and overpowered the flavor of the oysters. I think I just prefer them raw. I got the duck salad and I laughed out loud when I saw it. It was a huge portion of sliced duck breast with a tiny bit of of undressed spinach in the middle of the plate. Imagine the size of one scoop of ice cream. Yes, that was the portion size of the greens in my "entree" salad. All duck - no salad. You might be thinking, "What's wrong with that?" Well, I would say "nothing" if I had ordered the duck entree and not the duck SALAD. I don't like smoked foods and I think I either missed the "smoked" mention on the menu or it wasn't there. But, let's just say, my duck tasted like bacon. To me, everything smoked tastes like bacon. And, I don't like bacon. The only thing funnier than my salad was....my fiance's salad! His green salad with crabmeat was actually a scoop of shredded lettuce and crab meat mixed together and doused in mayo. Of course, the menu made NO mention of the mayo. (I tried to warn him having lived in New Orleans that I had never seen crab that wasn't was fried or doused in mayo or some sort of cream or cheese sauce, but he didn't believe me). Imagine getting scoop of tuna salad with some lettuce mixed in with it (and getting really soggy) and nothing else. Now, replace the tuna with crab meat. I know I sound bitter but Tommy's really put me over the edge. It's not even really Tommy's fault. But, I was so happy to get back on the plane and come back to Boston where greens are green, crunchy and plentiful and not everything tastes like bacon.
label: NEG

text: Diners craving hearty Mexican fare will find dishes more sophisticated than tacos at Café Poca Cosa. The exterior seems like just another downtown building. Once you step inside, you immediately feel the Mexican influence. The contemporary decor is edgy with fierce black and red tones. There was also some modern Mexican music in the background. It was a Thursday night before sunset, so there were probably only two other tables sat at the time. The rustic chalkboard menu showed the day's items available. There was a bottle of salad dressing on the table that was as decorative as it was functional. There was a whole chili pepper submerged with its buoyancy somehow allowing it to sink to the below the liquid but float above the vinegar. There were whole spices at the bottom such as bay leaves and peppercorns. As soon as I was sat, I was immediately presented with the chips and salsa with some glasses of water. It was a deep red salsa, spicy with subtle chipotle flavor. It was seasoned just right, making me devour more chips than I should have. The server came and explained the menu very thoroughly to us. It didn't really matter since my companion and I both ordered the Plato Poca Cosa, which has three random items from the menu. Since we both ordered it, the restaurant was smart enough to make sure that my three items were different from my companion's. My plate arrived with a carne asada with a creamy green sauce, a chicken mole, and a tamale pie with a creamy zucchini sauce. The garnish was a heaping pile of greens and a slice of pineapple. My companion had a carne asada with a pico de gallo type sauce, chicken with a tomato-based sauce, and tamale pie with a beet sauce. The garnish was also greens but with a slice of watermelon instead of pineapple. The carne asada was probably made of skirt steak or flank steak. It was tender so I didn't need to slice it. I just popped the big chunks in my mouth and chewed it just fine. The sauce brought out the richness of the meat, but it was not exceptional. The chicken mole was scrumptious though. I am usually prefer dark meat, but the white meat was prepared perfectly. It was still juicy and tender. The richness of the chocolate in the sauce probably would have been too rich for dark meat. The sauce was also the right consistency -- it clung to the chicken but was not a thick paste. The peanuts and pumpkin seeds provided body and flavor but was not overpowering. The tamale pie was rich yet left a refreshing aftertaste. The masa was soft and had a stringy cheese in the center. The zucchini was barely detectable to the palate but lightened up the dish. Every ingredient tasted fresh and made from scratch. The plate was beautiful from the abundant vibrant colors. It went for the festive instead of elegant look. Rice, beans, and tortillas came on the side but were not necessary since the starchy tamale pie was filling enough with the rest of the main dish. The rice and tortillas tasted standard but the beans were packed with flavor. The waitress overhead me speaking with my companion about my birthday, so she brought me a complimentary dish of delicate flan. It was drowning in the delicious caramel with a chocolate sauce drizzled along the side of the plate. The caramel was just the right sweetness; the sugar did not mask the gentle cinnamon flavor. The freshness and quality of the food was superb. I could not even resist nibbling on the garnishes. The stylish environment is also hard to find in a place like Tucson and makes it a great place to bring a date. It is about $15 per person for lunch and about $25 for dinner before drinks, tax and gratuity. Make sure to bring a little extra because they have great coffee and better margaritas. Any Mexican restaurant can brighten any plate with mixed greens with a random fruit slice, but only Café Poca Cosa has the blend of spices in its mole that will keep you coming back.

text: While you may find white table cloths on the table, this is anything but a standard white tablecloth establishment. Here you will find used newspapers available for patrons to read, french fries wrapped in paper, oysters shucked openly at the bar and a laid-back, casual atmosphere. Tips: If you like being near the action, ask for a table in the back where you get a nice view of the chefs at work behind a glass room. I've never eaten there for breakfast or brunch, but I have enjoyed many a lunch, dinner and happy hour there. Their lunch specials change daily, but they include some really good eats, if you can catch them on the right day. As appetizers go, you can't beat the deliciously cheesy, buttery, oniony, bacony lamenküche. Delicious! If you haven't guess it yet, I'm a cheeseburger girl. And Luke has one superb Cheeseburger; however, they have many other delectable selections to offer too. Luke's Shrimp and Grits rival some of the best in the city. If you'd rather fish, you won't be disappointed with the fish meunière... go ahead and splurge on the added jumbo lump crabmeat. It will definitely be worth it. A little warning, if you order the ravioli of local crabmeat you will absolutely love it.... for about 5 minutes when you realize that there are not nearly enough ravioli to satisfy you. The portion of this dish seems very small to me. Don't skip dessert! If you still have room left, go for the profiteroles. And make sure to get some coffee. Luke has some of the best restaurant coffee I have ever tasted. Another tip: Be mindful of the cheap oysters, appetizer and drink specials during Happy Hours throughout the week. Most importantly, it's not just the food that make this restaurant 5 star worthy... It's the cocktails. One cocktail in particular, actually. The French 75. I'm sure that their other cocktails are also good, but you will have to check that out for yourself. . You see... Luke is where I fell in love with the French 75. And Luke's French 75 is the French 75 by which all French 75s will be judged through my lifetime.

Unfortunately, there was, really, nothing that wowed me. And believe me if there was, I would say it every chance I could and to anyone who will listen. But the chicken was overcooked and boring (the carrot mustard sauce seemed to be, separately, mustard and carrot puree), the risotto was undercooked (which I suppose is better than overcooked) and the pear, champagne, chocolate float was made with chocolate that hardened by the time the glass made it to the table. Honestly, I would not be writing this review at all, if I thought the service was fantastic or if anyone had asked me how we enjoyed the meal. I understand it takes some time to get into a groove and perfect the dishes on your menu. I tend not to be critical early on. However when I tried to give feedback to the staff, I was left feeling like no one really cared what I thought. The server never once asked how anything was and in fact he really should have noticed because none of us finished our plates: I left the entire breast of chicken, except 2 bites. And when I asked to speak to someone I could give food feedback to (I preferred to tell them directly instead of just writing it here or telling "10 of my friends"), the manager never once looked at me (the only female at the table) nor did he ever apologize for our disappointment in the food (I didn't even mention the service). As someone who has been working in the food industry for more than 15 years, it is hard for me to write this. I really want restaurants to succeed. It's hard work. A friend likes this place and was keen on getting some late-night grub here, and she knows I hate the Chinese food in town. I was too nice in allowing to get myself involved with this mess. Utterly dreary, sterile, and cold interior, which set the mood perfectly. I tried to play it safe with the broccoli beef chow mein and was rewarded with reheated meat, noodles, and vegetables covered in chemically-enhanced goo. Her seafood curry was slightly better, but that's not saying much. The curry was really runny and didn't add to the seafood and vegetables much apart from turning them yellow. The egg roll was laughably bad. Cut up into smaller pieces, it tasted about as good as one you'd get in the frozen-food section at an Asian market, which it probably was. The thickness and consistency of the deep-fried batter reminded me of a frozen corn dog at the store. I asked if they had any dim sum there, which brought a look of confusion to the employee. I was told by another employee (who wasn't the most polite of sorts to the other customers in there and who seemed like she's been working there WAY too long) that they don't have any. text: "For the state to attempt to control what the people shall eat, drink and wear..is tyranny and not liberty" Gov. Malcom Patterson (1909) These words welcome you on the inside of every Patterson House drink menu. This place is for serious people who want a seriously well made drink. To some extent I thought they took some of the recipes to the extreme but I'm sure they had their reasons for doing things the way they do them. I was talking to one of the bartenders, Ed, an unusually chipper fellow, who was making drinks at such a fast and furious pace but with such precision as to remind me of an old school sushi chef. Every drink is tested by its maker once, twice even five times BEFORE it is served. I counted one drink that was tested five times. unbelievable. As an example they feature a drink called a 'Jennings', i guess its named after outlaw singer Waylon Jennings. Its made of Jack Daniels and hickory smoked cola. What the heck is hickory smoked cola? It was explained that the coke cola syrup is cooked with hickory chips, cooled and repackaged right there in Patterson House. I tasted a sample. It tasted like a coke served inside a wet chimney. Not for me. My first drink was the Juliet & Romeo, a Plymouth Gin, mint and cucumber concoction. The Oak Bar at the Plaza makes a drink called the Gin Mule, its kinda of like a Mojito but made with gin not rum. Its one of my favorites. The J&R was fresh and tasty with a thick delicious dose of lime. I love the flavor of lime. After a moment of intense inspection of the bar menu, it was easy to decide and try out the Dark and Stormy. If you are a D&S drinker then you know how rare it is to find a bar that actually makes them correctly. I've never had Matusalam rum or ginger syrup before but I'm a believer now. It was great. Served in a tall glass with a single shaft of ice, an obelisk...nonpareil. The space at the Patterson House is small, dark and is put together like part speakeasy part library. The people here are both young and old enjoying a good time. The music is a mix of house and alternative. Only a few of the tunes I recognized. The bartenders were skilled, no jokers here. Chauncy, the ponytailed blonde had the additional skill to hypnotize. Think half cheerleader and half love ninja. When she does this thing, shaking cocktail shakers in each hand, her hips do this thing, that...um, does some-thing to my brain. My friend had to hit my reset button a few times because I was locking up. Oh, well.. After the D&S and a consultation with James, another bartender, shaved head and athletic build, looks like a hitman but with an easy smile. He knew his stuff. I then moved onto the El Diablo. A tequila thing. After a few of these and maybe a few more I was in my zone, Jalisco Mexico. Its always warm and sunny there. I've never had the Lunazul Reposado Tequila before but It was great. The bar fare was interesting, mini hot dogs actually made in house and corn dogs made with shrimp, 'shrimpdogs'. Everything here was great and even a bit educational. At about $11 bucks a drink, this is cheap. in NYC you'd be paying $20 and in Europe $30. So, pretend you are drinking at a discount!

text: Having lived in South Philly for the better part of a decade, I have always meant to stop into Mr Martino's. I have heard such polarizing things about this joint- the service is slow, the food too salty and the portions too small. I have also heard it is homey, delicious, well-portioned and simply comfortable. From the moment the diner steps inside Mr Martino's, it's pretty apparent that this meal is going to be pretty unique, for better or for worse. The decor is splendid. You know how tacky places like Applebee's put random crap on their walls in a half-hearted attempt to make their establishments feel authentic? Well, Mr. Martino's is the sort of place they are ripping off. The walls are old. The tables are creaky. The space is cramped. It's kind of dark. There are somewhat creepy, kind of interesting pictures all over the place. I would say there is a hybrid of intimacy and comfort unlike any other restaurant I have ever entered. The service, from the very start, was awesome. We chatted with our server for a few minutes. She recommended a few dishes. Later, we chatted up Mr. Martino himself. Couldn't be a nicer fellow. I got the feeling that this is the sort of place that a lot of work has been put into, and that furthermore they could make a lot more money if, say, they opened up for more days or moved to a bigger establishment. That they haven't may account for the fantastic dishes. My fiance and I started by ordering an arugula and Asiago salad with a lemon-oil dressing. I loved the intense bitterness of the arugula contrasting with the sour tartness of the dressing. Crazy weird flavor. In fact, this salad was possibly the earthiest dish I have ever experienced. Though I mean that as a compliment, my fiance didn't care for it. "Go outside and lick the cement." Well then. As for our main dishes, I originally ordered the veal tortellini with Gorgonzola sauce. Unfortunately, the sauce was emptied for the nite. (We arrived pretty late.) So I switched to the apparently-endless special, the balsamic chicken. To me, this dish was heaven sent. It arrived with a few potatoes and 2 crunchy stalks of asparagus on the side. The sauce had that tangy sweetness which only balsamic could deliver. The chicken quite literally fell off the bone. Surprisingly, the dish had dark meat too. Quite a risk, considering the price point. It really lent itself to the dish, so tender and juicy. My fiance ordered the cheese tortellini with pesto sauce. The tortellini was obviously fresh and cooked perfectly. The pesto was sublime, not a hint overseasoned. She said it was one of the best pasta dishes she ever tasted. There are a few bum notes which obstruct a 5 star rating. The portion size has been discussed much. While I certainly agree that portion size at nearly every establishment is out of control these days, Mr Martinos goes the opposite way. I could literally have counted my fiance's tortellini on two hands. I MAY have need a few toes, but I doubt it. What it comes down to is this- if I am dropping a Grant on dinner, I should come out with my appetite satisfied. If it weren't for our bread, I would not have been. Also, as noted by other reviewers, the wait was excessive. I didn't particularly mind it, to be honest, but it is something to be considered if you are going out for dinner. There are nights when going out to dinner isnt the absolute centerpiece of the night. Going to Mr Martino's for dinner would preclude such nights. Overall, I loved it. I plan on going back, that much is for sure. The environment, the service, the atmosphere and, of course, the off the hook dishes are well worth stopping for a few hours every once in a while for a meal unlike any other.
label: POS

text: Four words: Fire Log Prime Ribs. DO NOT FALL FOR "KOBE BEEF". It is not at all what you would expect from anything you have ever heard about "kobe beef". Price: 13.99 for regular week days. More expansive on the weekends. I am a long time Harrahs goer. As a matter of fact, I only gamble at Harrahs when I am in Reno. Carving buffet is the one that I used to always go to. Aside from crappy comp points nowadays, Harrah's buffet has also really disappointed me in the past 2 trips. Their selection is actually ok, they have less buffet counter than many other casinos, but other places repeat their selections over and over to fill up the counter. King crab legs are just as salty as everyone else's. Snow crab legs are kind of small, but acceptable. Now prime ribs: MAN! How can you mess up prime ribs? For the past two trips, both time they have only had well done prime ribs. Yes well done though out! The whole thing! There were not "middle part that are more red", it is just one big chunk of fire log like thing that they somehow call "prime rib". An Asian chef was manning the carving station. I waited for an hour and half, for that "next one" to come, only to see more completely well done prime ribs, and there were nothing the chef was willing to do to solve the problem. Perhaps it was not his fault that he didn't understand what I was saying, but come on! It is called "carving buffet", so what about having an English speaking chef that knows how to cook prime ribs to man the "carving station"? Would it be the least the buffet can do to keep up its name? And the Kobe beef they had, as advertise in front of the buffet. It is nothing but a big chunk of beef shoulder roast. It had nothing to do with the tender, melt in your mouth legendary Kobe Beef, just a big tough chuck of roasted beef. I felt so scammed when I ate that thing, even though I somehow knew I shouldn't be expecting high grade Kobe beef with perfect marble distribution that melts in your mouth. Still I have no idea why and how dare they call it Kobe beef. I would have asked if the Asian chef understood English. The good thing is that they had "cook to order" New York steaks. And the lady was very nice and cooked everything according to my needs. This earned them an extra star, along with my personal year of good memory I had with Harrah's Casino in the past.

text: We had an absolutely fantastic time here watching the consolation (third place) game of the World Cup. A classy joint full of people who love beer and the people who love people who love beer. The bartenders are quick to show off samplers of the different varieties and recommend one for you. They seem to know their beer pretty well too. Here's my breakdown on the brews: Kolsch: very good beer with an especially good finish. Great if you are thirsty. Extra Pale Ale: Awesomely bitter. I love the aftertaste. Whale: I only had a sampler but opted for the EPA over this one. I think next time I will be down for a pint. Bavarian Hefeweizen: Oh..my..god. Simply amazing. There's so much flavor here that you almost can't believe this is beer. It's perfect. So perfect I opted for a second pint instead of trying the Whale. Word on the street is that the porter is good too but I am not a porter/stout kind of guy so I will pass. This is not the place to come when you have a large group to please or if you have that dull friend who only drinks bud light. Food selections are scarce, but satisfactory for a light meal. They have a limited bar for non-beer drinkers so those of you with non-beer-drinking-S.O's can come here without fear of a punishmnent shopping excursion to Bed Bath & Beyond or Pier 1. You can get their beer on draft at a few local establishments, but I think every beer lover owes themselves a visit here first. If you are looking for a classy bar to try some delicious craft beer, I can't recommend this place highly enough.

text: In theory, this is a good, neighborhood-y pub, and since I live in the neighborhood and like pubs, I find myself going there probably once a month or so. And there are reasons to. They have a top-notch draft beer menu, at good prices. Nice decor. It's a comfortable place to sit and have a beer and a bite, watch a game, whatever. It's not as noisy or crowded as neighboring Tin Can can get, and, unlike the Amsterdam Tavern down the street, Three Monkeys has a big menu. So, in theory, it's a good neighborhood bar. Except that every time I leave there, I'm sort of disappointed, and I feel like I have a brick in my stomach. That's because their food is mediocre at best. Bland and way too heavy. I've had the pizza, the burger, a couple of other sandwiches, various appetizers and I pretty much always leave feeling stuffed, and not in a good way. More like bloated and toting a massive block of congealing leftovers. I want to like the place, but I don't need to eat for three when I'm there. It's got potential, but unless the food improves, it's hard to give it more than two stars.

We eventually ran across the bark busters site which offered a few limited tips. My wife was pretty much fed up and asked me to call someone "professional" I called the local bark busters here in Tucson and they seemed fairly knowledgeable. After a couple lessons the marking has stopped and Reese is getting better about barking when the door bell rings. text: I had not quite the best experience here several months ago; I'd placed it out of my mind...but the stupid oil change reminder card and the incessant emails annoy me so much, I have to let it out. I've heard great reviews about Autotire as a chain, so when it came time for an oil change, Autotire was high on the list. That and the Sunday hours. I'm a bit of a newbie at this because my previous car had lifetime free oil changes at the dealership, so that was the only place I've ever gone to. That and my Dad. But I digress. Doing the ever essential research online, I printed out the $19.99 coupon they have on their site for the Oil Change +Plus. It's an oil and filter change, brake inspection, tire pressure check, and a four tire rotation deal with a $2.25 disposal charge and a warning that additional charges may apply. Fair enough. I see these coupons all the time. So I go in, and it starts off with yellow flags. The guy at the counter takes my coupon, does a bunch of inputting of sorts, and gives me a printout with a total of approximately $28, which means approximately another $6 in fees and taxes. He sort of defensively / apologetically states that these are just extra fees they tack on. Um, ok. I guess so, I mean, just look at my cell phone bill; they do that all the time. They take my car back then and some time later, an employee pops out to tell me that a) my right strut is leaking and needs to be fixed immediately, b) would I like my air filters changed while I'm at it? and c) would I like to upgrade my oil change? What? It's a new car! I just came in for a simple oil change and a tire rotation!! To give them credit, the employee did say that since it was a newer car, the warranty ought to cover the strut. He looked at me askance when I said I'd save the air filter change until the next time and stated that a regular oil change was just fine - I mean, really, it hadn't even been 12,000 miles yet! Plus, I think the filter change is one of the easier things that you can do by yourself and save $20 in the meantime. I mean, I'm a girl, but I'm not DUMB. Then as a final snub, after he's all done, and I'm ready to leave, I restart my car and notice that all of my tire pressures are unchanged on the monitor. As in, my tires were never checked or rotated. Huh. That was corroborated later by looking at the wheels as one of them already is slightly dented. I wish I could say something positive, but now that I'm at another 3,000 miles further, I'll be looking for another oil change place and staying far away for this one. The final insult? This new coupon card they sent me has the same online deal for $24.99, which is $5 more than the online coupon...and the same price they advertise in store!

Also, we had to call a waitress over to refresh our water glasses, and she reached over people to do so, instead of actually coming around and doing it from behind you. There was only one lonely little jug of creamer, meant for ten people at the table. We were seated in the back, and were right by the doors to the kitchen. My mother said that she was surprised to be able to hear the staff calling out to one another in there. I had to constantly duck because the one waiter is short and held the tray just above my head as he walked by in the pitiful amount of space between tables. We figure that in the future, the staff should be assigned one to a table, instead of the milling around, then frantically dealing with one table like it's an emergency. Also, if a dish requires a special thing added to it, like the cheese, it should have been left out on the table from the beginning. They had done that with the Cesar dressing, so why not the mozzarella/parmigiana? Mind you, we were just there as guests at a luncheon, so we don't know what was paid for what type of service. But if you plan on having an event in their ballroom, please keep in mind this review and insist on better service. I have to admit, the ballroom is lovely and the china/silverware was very nice. text: As you may or may not know, Copia had a fire back in 2008 and they've finally reopened. Thank goodness they have because my initial reaction is "freaking awesome." The beautiful wife and I trekked here for lunch this afternoon. I'll start of saying that it was delicious, but that I wish we had come here for dinner (more on that later). The interior (normally something I don't care about) is really nice, very "fashionable upscale" -- not snooty, but rather there was a lot of thought put into it. And there are those cascading water panes of glass separating the bar area from the main dinning room. It's pretty cool, but admittedly, if you focus on them, you go might into a trance. We perused the wine list. Here's the great thing about having a restaurant connected to a wine shop -- the prices are LOW. Freaking wonderful low. Now, they do charge a corkage fee ($8), but eve with that, you're still great a pretty decent value. So, if you're a person that enjoy more than a glass or two, this is the spot. Admittedly, I didn't know about the corkage fee initially -- maybe it was mentioned on the wine list and I skipped over it, but our server explained this after we got the bill. On to the food. I had the prime rib French dip with housemade chips. This wasn't Sunday crappy buffet prime rib -- it was all meat and barely any fat. Delicious. And they put the horseradish in a condiment cup on the side, so you can heat to your own desire. I'll let the beautiful wife do a recap of her dish (the pulled pork sandwich), but I tasted it and its accompanying sides and thought it was tasty. Now, why did I wish we had gone there for dinner? While the lunch menu was very "Downtown business lunch" the dinner menu was "rival your favorite spot" interesting. Unfortunately, they don't have a web site up, but there were a number of dishes that sounded excellent. Note that while the average lunch offering was around $9-12, dinner is in the $25-30 range. Service was friendly and efficient (though admittedly, there was only two other people eating). But I got that nice feeling that our server was happy he was working there. They're still getting things in order on the wine shop side of things, but they should be offering a lot of different bottles. I can't wait to go back here for dinner, though I'll have to clean up a little bit. Not sure about things like wine flights, but that may develop as things settle down.

text: Pho is essentially a hot noodle and meat soup and takes hours upon hours to make. It's a time consuming process but the end result speaks for itself. I should know; I've eaten it all my life. Trust me, I've had my fair share of bad pho and it's not good at all. However, Pho Ha makes a damn tasty bowl of pho hands down. I ordered the pho tai nam gau gan sach (steak, fatty flank, tendon and tripe - yes, tripe!). It was delicious, comforting and filling - everything you want in a hearty bowl of pho. A very well flavored broth adorned by copious amounts of meats makes me a very happy camper. And at about $5 for an immense bowl, it was a friggin steal! text: I stopped in here with a friend because I read about their gluten free pizza menu online. My doctor recently recommended I go gluten free so I'm working on giving it a go. While the gluten free pizza menu was significantly more expensive than the regular pizza menu, that was quickly cleared up: they don't make the gluten free dough in house. Why? They make their gluten laden dough in house and can't guarantee against cross-contamination, so they buy the dough from a wholesaler. Obviously more expensive. The pizza was nicely thin crusted, as opposed to the other pizzas I saw leaving the establishment. It also had a crunch I rarely find in any pizza, but was delicious. We shared the Old time (old school, old way, something) pizza with pepperoni and it was so delicious. Also, it was the first time in a while that I had a meal at a restaurant that didn't make me want to throw up. I didn't feel sick at all eating this, sorta like my ramen/pho experiences, and completely opposed to my beyond bread meals that often made me ill immediately afterward. So, for the gluten free/celiac crowd out there: this is your joint. For someone like me, it was an eye-opening experience. Thankfully, a tasty one. The prices are a bit higher than at other places, but they use only recyclable materials (which are, frankly, more expensive) and high quality ingredients: generally organic veg, free-range (and hormone/antibiotic free) chicken, etc. All of that leads to higher base cost levels for a product. Because I appreciate their effort to both save the environment and my body, I'm willing to pay the price. But be forewarned: a 10" gluten free pizza can run you $19. If that's out of your budget, go to Sunflower and buy the gluten free pizza mix for $8.

It's a small place, a converted house a good distance away from the French Quarter. (It's a great St. Charles streetcar trip, if you have the time.) Thoroughly decorated with their awards too prominently displayed, it's a wonderful place for foodies to dine. For starters, my wife had butternut shrimp bisque and I had sautéed sweetbreads on lemon thyme brioche with shitake mushrooms, capers, and veal demi-glace. Tell me that isn't creative! Our mains were equally interesting: roast duck with popcorn dirty rice and honey pecan gravy, and paneed rabbit with sesame crust, spinach, and Creole mustard sauce. Everything was outstanding. The dining rooms are intimate, the service is excellent, and the food is fabulous. And since Chef Frank is a native who has been cooking in New Orleans for decades, he's not likely to leave. text: First, the good: the salad bar is great. Everything except meat that you could possibly want to eat, ranging from salads to other vegetables to cheeses to breads. All of it delicious. I'm not going to cover the serving style at this place because the other reviewers here have done that for me, so let's just say it's essentially all you can eat portions of "16 types" of meat. I put "16 types" in quotation marks because every cut from the same animal tastes the same. Yeah, you can tell the difference between beef and chicken, but that's about it. "Filet mignon" = "bottom round" = "top sirloin" - all greasy, all salty, and all indistinguishable. I'd go as far as to call most of the meat slimy. It's not bad if you're famished, but marginal utility goes down pretty quickly. I'm not gonna lie, I'm a skinny guy who doesn't have the biggest appetite. But I couldn't possibly get my money's worth here. If you're capable of eating a pound of steak without losing any of your hunger, then Fogo de Chao is the right place for you. But if you're not, spend less on a good old fashioned buffet (New Delhi in University City comes to mind) or sacrifice a bit of quantity for quality and go to virtually any traditional steakhouse in the area. A footnote to the international travelers out there: there's a chain in the Johannesburg area called Rodizio that offers a similar experience (sans salad bar) for ~120ZAR, or about $15 depending on the exchange rate. I've been to the one in Bedfordview a few times, and the meat is just as good (for better or worse) as at Fogo de Chao.

text: How long would you be willing to wait for a fantastic, memorable meal? How long would you be willing to wait for a really good meal? How long would you wait for a decent meal? Those questions begged for an answer last night, as the DH and I sat for close to FOUR hours at this restaurant, trying, mostly in vain, to enjoy a five course meal. It wasn't any other night, Ms. Top Chef, was in the kitchen, (or she was supposed to be as she was shaking hands and kissing babies on the dining floor), it was her night in the big lights, as the season opener of Top Chef 10 was being shown on all screens. Featuring Ms. Jennifer Carroll and her winning Top Chef dishes. Oy vey. Of all nights, this night should have been the night when Ms. Top Chef and her kitchen shone - pulled out all the stops - and impress their adoring foodie public. However, this was not to be - I was not impressed in the least. I was utterly and completely disappointed. Angry, even. The meal, our experience from beginning to end, was totally average, almost bordering on not so good at all. Top Chef, my derrière. First of all, the kitchen became mysteriously slammed (the bar was packed - not many eaters there- and the dining room was about two-thirds full-- and servers just hanging around) and the service took on an immediate glacial pace. This really set the tone for the entire night. Had we not ordered the tasting menu, we would have left before the second course was even served. The first two courses of our tasting menu, a ceviche, and steamed mussels (two dishes that should not take that long to plate) took nearly two hours to serve. TWO hours. For TWO very mediocre dishes. Meanwhile, a large number of VIPs who had arrived long after us lowly general public, were being served quickly - in front of our very eyes, and we seemed just a general afterthought. The final three courses, improved sightly, a poached halibut was served very dry, with little flavor - the only saving grace being the accompanying peppercorn lobster bourbon sauce. Followed by, our fourth course, a kobe skirt steak that was cooked to the correct temperature, but served not even warm. Which brings me to the following, did I mention that save for the ceviche (of course), all meals were less than room temperature - even with the accompanying sauces? Yes, it seemed as though each dish had been assembled and set aside and forgotten about. To wait three and a half hours, for a semi-warm, not terribly special or delicious meal, at $75 a pop - I felt cheated... and almost violent. Obviously, I had set my expectations pretty high for Ms. Top Chef and her Ripert-approved cuisine. Finally, the only star that shone that night, were the desserts. None of which were prepared by Ms. Top Chef, but her pastry chef Monica Glass. Thank god for that dish - a delectable take on S'mores - graham cracker ice cream (sweet jesus!), soft chocolate, toasted marshmallows and pomegranate. That dish brought me to my senses, but only temporarily. The real nail in the coffin though, was that our meal only ended nearly four hours later, and though we got complimentary glasses of dessert wine (which was appreciated), we also got the bill - a hefty one at that. Had we experienced an incredible meal, even within that time frame, perhaps I would have been more forgiving, but an average meal? With no true, balanced service progression, on a night that was supposed to be a true representation of 10Arts' worth, with meals served barely lukewarm and then we've got to fork over the $300? We felt robbed. Basic and simple. Not tempted to give this place another chance, I don't think my wallet or my schedule could afford that.
label: NEG

text: How good is The Dish? As good as it gets. I've been to the "old" Dish, back when it had more space, and I've been to the "new" DIsh, where there are really only 4-5 tables and a big bar. To let Yelpers know, when they renovated the restaurant and the liquor store it is connected to, they had hoped to expand the restaurant out into the parking lot and make it a lot bigger than it was. But then they ran into some obscure Tucson building code that required the restaurant to have a certain number of private parking spaces that couldn't be shared with the liquor store, which makes no sense since they are one in the same! Since the Dish couldn't just buy another parking lot somewhere else, they had to cancel the expansion, and so now it is what it is. But, what is it? It's the best food in Tucson. HANDS DOWN. I've eaten at all the other "nice" restaurants in Tucson, most of which are tacky over-priced conveyor belts of "Southwestern international" blah-food contained within tackier resorts. The Dish creates super creative, richly flavored, top-notch food in a low-key friendly atmosphere. We went there the other night, and while the long-stemmed artichokes with white-corn polenta were delicious, the cane-braised short ribs were jaw-droppingly good. The best think about this place, though, is that it's attached to a good liquor store. You show up 10 minutes before your reservation, you pick out the wine you want to drink, you hand it to the hostess, and then you're seated and your wine is already selected! Corkage is $12, which on most good bottles is a lot less then the normal mark-up you'd pay off of a wine list.

text: There isn't a doubt in my mind that one of the very rarest slices of culinary heaven on earth can be found inside the doors of Link's eateries and if there is one in particular that rises to the status of Godlike it is indeed Cochon. I lived in New Orleans for years, went through Katrina and came back and was so very happy to see that Link's commitment to the city just got stronger. This is undeniable in the warm familial atmostphere and stunning bites that define Cochon. I LOVE food but occasionally when I open a menu and see items that have been served up SO BADLY, SO OFTEN I shudder at the thought of trying said things again (see alligator often too tough to swallow much less use for anything other than a fleshy baseball OR Boudin often so dry and just horribly gamey it is inedible) but I was heading to Cochon with a group of 5th generation cajuns and it was a Link eatery so I dove in...and we were all thrilled we did. GET A RESERVATION. This is not optional. No reservation? Unless it is the middle of summer with 180% humidity and everyone has left town you won't get a seat. The local liquor selection is divine. They usually carry at least 4 Abita's on draft at any given time. The bartenders there are true mixologists and will not steer you wrong. Don't know what to drink with your dinner? Ask them. They know exactly the perfect compliment. The fried alligator with Garlic aioli was like a bit of "fried fried heaven" in my mouth. The alligator was firm but not tough and the seasoning scrumptious. The boudin with the mustard and pickled peppers looked a bit tart to me on paper but turned out to be a revelation when served. The rabbit and dumplings was just one of the most amazing things I have ever put in my mouth EVER. It was so fresh tasting with the veggies and the rabbit was fall apart tender. The brisket was almost obscene it was so good with the smokey, seasoning playing perfectly against the kick of the horseradish in the potato salad. It was beautifully executed, lacking the snobbery and just simple, brilliantly paired food that was clearly created by someone who loves Louisiana cuisine. Is it a bit "much"? HELL YES! But isn't that by definition what New Orleans is all about. It is a celebration of excess and it succeeds perfectly! I could eat here everyday. I am sure I would die young with all the butter that is notorious in cajun cooking but damn it if it were being served by Cochon I can promise you I would also die happy in one of my favorite eateries on the planet in my favorite city in the world.. Always hungry...and Sadly STILL stuck and lost in LA. GG

text: Like a previous post, I thought the Treehouse Restaurant, next to a Best Western would be decent. MAN was I wrong... There are only two cute things about this place. One is the name, "Treehouse"... ooohhh, so artsy... so safe... so inviting... so wrong (shaking my head no like a two year old)... The other was the old fashion cash register. I haven't seen something like that in years. I'm thinking like something from the "Gunsmoke" tv show... Old West... 1920's... that type of cash register. That should have been a warning to me, but I was stuck in the Twilight Zone (cue the music) because I missed all the clues. Clue number one. The inside of this place is stuck in a timewarp from the 1950's - and that's not by design like Johnny Rockets. The primary difference is Johnny Rockets is clean. You see where I'm going here? The interior looks like the owners haven't put one single dime into redecorating the inside. Basically the interior looks like a restaurant in one of those horror movies where you know you shouldn't stop, but you stop anyway. Well, keep driving. You'll thank me - and yourself later. Clue number two. I don't drink coffee, so I ask if you should be able to "see" thru it - should you? I've never seen coffee that was so watered down, you could almost see the bottom of the cup. But to have the nerve to pour and serve it like it was completely normal - something is frighteningly wrong with that. Gives me the chills. Try sending it back and getting another one. Whew, do so at your own risk. Clue number three. Our waitress never smiled. Not once. Not even when I thanked her for politely telling me - although I didn't ask - what the difference was between one thing on the menu and another. That scared me. Clue number four. When you order your food, shouldn't it look appealing to eat? I mean really. As a kid, even when my mother was mad at me and made my breakfast, she still made it look appealing. The breakfast served was absent any personality - or appeal - and I'm talking about simple sausage and eggs. By the way, my hash browns were cold, but they looked like they were cooked. How does that happen? Nevertheless, I'm sure you get the picture. Needless to say, I'm not a fan. I believe the only way they survive is on unsuspecting tourists from Eastern Europe staying at the BW and on locals who don't know any better. Do yourself a favor, no matter how warm and inviting BW looks from the outside, the Treehouse out front is a horror movie. There are too many other places to eat, that are "one million times better" in Santa Barbara than eating here. Do yourself a favor, save yourself and go elsewhere.

text: I'm not big on smoothies. There, I've said it. In my life, I just found smoothies to taste like frothy ice with bits of fruit in it here and there. Then there's Jamba Juice. All of the flavors, from the Peanut Butter Moo'd to the Aloha Pineapple, are "to die for" good, but are "love live the king" good for you. There are also seasonal smoothies, such as the Pumpkin Spice in the fall (which absolutely must be tried), and what some call "secret smoothies", such as the Strawberry shortcake and White Gummy Bear (equally awesome). Apart from the smoothies, they sell some really tasty baked goods and various packaged health snacks; they both make a great meal on the go when combined with an original or power sized smoothie. The establishment has a modern look to it, with brushed steel and wood. The place is big on being healthy; there are workout books, workout equipment, juicers, and other paraphernalia, have wheatgrass shots and also give you the opportunity to put what they call "boosts" in your smoothie. These boosts are various supplements such as daily vitamins, fiber, protein and even an immunity boost. Some of these boosts are free, and others cost 50 cents. Speaking of immunity, if you ever have a cold, I highly advise one of their smoothies known as the "Coldbuster"; every time I have a cold, I drink one and my disease goes away within three days. Tastes better than anything over the counter liquid, and seems to work just as well. This place can get very busy, but the staff seem to make it all breeze by quickly. They are all friendly and cheerful people, adding even more lightness into the store. These people remember you too, I was absent for a good two or three weeks and they smiled and remembered what I liked to order without a second's thought. Redefine smoothie for yourself. Go have a Jamba Juice.

text: I discovered Chadwick's on restaurant.com and one glance at their kids' menu determined that we HAD to check it out. My husband and I went last week to try it out, figuring that if we liked it, it could become a regular place to take the kids, with food they would actually eat, and at reasonable prices! Pulling up we were impressed with the building, the golf course location, and the decor. The restaurant was almost empty, with one small table, and one larger family gathering of about 10-12 as the only other customers at the time. We decided we would try the sampler, but with seasoned fries rather than portabello fries. Note that the portabello fries on their own are $7 and the seasoned fries are $4. Our waitress told her that there was no way they could replace them, and that she could ask, but it would be pointless. Ok, either you know for sure that it's not a possibility, or you don't know and you ask, without making it seem like it's wasting your time. So we decided to try the "asian" chicken wraps. There were no drinks on the menu, but considering we walked past a bar on the way in, "Do you serve alcohol?" seemed like a legitimate question. She seemed shocked that we were asking, and then said that they didn't have a drink list, so what kind of drinks did we want? We asked what wines they had, and she came back from the bar with the names written down. We ordered the Riesling and Pinot Grigio and when she brought them back, she said she had no idea which was which. My husband got the Cowboy cut Prime Rib, described as being lightly seasoned with steak sauce, and served on top of fizzled onions. We knew there might be trouble when she asked how well he wanted his prime rib done... I went with the top sirloin steak, medium well. Neither one of us noticed that she didn't give us the choice between baked potato, fries, or mashed, as was listed on the menu. One of the other waiters brought our appetizer. On first glance, I was super excited. They had the typical choices...chicken, shredded carrots and cucumber... and they had what they called lo mein noodles, wonton strips, and three sauces. Then we dug in. The lettuce was small spring mix type lettuce, not typical iceberg, and it wasn't crisp enough to be able to hold anything inside of it. The lo mein noodles were spaghetti with no flavor, the wonton strips were stale, and the three sauces were an italian type vinagrette, a duck sauce, and something of barbecue consistency that tasted like a black jellybean. Our entrees arrived and Jason's prime rib had grill marks on it. Contrary to what we both thought "fizzled onions" would be (sauteed onion slices), they are actually the crispy onions from a can that you put in green bean casserole, and the whole thing was drenched in a less-spicy A-1 knockoff steak sauce. My steak looked alright, but tasted like liver. We both got baked potatoes. I got butter and sour cream. Jason got neither. At least our steamed vegetables were good (and like an old folks' home dining room, they are all you smell as soon as you walk in the door.) Halfway through we ordered another glass of wine each. She brought it to is explaining that she found out how to tell the difference... that Pinot is almost clear, and Riesling is darker.... Ummmmm not most ones that I've tried but ok. The confusing part being that neither one of the glasses tasted quite the same as our first. We chalked it up to being a little wine buzzed and having traumatized taste buds, but when we got the bill, we realized that they had given us four completely different (and differently priced) glasses of wine. But hey, at least we had shirtless rednecks rebuilding engines on the Speed channel to watch on the big screen TVs on the walls...

text: If Atlantis is a beautiful lost underwater paradise, then the Motor Lodge is the decaying shipwreck right next to it. I booked my trip using Mobissimo, and was redirected to a German hotel website (and could not cancel later due to them only being open M-F) where a room at this 3.5 star resort could be had for about $109. Since it was a spontaneous trip, this rate seemed reasonable to me, given the comparable rates from Silver Legacy and Peppermill. We arrived late and checked out a show at the Eldorado, then came back to regroup and drop our bags at the hotel with the premise of going out later to continue the evening. However, the walk to this Sinatra-era backwoods location at the other side of the parking lot quickly killed our spirits. Take every cliche from every generic off the Interstate motel you've stayed at, and you have this place. If I were a truck driver hauling corn thousands of miles and needed a place to crash, this would be fine, but not for the rate we paid in this city. The decor, pillows and mattresses felt like they've been recycled since Ted and Maude Okie rented a room here to go see Bobby Darin live. My memory is fresh, as I'm in the actual room now, and am continually reminded of its inadequacy. Such as when I went to go plug in my laptop, I could hear the walls shake and the TV rattle as I walked. This is not to mention that the walls are about as hollow as the deceptive marketing Atlantis used to get me here. My advice to them is this: sure, you might have a 3.5 or maybe even a 4 star hotel, but allowing people to book for the motor lodge using sites such as travelocity, expedia, or wherever, when they don't know what they'ere getting into is bad business. Just putting a guest services directory and a $11.95 movie option in a motel room does not magically make it up to par. On the plus side, the bathroom was clean, with newly replaced faucets and showerhead. EDIT: After looking around, it appears that some sites do in fact call it the motor lodge. However, the site I booked from did not. However, my point remains that the economy class accomodations here should not be considered to be nearly the same star rating.

It seems that the older family members of the owners started sending in secret shoppers (3 separate employees told us this, in person, face to face, which was then confirmed by the front of the house owner, Gian (if you don't want customers finding out about your establishment's secrets, maybe you shouldn't get wasted at your own bar several times a week). After this, and several poor service experiences (a plate of clams poured over my friends back, which only one employee responded to, and said owner never apologized for), we just stopped going for about a year. Recently, my friend went back at the behest of another friend of ours, and after 5 minutes, wasn't just asked to leave, but was openly accosted and yelled at in a full dining room by the one owner, Gian, because he had dropped the review from 5 to 4 stars. This occurance was confirmed not only by the friend that accompanied him, but by 2 close friends (that I had told to try Gias) that happened to be in the dining room that night. It's so great to get a call from them, asking me why I would reccomend a place where the owner would behave so unprofessionally (their exact words). I've been at the bar when an old creeper regular has loudly commented on how one bartender's genitals would taste, and that vulgar guy was not yelled at, was not asked to leave, and was not banned, yet my friend gets embarrassingly yelled at and banned for giving a 4 star review? The proper way to handle this would have been to pull him aside privately. Not to mention maybe taking ownership of the problem. So for completely unprofessional behavior on the owners part, they now get one star. text: I love Saigon In-N-Out. I even have cravings for it,. My boyfriend and I come here pretty frequently and we always start with the spring rolls. They're good and come out quickly. For some reason we always come here ravenously hungry, maybe just to stuff our faces??! No clue. I've had a few things here, but my all out favorite is the #64, the Golden Fried Tofu Soup. It's awesome, even if you're not a vegetarian. I'm not and I love it! The tofu is fried until crispy and served with an onion based soup and rice noodles. When you add the tofu to the soup, it softens a little but still remains firm and not squishy like some tofu can be. There is usually chopped ginger at the bottom of the bowl, which adds a nice crunch and zing of ginger to the meal, which I love. The soup (does is count as pho if there's no beef base? I'm guessing not) comes with the standard lime, bean sprouts, basil, cilantro, and jalapeno. The restaurant isn't cheap about the extra stuff, which is great because some places are. I can't stand it when I go to a pho place and they give you one wilted basil leaf. Saigon in-n-out doesn't do this. The restaurant chain is much better than others in the area, such as Saigon Noodle House in Goleta. My only gripe about the place is that usually we're left waiting for refills on water. We've gotten used to asking for more water early because the servers don't come to the table often. It's not bad, you can kind of expect that from any small, inexpensive restaurant. We don't like anyone interrupting us stuffing our faces anyway. =)

text: I just completed a review of this restaurant, but it is under "El Dorado Tortilla Factory." In a nutshell, this place is the real deal: truly authentic truck stop Mexican food, you know, the kind that locals in central Mexico may prefer and probably snowbirds from Chicago would not. You can happily avoid the typical gringo/Mexican chimichangas, fajitas, burros, taco salads and hamburger tacos you find at most Tucson restaurants. Instead you can get machaca, pozole, menudo, huevos con nopalitos, picadillo, chilaquiles and other not-smothered-with-lettuce-and-kraft-cheese food. It may not be healthy, but for sure tastes good and is real Mexican food. Call it ethnic comfort food. Lunch buffet was very tasty with lots of choices, under $8 per humanoid including drinks. Compare that to a boring taco combo plate for over $10 and $2 more for an iced tea at most Tucson "Mexican" restaurants. Service was quite good. We were the only gringos eating there, and the servers (yes, several of them) stopped by to see if we were happy with our food.
